courses.title: Build Your Home Lab
courses.summary: Stand up a Windows domain with two clients and a Linux box on a used PC, learn to snapshot and roll back without fear, and document the whole build on GitHub. Every later course runs on what you build here.
outcomes: Run a hypervisor (Proxmox or VMware Workstation) on a used PC with 32 GB RAM
Operate a Windows Server domain controller with two joined Windows clients and one Linux server
Use snapshots to break things on purpose and recover in under a minute
Publish a lab README, network diagram, and addressing plan to a GitHub repo

lessons.title: Why a lab, and what it has to do
lessons.objective: Explain what a home lab is for, name the five machines you will build, and state the one rule of lab work: nothing you break matters.
lessons.lab: In a text file, write one paragraph describing the lab you are about to build: hypervisor, a Windows Server domain controller, two Windows clients, one Linux server. Then list three things you expect to break. Keep this file — it becomes the first section of your GitHub README.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to run a home lab instead of practicing on your daily-use laptop?
choices: You can break, infect, and rebuild lab machines with no consequences to your real data
Employers require a lab before hiring
Lab software is free and laptop software is not
quiz.explain: A lab is a disposable environment. Its value is that mistakes cost nothing, so you can be aggressive about experimenting.

quiz.q: A hypervisor is software that…
choices: Scans a network for open ports
Runs several virtual machines on one physical computer
Manages user passwords in a domain
quiz.explain: The hypervisor divides one physical box into multiple isolated virtual machines, each with its own OS.

quiz.q: How many virtual machines does this course's core lab call for?
quiz.explain: One domain controller, two Windows clients, one Linux server — four VMs on the hypervisor.

lessons.title: Spec the box: CPU, RAM, storage
lessons.objective: Choose hardware that will comfortably run four VMs at once: a CPU with virtualization extensions, 32 GB RAM, and an SSD of at least 500 GB.

resources.label: Intel: How to check if your processor supports virtualization (VT-x)

lessons.lab: Build a RAM budget spreadsheet: hypervisor overhead 2 GB, domain controller 4 GB, each Windows client 4 GB, Linux server 2 GB. Total it, then add 25% headroom. Confirm the total fits in 32 GB and write down how much is left for a fifth VM later.

quiz.q: Which CPU feature must be enabled in BIOS/UEFI for a hypervisor to run 64-bit guests efficiently?
quiz.explain: Intel VT-x or AMD-V lets the hypervisor hand hardware directly to guests. Without it, most hypervisors refuse to start 64-bit VMs.

quiz.q: Why is an SSD strongly preferred over a spinning hard drive for a lab host?
choices: Four VMs booting at once produce random I/O that spinning disks handle very poorly
Hypervisors will not install on hard drives
quiz.explain: Multiple VMs mean lots of small random reads and writes. Spinning disks crawl under that load; SSDs do not.

quiz.q: With 32 GB total RAM, roughly how much should you keep unallocated for the hypervisor itself?
choices: 0 GB — give it all to VMs
quiz.explain: The host OS needs a couple of gigabytes to manage the guests. Overcommitting RAM leads to swapping and a very slow lab.

lessons.title: Buying used without getting burned
lessons.objective: Find an off-lease business desktop or small-form-factor PC (Dell OptiPlex, HP EliteDesk, Lenovo ThinkCentre class) for a fair price and verify it before you commit.

resources.label: eBay — search 'OptiPlex 32GB' (filter: Buy It Now, US only)

lessons.lab: Find three listings for a used business desktop with an 8th-gen Intel Core or newer (or Ryzen 3000+), 32 GB RAM or an easy upgrade path, and an SSD. Record price, CPU, RAM, storage, and seller rating in a table. Pick one and write two sentences on why. Do not buy yet unless the price is clearly right — the point is comparison.

quiz.q: Why are off-lease business desktops a good lab buy?
choices: They come with Windows Server licenses
They are built for reliability, easy to open, and sold cheaply in bulk when companies refresh
They have the newest graphics cards
quiz.explain: Corporate refresh cycles flood the used market with sturdy, standardized machines at low prices.

quiz.q: Before paying, which spec is most important to confirm supports virtualization?
quiz.explain: Look up the exact CPU model. It determines core count, virtualization support, and how many VMs you can realistically run.

quiz.q: A listing says '16 GB RAM, 2 slots free.' What does that tell you?
choices: You can add two more sticks to reach 32 GB — check max supported RAM first
quiz.explain: Free slots mean an upgrade path, but always check the motherboard's maximum supported RAM before assuming 32 GB is possible.

lessons.title: Proxmox or VMware Workstation?
lessons.objective: Choose a hypervisor: Proxmox VE as a dedicated bare-metal host, or VMware Workstation Pro running on top of an existing Windows install. Understand the trade-offs of each.

resources.label: VMware Workstation Pro (free for personal use — download via Broadcom support portal; verify current)

lessons.lab: Write a one-page decision record: which hypervisor you chose, three reasons, and one thing you give up by choosing it. Commit it to your lab repo later as docs/decisions/001-hypervisor.md.

quiz.q: Proxmox VE is a 'Type 1' (bare-metal) hypervisor. What does that mean?
choices: It runs as an app inside Windows
It installs directly on the hardware as the operating system, with VMs running on top
It only runs one VM at a time
quiz.explain: Type 1 hypervisors own the hardware. Type 2 (like Workstation) run as software inside another OS.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason to pick VMware Workstation for a first lab?
choices: It is the only option that supports Windows guests
You want to keep using the PC as a normal Windows desktop while running VMs
It is faster than Proxmox in every case
It supports more than 32 GB RAM
quiz.explain: Workstation lets one machine be both your desktop and your lab. Proxmox needs a dedicated box.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason to pick Proxmox?
choices: It matches how enterprise virtualization actually runs — dedicated host, web management, clustering later
quiz.explain: Proxmox behaves like the vSphere/Hyper-V hosts you will meet at work: managed remotely, always on, no desktop.

lessons.title: Install the hypervisor and reach the console
lessons.objective: Install your chosen hypervisor, give it a static IP on your home network, and log into its management interface from another device.

resources.label: Rufus — write an ISO to a USB stick

lessons.lab: Write the installer to USB, boot the box, install. For Proxmox: set a static IP (for example 192.168.1.250/24), then open https://<that-ip>:8006 from your laptop. For Workstation: install on Windows and confirm 'Virtual Network Editor' opens. Take a screenshot of the working console for your README.

quiz.q: Why should the hypervisor host have a static IP rather than DHCP?
choices: So the management address never changes and you can always find it
quiz.explain: If the host's address moved every reboot you would spend your life hunting for the console. Infrastructure gets static addresses.

quiz.q: Proxmox's web console listens on which port by default?
quiz.explain: https://host:8006 is the Proxmox management interface. Memorize it — you will type it hundreds of times.

quiz.q: You wrote the ISO to USB but the PC boots straight to the old OS. Most likely fix?
choices: Change the boot order or use the one-time boot menu in BIOS/UEFI
quiz.explain: The firmware decides what boots first. Enter setup (often F2, F12, or Del) and choose the USB device.

lessons.title: Storage layout and the ISO library
lessons.objective: Understand where VM disks live, upload the four installer ISOs you need, and keep them organized.

resources.label: Windows Server 2022 evaluation (180-day) — Microsoft Evaluation Center

lessons.lab: Download the Windows Server eval, Windows 11 Enterprise eval, and Ubuntu Server ISOs. Upload them to the hypervisor's ISO storage (Proxmox: local → ISO Images). Record each file's SHA-256 hash and compare it to the vendor's published value. Note the results in your README.

quiz.q: Why verify an ISO's checksum after downloading?
choices: To confirm the file was not corrupted or tampered with in transit
It is required by the installer
quiz.explain: A matching hash proves you have exactly the bytes the vendor published. This habit matters enormously in security work.

quiz.q: Microsoft's evaluation editions of Windows Server are…
choices: Fully functional for a limited period (typically 180 days), ideal for labs
quiz.explain: Evaluation media is full-featured but time-limited. Snapshots and rebuilds make the expiry a non-issue in a lab.

quiz.q: A 'thin-provisioned' virtual disk…
choices: Consumes physical space only as data is written, not the full declared size up front
Is always faster than thick provisioning
quiz.explain: Thin disks let you declare 80 GB but use 15 GB until the guest actually fills it — handy on a single SSD.

lessons.title: Virtual networking: bridged, NAT, isolated
lessons.objective: Explain the three common virtual network modes and build one isolated lab network so your domain traffic never touches your home Wi-Fi.
lessons.lab: Create a second virtual bridge or virtual network (Proxmox: vmbr1 with no physical port; Workstation: a custom 'LAN Segment' or host-only network). Decide your lab subnet — 10.10.10.0/24 is a good choice — and write down which IPs the DC, clients, and Linux box will use. This becomes your addressing plan.

quiz.q: A VM in 'bridged' mode…
choices: Appears on your home network as if it were a physical device, getting its own IP from your router
Can only talk to the host
quiz.explain: Bridged puts the VM directly on the physical LAN. Convenient, but it means your lab domain controller is visible to every device at home.

quiz.q: Why run the domain on an isolated (internal-only) network?
choices: So lab DHCP, DNS, and attack traffic cannot interfere with or leak onto your real home network
quiz.explain: Your DC will run DNS and possibly DHCP. On the home LAN that fights your router. Isolation also makes later attack labs safe.

quiz.q: In the plan 10.10.10.0/24, how many usable host addresses are there?
quiz.explain: A /24 has 256 addresses; the first (network) and last (broadcast) are reserved, leaving 254. Network+ will drill this hard.

lessons.title: First VM and your first snapshot
lessons.objective: Create a VM, install an OS, take a snapshot, deliberately break the machine, and roll back.
lessons.lab: Create the Ubuntu Server VM (2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, 32 GB thin disk, attached to the isolated network). Install it. Take a snapshot named 'clean-install'. Then run 'sudo rm -rf /usr/bin' — yes, really — reboot, watch it fail, and roll back to the snapshot. Time how long recovery takes and write it in your README.

quiz.q: A snapshot is…
choices: A full copy of the VM stored on another drive
A point-in-time record of the VM's disk (and optionally memory) you can revert to
quiz.explain: Snapshots capture state so you can return to it. They live on the same storage as the VM, which is why they are not backups.

quiz.q: Why is a snapshot NOT a backup?
choices: If the underlying storage or host fails, the snapshot is lost along with the VM
quiz.explain: Snapshots protect against your own mistakes, not against disk death. Backups live somewhere else.

quiz.q: What is the best moment to take your first snapshot of a new VM?
choices: Immediately after a clean install and updates, before you change anything
quiz.explain: A 'clean' snapshot is your reset button for the whole course. Take it before you start experimenting.

lessons.title: Install Windows Server
lessons.objective: Create the DC VM and install Windows Server with the Desktop Experience, then apply updates and snapshot.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Get started with Windows Server

lessons.lab: Create a VM: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 60 GB thin disk, isolated network. Install Windows Server (Standard, Desktop Experience). Set a strong local Administrator password and store it in a password manager. Snapshot as 'clean-install'.

quiz.q: 'Desktop Experience' vs 'Server Core' — which is right for your first DC and why?
choices: Server Core, because it has more features
Desktop Experience, because it has a GUI and you are still learning where everything lives
Server Core, because Desktop Experience cannot run AD
quiz.explain: Core is what production often uses, but the GUI teaches you the concepts first. You can rebuild as Core later.

quiz.q: Where should the local Administrator password be stored?
choices: A sticky note on the monitor
quiz.explain: Lab or not, build the habit now. Secrets never go in a repo, even a private one.

quiz.q: Why apply Windows updates before promoting the server to a domain controller?
choices: Updates are required to install AD DS
A patched, stable baseline avoids chasing bugs later that were already fixed, and reboots are simpler before AD is running
There is no reason; order does not matter
quiz.explain: Patch first, then add roles. Every reboot of a DC is more disruptive than a reboot of a plain server.

lessons.title: Static IP, hostname, and time
lessons.objective: Give the server a fixed address on the lab network, a meaningful hostname, and correct time — the three things AD refuses to work without.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Configure IP settings in Windows Server

lessons.lab: Set the DC to 10.10.10.10/24 with no gateway (isolated network) and DNS pointing to itself (127.0.0.1 or 10.10.10.10). Rename it to something like LAB-DC01. Confirm the time zone is correct. Reboot and snapshot as 'pre-promotion'.

quiz.q: Why must a domain controller have a static IP?
choices: Clients find the domain through DNS records pointing at the DC; if its IP changes, the domain breaks
So it can be reached from the internet
quiz.explain: AD is glued together by DNS. A moving DC address means clients can no longer locate authentication services.

quiz.q: What should the DC's preferred DNS server be set to after promotion?
quiz.explain: The DC hosts the domain's DNS zone. It should query itself so it can resolve its own service records.

quiz.q: Why does Active Directory care so much about time?
choices: Kerberos authentication rejects tickets when clocks differ by more than about five minutes
It does not; time is optional
quiz.explain: Kerberos uses timestamps to prevent replay attacks. Clock drift is one of the most common 'the domain is broken' causes in real environments.

lessons.title: Promote to domain controller (AD DS + DNS)
lessons.objective: Install the Active Directory Domain Services role, create a new forest, and understand what just got built.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Install AD DS and create a new forest
Microsoft Learn — Active Directory Domain Services overview

lessons.lab: Add the AD DS role in Server Manager, then promote: new forest, root domain name 'lab.nextgen-tech'. Let it install DNS. Set the DSRM password (store it in the password manager). After reboot, open 'Active Directory Users and Computers' and DNS Manager. Screenshot both. Snapshot as 'dc-promoted'.

quiz.q: What is a 'forest' in Active Directory?
choices: The top-level security boundary containing one or more domains that share a schema and configuration
quiz.explain: Your first domain is also the forest root. Companies with many domains still usually have just one forest.

quiz.q: Why does the promotion wizard insist on installing DNS?
choices: Because AD publishes its services as DNS records; clients cannot log in without them
It is optional and only for convenience
quiz.explain: Records like _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs tell clients where to find a DC. No DNS, no domain.

quiz.q: The DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) password is used…
choices: To log into the DC locally when Active Directory itself is offline or being repaired
By domain users to reset their own passwords
quiz.explain: When AD is broken you cannot authenticate against it. DSRM is the break-glass local account for exactly that.

lessons.title: Organizational units, users, and groups
lessons.objective: Design a small OU structure, create test users and security groups, and explain why groups — not users — receive permissions.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Create an OU design
Microsoft Learn — Active Directory security groups

lessons.lab: Create OUs: LAB > Users, LAB > Workstations, LAB > Groups, LAB > Servers. Create four users (two 'staff', one 'helpdesk', one 'admin' — never use your real name for the admin). Create groups HelpDesk-Staff and Workstation-Admins; add the helpdesk user to both. Export the OU tree with PowerShell: Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | Select Name,DistinguishedName. Save the output to your repo.

quiz.q: Why grant permissions to groups instead of directly to users?
choices: When people join or leave, you change one membership instead of hunting permissions across every system
Windows does not allow user-level permissions
quiz.explain: This is the foundation of access management and a favorite interview question. Users go in groups; groups get rights.

quiz.q: What is an Organizational Unit (OU) mainly used for?
choices: Organizing objects so you can delegate administration and apply Group Policy to specific sets of users or computers
quiz.explain: OUs are containers for delegation and policy. Groups are for permissions. New admins confuse the two constantly.

quiz.q: Why should a separate admin account exist rather than doing admin work as your daily user?
choices: Windows requires two accounts per person
If your everyday account is phished or compromised, the attacker does not automatically get admin rights
quiz.explain: Separation of privileged and everyday identities is core security hygiene. Security+ and every job you will hold expect it.

lessons.title: Install two Windows clients
lessons.objective: Build two Windows 11 client VMs on the isolated network with DNS pointing at the domain controller.
lessons.lab: Create LAB-WS01 (10.10.10.101) and LAB-WS02 (10.10.10.102), 2 vCPU / 4 GB each, DNS 10.10.10.10. Bypass Microsoft account sign-in with a local account during setup. From each client, run 'nslookup lab.nextgen-tech' and confirm it resolves to the DC. Snapshot both as 'clean-install'.

quiz.q: Before joining a domain, what must the client's DNS server setting point to?
choices: Nothing — DNS is set automatically after joining
quiz.explain: The client locates the domain through DNS. If DNS points elsewhere, the join fails with 'domain could not be contacted'.

quiz.q: 'nslookup' returned the DC's IP for your domain name. What does that prove?
choices: Name resolution to the domain works, which is the prerequisite for a successful join
quiz.explain: Test the smallest thing first. If DNS works, the join will almost certainly work; if not, nothing downstream will.

quiz.q: Why build two clients instead of one?
choices: Later labs test policy, lateral movement, and log correlation between machines — you need more than one endpoint
quiz.explain: Detection and attack scenarios in Phase 2 need traffic between hosts. Two endpoints is the minimum realistic network.

lessons.title: Join the domain and log in as a domain user
lessons.objective: Join both clients to the domain, move their computer objects into the Workstations OU, and log in as a standard domain user.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Join a computer to a domain

lessons.lab: Join LAB-WS01 and LAB-WS02 to the domain using your admin account. On the DC, move both computer objects from the default Computers container into LAB > Workstations. Log into WS01 as one of your 'staff' users. Try to install software — note what happens. Screenshot the 'Access denied' or UAC prompt.

quiz.q: After joining, computer objects appear in which container by default?
quiz.explain: The built-in Computers container cannot have Group Policy linked to it, which is why you move machines into a real OU.

quiz.q: A standard domain user cannot install software on the workstation. This is…
choices: Correct behavior — least privilege means users do not have local admin rights by default
quiz.explain: Removing local admin from users blocks most commodity malware. It is one of the highest-value controls in any environment.

quiz.q: Which credential is required to join a computer to the domain?
choices: Any local account on the client
A domain account with rights to create computer objects (by default, Domain Admins, or any user for up to 10 machines)
quiz.explain: The join creates an object in AD, so AD must trust who is asking. Note the default 10-machine quota for ordinary users — a real-world gotcha.

lessons.title: Group Policy basics
lessons.objective: Create and link a Group Policy Object, apply one setting to the Workstations OU, and verify it took effect.
lessons.lab: In Group Policy Management, create a GPO called 'WS - Baseline' linked to LAB > Workstations. Set: a logon banner message (Computer Config > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Interactive logon: Message text'), and disable the Guest account. On WS01 run 'gpupdate /force', reboot, and confirm the banner appears. Run 'gpresult /r' and save the output to your repo.

quiz.q: A GPO is linked to an OU. Which objects receive its settings?
choices: Every object in the entire domain
Users and/or computers located in that OU (and its child OUs)
quiz.explain: Scope follows the OU tree. This is why OU design matters — it decides who gets which policy.

quiz.q: You changed a GPO but the client still shows the old behavior. First thing to try?
choices: Run 'gpupdate /force' on the client (and reboot for computer settings)
quiz.explain: Clients refresh policy on a timer (roughly every 90 minutes). gpupdate pulls it immediately; some computer settings need a reboot.

quiz.q: What does 'gpresult /r' show you?
choices: Which GPOs actually applied to this user and computer — the first step in troubleshooting policy
quiz.explain: Resultant Set of Policy tells you what really landed. Never guess — check.

lessons.title: The Linux server: SSH, users, and a service
lessons.objective: Harden basic SSH access to the Ubuntu server, create a non-root user, and run one service so the box has a job.
lessons.lab: Set the Ubuntu VM to 10.10.10.20. Create a user 'labadmin' with sudo. Generate an SSH key pair on your laptop, copy the public key to the server, then disable password authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and restart sshd. Install nginx and confirm you can browse to http://10.10.10.20 from WS01. Snapshot as 'ssh-hardened'.

quiz.q: Why disable SSH password authentication in favor of keys?
choices: It eliminates password brute-force attacks, the most common attack against exposed SSH
Passwords do not work on Ubuntu
quiz.explain: A private key cannot be guessed. Internet-facing SSH with passwords enabled gets hammered within minutes.

quiz.q: Which file goes on the SERVER when setting up key-based SSH?
choices: Neither — keys stay on the client
quiz.explain: Public key on the server, private key stays with you, always. Sending a private key anywhere is a security incident.

quiz.q: Why run as 'labadmin' with sudo instead of logging in as root?
choices: Root is disabled on all Linux systems
Every privileged action is logged to a named account and you cannot accidentally run everything as root
quiz.explain: Accountability and mistake-proofing. 'Who ran this?' has an answer when everyone uses their own account.

lessons.title: Snapshot strategy and backups
lessons.objective: Define a snapshot naming convention, set a rule for how many to keep, and take one real backup off the host.
lessons.lab: Write a snapshot policy in docs/snapshots.md: naming (yyyy-mm-dd-purpose), max three snapshots per VM, and which snapshot is the 'golden' reset point for each machine. Then back up the DC VM to an external USB drive or NAS (Proxmox: Datacenter > Backup, or vzdump). Confirm the backup file exists somewhere other than the lab SSD.

quiz.q: Why limit the number of snapshots per VM?
choices: Hypervisors allow a maximum of three
Long snapshot chains consume space and slow disk I/O, and make it unclear which state is which
quiz.explain: Every write after a snapshot goes to a delta file. Deep chains get slow and messy. Consolidate regularly.

quiz.q: The single test of whether something counts as a backup is…
choices: It was made with backup software
It survives the loss of the original host and storage — it lives somewhere else
It is less than a week old
quiz.explain: Same disk, same host = not a backup. The 3-2-1 rule (three copies, two media, one offsite) formalizes this.

quiz.q: Which VM in the lab is most important to back up, and why?
choices: A Windows client — it has the most software
The domain controller — every other machine's identity depends on it, and it is slowest to rebuild
The Linux box — Linux is fragile
quiz.explain: Lose the DC and the clients can no longer authenticate. Protect the thing everything else depends on.

lessons.title: Network diagram and addressing plan
lessons.objective: Produce a one-page network diagram and an IP addressing table that a stranger could use to understand the lab.

resources.label: Mermaid — diagrams in Markdown (renders on GitHub)

lessons.lab: Draw the lab: hypervisor host, home LAN bridge, isolated lab bridge, and the four VMs with hostnames and IPs. Export as PNG (or write it in Mermaid so GitHub renders it). Build an addressing table in Markdown: hostname, role, IP, OS, RAM, vCPU, notes. Both go in your repo.

quiz.q: Why does an addressing plan matter in a four-machine lab?
choices: It does not; it is only for large networks
It is the habit that scales — the Network+ VLAN lab and the SIEM course will both extend this exact table
quiz.explain: Documentation habits are built small. Every job you get will ask for this table and be surprised you already keep one.

quiz.q: Which is a good reason to write the diagram in Mermaid inside Markdown?
choices: Mermaid produces prettier diagrams than any tool
The diagram is plain text, versioned with the repo, and renders directly on GitHub
PNGs cannot be uploaded to GitHub
Mermaid is required for GitHub Pages
quiz.explain: Text-based diagrams diff cleanly and never go stale in a separate file you forgot to update.

quiz.q: What should NOT appear in a network diagram committed to a public repo?
choices: Passwords, keys, or your real home public IP
quiz.explain: Private RFC 1918 addresses are harmless. Secrets and anything that identifies your real home network are not.

lessons.title: Publish the build on GitHub
lessons.objective: Create a public 'homelab' repository with a README, decision records, diagrams, scripts, and a changelog — your first portfolio piece.

resources.label: GitHub Docs — Hello World (create a repo, branch, commit, PR)
GitHub Docs — Basic writing and formatting syntax (Markdown)

lessons.lab: Create github.com/<you>/homelab. Structure: README.md (purpose, hardware, diagram, addressing table, how to rebuild), docs/decisions/, docs/snapshots.md, scripts/ (your Get-ADOrganizationalUnit export and any PowerShell), CHANGELOG.md. Add a .gitignore. Make at least five meaningful commits with clear messages. Send the link to your mentor.

quiz.q: Why publish the lab publicly instead of keeping notes on your laptop?
choices: It becomes proof of skill a hiring manager can read in two minutes — and it forces you to write clearly
quiz.explain: Entry-level candidates rarely have a portfolio. A documented lab puts you ahead of most of the stack before the interview.

quiz.q: A good commit message…
choices: Explains what changed and why in one short line, e.g. 'Add WS-Baseline GPO export and gpresult output'
quiz.explain: Commit history is documentation. Future-you and every reviewer read it.

quiz.q: You accidentally committed a file containing a password. What is true?
choices: Deleting the file in the next commit removes it completely
It is still in the repo's history; treat the password as compromised, rotate it, and rewrite history if the repo is public
Passwords in private repos are safe
quiz.explain: Git never forgets. Rotate the secret first; cleaning history is secondary. This exact mistake causes real breaches.

lessons.title: Lab checkpoint: break it, fix it, explain it
lessons.objective: Demonstrate the lab works end to end, recover it from a deliberate failure, and explain the build to someone else in five minutes.
lessons.lab: Checkpoint: (1) log into WS02 as a domain user and browse to the nginx page on the Linux box; (2) shut down the DC and try to log into WS01 with a domain user you have never used on that machine — observe the failure; (3) start the DC, confirm login works again; (4) roll WS01 back to 'clean-install' and re-join the domain in under 15 minutes; (5) record a five-minute screen walkthrough of your lab and repo. Add 'Checkpoint passed' with the date to CHANGELOG.md.

quiz.q: With the DC offline, a user who has logged into WS01 before can still sign in, but a brand-new user cannot. Why?
choices: The new user's password is wrong
Windows caches credentials of previous logons; a first-time logon needs the DC to authenticate
quiz.explain: Cached domain logons keep laptops usable off-network. Understanding this explains dozens of help desk tickets.

quiz.q: After rolling WS01 back to a pre-join snapshot, why might rejoining fail until you reset or delete the computer object in AD?
choices: The computer account password in AD no longer matches the reverted machine's — a stale trust relationship
quiz.explain: Computers have passwords too. Reverting the machine desyncs it from AD. 'Trust relationship failed' is a classic ticket.

quiz.q: What is the point of the five-minute recorded walkthrough?
choices: Explaining a system out loud is the skill interviews actually test, and the recording becomes a portfolio artifact
quiz.explain: You will be asked 'walk me through your home lab' in nearly every entry-level interview. Rehearse it now.

courses.title: CompTIA A+ Core 1 & 2
courses.summary: Hardware, operating systems, basic networking, security fundamentals, and the troubleshooting method that every later course assumes. Built around Professor Messer's free video series, the Mike Meyers book, and Jason Dion's practice exams.

Install, configure, and support Windows, macOS, Linux, and mobile OSes
Explain TCP/IP basics, common ports, and SOHO networking
Apply the six-step CompTIA troubleshooting methodology to any ticket

sections.title: Study plan and the troubleshooting method

lessons.title: How the exams work and how to study them
lessons.objective: Describe the two-exam structure, question types, passing scores, and build a 10-week study calendar.

resources.label: CompTIA A+ exam objectives (download both Core 1 and Core 2 PDFs)
Professor Messer — free A+ 220-1201 video course

lessons.lab: Download both objectives PDFs. Print or copy each top-level domain into a checklist in your homelab repo (docs/a-plus-tracker.md). Schedule ten weeks: weeks 1–5 Core 1, weeks 6–9 Core 2, week 10 practice exams. Put Core 1 exam date on the Certification Tracker as 'Scheduled' only once you score 85%+ on two Dion exams.

quiz.q: How many exams must you pass for A+?
quiz.explain: Core 1 covers hardware, networking, and mobile; Core 2 covers operating systems, security, software troubleshooting, and procedures.

quiz.q: Performance-based questions (PBQs) on CompTIA exams are…
choices: Simulations where you perform a task, usually appearing at the start of the exam
quiz.explain: Many candidates flag PBQs and return to them after the multiple choice so they do not burn time early.

quiz.q: A sound rule for scheduling the real exam is…
choices: Book it the day you start studying
Book it once practice exam scores are consistently above the passing threshold with margin
Never book until you feel perfect
Book both exams on the same day
quiz.explain: A firm date creates urgency, but booking before you are scoring well wastes money. 85%+ on fresh practice exams is a reliable signal.

lessons.title: The six-step troubleshooting methodology
lessons.objective: Recite and apply CompTIA's six-step troubleshooting method, and explain why it is on every exam and in every good technician's head.
lessons.lab: Break something in the lab on purpose: set WS01's DNS to 1.2.3.4. Now write a ticket as if a user reported 'I can't log in.' Work the six steps in writing — identify the problem, establish a theory, test it, plan and implement, verify full functionality, document. Save the write-up as your first entry in docs/tickets/.

quiz.q: What is the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
choices: Identify the problem (gather information, question the user, identify changes)
quiz.explain: Most failed troubleshooting comes from skipping this step and fixing the wrong problem.

quiz.q: Before making changes to a system, the methodology says you should…
quiz.explain: Backups are explicitly part of 'identify the problem.' A fix that destroys data is worse than the original fault.

quiz.q: 'Question the obvious' belongs to which step?
choices: Establish a theory of probable cause
quiz.explain: Is it plugged in? Is Caps Lock on? Simple causes first, then escalate the theory if testing disproves it.

lessons.title: Safety, ESD, and professional conduct
lessons.objective: Explain electrostatic discharge protection, safe handling of components and power supplies, and the professionalism expectations tested in Core 2.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Safety Procedures and Communication videos

lessons.lab: Open your lab PC's case (powered off and unplugged). Identify: PSU, motherboard, CPU cooler, RAM slots, storage, expansion slots. Photograph each labeled for your README. Ground yourself first and describe how you did it.

quiz.q: Which component should you NEVER open, even when powered off?
choices: Power supply unit — capacitors can hold a lethal charge
quiz.explain: PSUs and CRT monitors retain dangerous voltage. Replace, do not repair.

quiz.q: An anti-static wrist strap works by…
choices: Keeping you and the chassis at the same electrical potential so no discharge occurs
quiz.explain: ESD you cannot even feel (under ~3,000 volts) can still destroy a chip.

quiz.q: A user is angry and blaming you. The professional response is to…
choices: Stay calm, listen without interrupting, avoid jargon, and set clear expectations
quiz.explain: Core 2 tests soft skills directly. Real jobs test them daily.

lessons.title: Motherboards, CPUs, and RAM
lessons.objective: Identify motherboard form factors, CPU sockets and features, and RAM types, speeds, and channels.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Motherboards, CPUs, and Memory (Core 1 domain 3)
Mike Meyers, CompTIA A+ All-in-One Exam Guide — hardware chapters

lessons.lab: Run 'msinfo32' and 'wmic memorychip get Capacity,Speed,MemoryType' on your lab host. Record CPU model, socket, RAM type (DDR4/DDR5), speed, and whether it runs dual-channel. Look up the motherboard's max RAM and note the upgrade path.

quiz.q: Which motherboard form factor is the smallest of ATX, microATX, and Mini-ITX?
quiz.explain: Mini-ITX is 17 × 17 cm with a single expansion slot — common in small business desktops.

quiz.q: Dual-channel memory requires…
choices: Two identical sticks in the correct paired slots
quiz.explain: Matched pairs in the right slots double the memory bus width. Populating wrong slots silently loses performance.

quiz.q: ECC RAM is used in servers because it…
choices: Detects and corrects single-bit memory errors
quiz.explain: Error-correcting code memory prevents silent data corruption. Consumer boards usually do not support it.

lessons.title: Storage: HDD, SSD, NVMe, and RAID
lessons.objective: Compare storage interfaces and media, and explain RAID 0, 1, 5, and 10 with their fault tolerance.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Storage Devices and RAID videos

lessons.lab: In Proxmox (or Workstation), add a second virtual disk to the Linux VM. Use 'lsblk' to find it, partition with 'fdisk', format ext4, and mount it at /data. Then write a paragraph on which RAID level you would use for the DC's disks if this were production and why.

quiz.q: RAID 1 provides…
choices: Mirroring — the same data on two disks
Striping with parity across three or more disks
Nothing; it is a single disk
quiz.explain: RAID 1 survives one disk failure at the cost of half the raw capacity.

quiz.q: Minimum number of disks for RAID 5?
quiz.explain: RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity; it needs at least three disks and survives one failure.

quiz.q: NVMe SSDs connect via…
choices: The PCIe bus, typically in an M.2 slot
quiz.explain: NVMe bypasses the SATA bottleneck; it is several times faster than a SATA SSD.

lessons.title: Power, cooling, and peripherals
lessons.objective: Size a power supply, identify connectors, explain cooling methods, and troubleshoot common peripheral and display issues.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Power Supplies and Cooling videos

lessons.lab: Record your lab host's PSU wattage and connector types (24-pin ATX, EPS, SATA power, PCIe). Use an online PSU calculator to estimate load if you added a mid-range GPU. Then clean the CPU cooler and fans with compressed air and note the before/after idle temperature (use HWMonitor or 'sensors' on Linux).

quiz.q: The 24-pin connector on a motherboard is…
quiz.explain: The 24-pin ATX connector powers the board; the separate 4/8-pin EPS connector powers the CPU.

quiz.q: Thermal paste is applied…
choices: Between the CPU and its heatsink
quiz.explain: It fills microscopic gaps for heat transfer. A pea-sized dot is enough; more is not better.

quiz.q: A monitor shows 'No Signal' but the PC powers on. Best first step?
choices: Check the cable and the input source on the monitor, and confirm the cable is in the GPU not the disabled onboard port
quiz.explain: Question the obvious. Wrong input or a cable in the motherboard's disabled port causes most 'no signal' tickets.

lessons.title: Laptops, mobile devices, and printers
lessons.objective: Troubleshoot laptop-specific hardware, configure mobile devices for email and security, and support common printer types.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Laptops, Mobile Devices, and Printers (Core 1 domains 1 and 3)

lessons.lab: On your own phone: enroll a device PIN plus biometric, enable remote wipe (Find My / Find My Device), and add a work-style email account with IMAP settings by hand — record which ports you used. Then set up a printer (or PDF printer) as a shared network printer from the DC and print from WS01.

quiz.q: Laser printer imaging process order begins with…
quiz.explain: Processing → charging → exposing → developing → transferring → fusing → cleaning. Expect it on the exam.

quiz.q: IMAP typically uses which port with TLS?
quiz.explain: IMAPS is 993; POP3S is 995; SMTP submission is 587. Ports are a heavy A+ and Network+ topic.

quiz.q: A laptop screen is very dim but visible with a flashlight. Likely cause?
quiz.explain: The panel is drawing the image; the light behind it has failed.

lessons.title: TCP/IP essentials and common ports
lessons.objective: Explain IP addressing, DHCP, DNS, and memorize the ports and protocols on the Core 1 objectives.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Ports and Protocols video

lessons.lab: On WS01 run 'ipconfig /all' and explain every line in a document: IP, subnet mask, gateway, DNS, DHCP lease, MAC. Then run 'netstat -an' and identify five listening ports and the services behind them. Make flashcards for every port on the objectives.

quiz.q: Which protocol assigns IP addresses automatically?
quiz.explain: DHCP uses the DORA sequence: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

quiz.q: RDP uses port…
quiz.explain: 3389 is Remote Desktop. 22 is SSH, 445 is SMB, 443 is HTTPS.

quiz.q: An APIPA address like 169.254.x.x means…
choices: The device has a public IP
The client could not reach a DHCP server
quiz.explain: Windows self-assigns 169.254.0.0/16 when DHCP fails — a top help desk clue.

lessons.title: SOHO networks, Wi-Fi, and network hardware
lessons.objective: Configure a small office router, distinguish switches, routers, access points, and firewalls, and secure Wi-Fi.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Networking Hardware and Wireless videos

lessons.lab: Log into your home router. Document: WAN IP, LAN subnet, DHCP range, Wi-Fi security mode, and firmware version. Change the admin password if it is default, set WPA3 or WPA2-AES, disable WPS, and create a guest network. Record the changes as a mini change log.

quiz.q: A switch forwards frames based on…
quiz.explain: Switches are layer 2; routers are layer 3 and forward on IP.

quiz.q: Which Wi-Fi security setting should be disabled on a SOHO router?
quiz.explain: Wi-Fi Protected Setup PINs are brute-forceable and a known weak point.

quiz.q: The 5 GHz band compared with 2.4 GHz…
choices: Offers more bandwidth and less interference but shorter range
Is not supported by modern devices
quiz.explain: Higher frequency, more channels, less crowding, but walls absorb it more.

lessons.title: Virtualization and cloud basics
lessons.objective: Explain virtualization concepts you already use in the lab, plus cloud service and deployment models tested on Core 1.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Cloud Models and Virtualization videos

lessons.lab: Write a one-page comparison of your home lab versus what the same four machines would look like in Azure or AWS: IaaS vs on-prem, what you would pay for, and what you would not have to manage. Create a free-tier cloud account (AWS or Azure) but do NOT deploy anything yet.

quiz.q: Office 365 / Microsoft 365 is an example of…
quiz.explain: Software as a Service: you use the application; the vendor runs everything beneath it.

quiz.q: A virtual machine that runs an old OS to keep legacy software working is an example of…
quiz.explain: One of the classic virtualization use cases the exam names.

quiz.q: A 'hybrid cloud' means…
choices: A mix of on-premises/private and public cloud resources
quiz.explain: Most real companies are hybrid — including the one you will work for.

lessons.title: Windows editions, installation, and the command line
lessons.objective: Compare Windows editions, perform clean and in-place installs, and use the Core 2 command-line tools.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Windows Editions and Command Line Tools videos

lessons.lab: On WS02, from an admin command prompt, run and document what each does: ipconfig, ping, tracert, nslookup, netstat, sfc /scannow, chkdsk, diskpart (list disk only), gpupdate, gpresult, shutdown /r /t 0, winver. Paste sanitized output into docs/windows-cli.md.

quiz.q: Which Windows edition is required to join an Active Directory domain?
quiz.explain: Home lacks domain join and Group Policy — a frequent surprise on small-business tickets.

quiz.q: 'sfc /scannow' does what?
choices: Scans and repairs protected system files
quiz.explain: System File Checker; chkdsk handles disk errors, DISM repairs the component store.

quiz.q: An 'in-place upgrade' differs from a 'clean install' because it…
choices: Keeps files, settings, and apps while replacing the OS
quiz.explain: Clean installs start fresh; in-place upgrades preserve user state.

lessons.title: Control Panel, Settings, and management consoles
lessons.objective: Navigate the Windows tools on the objectives — Device Manager, Disk Management, Task Manager, Event Viewer, Services, Local Users and Groups, and more.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Windows Utilities and Control Panel videos

lessons.lab: On WS01: open Event Viewer and find the last failed logon (Security log, Event ID 4625). Open Services and set a non-critical service to Disabled, reboot, observe, restore it. In Disk Management, shrink the C: volume by 5 GB and create a new D: partition. Screenshot each for your notes.

quiz.q: Which console shows hardware with missing or bad drivers?
quiz.explain: A yellow triangle in Device Manager means a driver problem.

quiz.q: Event Viewer's Security log records…
choices: Logon events, privilege use, and audit results
quiz.explain: The Security log is where SOC analysts live. Event ID 4624 is a successful logon, 4625 failed.

quiz.q: 'msconfig' is used to…
choices: Control boot options and startup settings
quiz.explain: System Configuration handles Safe Boot and startup selection.

lessons.title: macOS, Linux, and mobile operating systems
lessons.objective: Perform basic support tasks on macOS and Linux, and understand mobile OS features tested on Core 2.

resources.label: Professor Messer — macOS and Linux videos

lessons.lab: On the Linux VM, complete these and save the commands: check disk space (df -h), memory (free -m), running processes (top / ps aux), update packages (sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade), find a file (find / -name sshd_config), change permissions (chmod 640 on a test file) and explain the resulting mode.

quiz.q: Linux command to see disk usage by filesystem?
quiz.explain: df reports free space; du reports usage of directories.

quiz.q: macOS's built-in backup utility is…
quiz.explain: Keychain stores passwords, Spotlight searches, Finder browses files.

quiz.q: chmod 640 gives…
choices: Owner rwx, group rwx, others rwx
Owner rw, group r, others none
quiz.explain: 6 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. Octal permissions are on both A+ and Linux+.

lessons.title: Security fundamentals: malware, social engineering, authentication
lessons.objective: Identify malware types and social engineering attacks, and explain authentication and authorization controls at the desktop level.
lessons.lab: Build a phishing-awareness one-pager for a fictional small office: five red flags with an example each. Then on WS01, enable BitLocker (or confirm why the VM cannot — TPM) and turn on Windows Defender's controlled folder access. Document what you did.

quiz.q: Ransomware…
choices: Encrypts files and demands payment for the key
quiz.explain: Backups that are offline or immutable are the primary defense.

quiz.q: Following someone through a badge-controlled door is called…
quiz.explain: A physical social engineering attack. Whaling is phishing aimed at executives.

quiz.q: Multifactor authentication combines at least two of…
choices: Something you know, have, and are
quiz.explain: Two passwords are the same factor twice. MFA needs different factor types.

lessons.title: Malware removal and Windows troubleshooting
lessons.objective: Apply the seven-step malware removal process and diagnose common Windows symptoms: slow boot, BSOD, no boot, application crashes.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Malware Removal and Troubleshooting Windows videos

lessons.lab: Snapshot WS02, then download and run the EICAR test file to trigger Defender. Walk the seven malware-removal steps in writing as if it were real: investigate, quarantine, disable System Restore, remediate, schedule scans, enable System Restore, educate the user. Roll back the snapshot afterward.

quiz.q: In CompTIA's malware removal process, why disable System Restore before remediation?
choices: So infected restore points are not reintroduced later
It is required by antivirus software
quiz.explain: Restore points can contain the malware; remove them, clean, then create a fresh one.

quiz.q: A blue screen (BSOD) most often points to…
quiz.explain: Note the stop code and recently installed drivers or hardware.

quiz.q: The EICAR file is…
choices: A harmless standard test string every antivirus detects
quiz.explain: Safe way to confirm AV is working.

lessons.title: Operational procedures: documentation, change management, backups
lessons.objective: Describe ticketing, asset management, change management, backup schemes, and the scripting basics on Core 2 domain 4.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Operational Procedures (Core 2 domain 4) videos

lessons.lab: Write a change request for a real lab change (for example, enabling BitLocker on WS01): purpose, scope, risk, rollback plan, approval, date. Then define a backup scheme for the lab using 3-2-1 and note which backup types (full, incremental, differential) you would run on which days.

quiz.q: A rollback plan in change management is…
choices: How you undo the change if it fails, written before you start
quiz.explain: Every change gets a rollback. Interviewers love this question.

quiz.q: An incremental backup copies…
choices: Only data changed since the last backup of any type
Only data changed since the last full
quiz.explain: Differential copies changes since the last full; incremental since the last backup of any kind. Incrementals are smaller but slower to restore.

quiz.q: Which file extension is a PowerShell script?
quiz.explain: .bat is batch, .sh is shell, .py is Python. Core 2 expects you to recognize all of them.

lessons.title: Final review and exam day
lessons.objective: Run timed practice exams, close weak domains, and execute an exam-day plan.

resources.label: Professor Messer — A+ Pop Quizzes and study groups

lessons.lab: Take two full timed Dion exams per core. For every wrong answer, write one sentence on why the right answer is right. Re-watch Messer videos only for domains under 80%. Schedule Core 1 for two weeks out once you hit 85% twice. Update the Certification Tracker to 'Scheduled' with the date.

quiz.q: The most useful thing to do after a practice exam is…
choices: Review every wrong answer and understand why the right answer is right
quiz.explain: Practice exams are diagnostic tools, not the study material.

quiz.q: Good exam-time strategy for PBQs is…
choices: Spend as long as needed on them first
Flag them, complete the multiple choice, then return
quiz.explain: Protects your time; multiple choice questions are worth solid points and go faster.

quiz.q: After passing Core 1, you should…
choices: Schedule Core 2 within 4–6 weeks while the material is fresh
Retake Core 1 for a higher score
quiz.explain: Momentum matters. The cores overlap; do not lose it.

courses.title: CompTIA Network+
courses.summary: TCP/IP, subnetting, switching and routing, wireless, and network troubleshooting — with a capstone that segments your home lab into VLANs and publishes the addressing plan.
outcomes: Subnet IPv4 networks by hand quickly and correctly
Explain switching (VLANs, STP, trunking) and routing (static, OSPF, BGP concepts)
Design and secure a small wireless network
Capture and read packets in Wireshark
Segment the home lab into VLANs with documented addressing
Pass N10-009

lessons.title: OSI and TCP/IP models
lessons.objective: Name all seven OSI layers with a protocol and device at each, and map them to the four-layer TCP/IP model.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Network+ N10-009 free video course

lessons.lab: Start Wireshark on WS01 and browse to the nginx page on the Linux box. Pick one HTTP packet and, in a document, label every header from layer 2 up to layer 7 with the layer number. Save the .pcapng to your repo (it contains no secrets — lab traffic only).

quiz.q: Switches primarily operate at OSI layer…
quiz.explain: Layer 2, using MAC addresses. Layer 3 switches also route.

quiz.q: TCP and UDP live at which OSI layer?
quiz.explain: Layer 4. IP is layer 3.

quiz.q: Which is a layer 1 problem?
quiz.explain: Physical layer: cables, connectors, signals. Always rule it out first.

lessons.title: Cables, connectors, and Ethernet standards
lessons.objective: Identify copper and fiber media, connectors, categories, and Ethernet standards, and terminate a patch cable.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Cables and Connectors videos

lessons.lab: Buy a crimper, a bag of RJ45 ends, and a cable tester (under $30 total). Terminate two straight-through patch cables to T568B. Test them. Photograph the pinout for your README. Then identify every cable and port type on your lab host and router.

quiz.q: Cat 6 cabling supports 10 Gbps up to…
quiz.explain: Cat 6 does 10GBASE-T to 55 m; Cat 6a to the full 100 m.

quiz.q: Single-mode fiber compared with multimode…
choices: Uses a laser and supports much longer distances
quiz.explain: Single-mode for long haul; multimode for within buildings.

quiz.q: T568A and T568B differ in…
choices: The position of the orange and green pairs
quiz.explain: Same standard both ends = straight-through; A on one end and B on the other = crossover.

lessons.title: Network topologies and types
lessons.objective: Compare LAN, WAN, MAN, SAN, and WLAN, and star, mesh, hybrid, and three-tier topologies.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Network Topologies and Types videos

lessons.lab: Redraw your home lab diagram to show the topology explicitly: which devices are the core/distribution/access equivalents in a tiny network, and where a collapsed core applies. Add the diagram to your repo.

quiz.q: In a star topology, all devices connect to…
quiz.explain: The dominant LAN design; the switch is the single point of failure.

quiz.q: A 'collapsed core' design…
choices: Merges core and distribution layers into one, common in small networks
quiz.explain: Your lab and most small businesses run collapsed core.

quiz.q: A SAN is…
choices: A dedicated network for block-level storage access
quiz.explain: Storage Area Network — iSCSI or Fibre Channel.

lessons.title: IPv4 addressing and classes
lessons.objective: Convert between binary and decimal, identify address classes and private ranges, and explain CIDR notation.
lessons.lab: By hand, convert 10 random IP addresses to binary and back. Then list the three RFC 1918 private ranges with their CIDR masks and mark which one your lab and your home network use.

quiz.q: Which is a private (RFC 1918) address?
/24 in CIDR equals the mask…
quiz.explain: 24 network bits, 8 host bits.

quiz.q: 192.168.1.255 in a /24 network is…
quiz.explain: Last address is broadcast; first (.0) is the network address.

lessons.title: Subnetting by hand
lessons.objective: Given an address and mask, compute network, broadcast, usable range, and host count in under a minute; split a network into equal subnets.

resources.label: Subnetting practice (do 10 a day until fast)

lessons.lab: Split 10.10.0.0/16 into subnets for your lab: Servers, Workstations, Management, Guest, and a spare — each /24. Write the network, gateway, usable range, and broadcast for each. This table is your VLAN plan for the capstone.

quiz.q: Usable hosts in a /26?
quiz.explain: 6 host bits = 64 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 62.

quiz.q: Which subnet contains 192.168.10.77/27?
To create at least 5 equal subnets from a /24 you need…
quiz.explain: Borrow 3 bits → 8 subnets of 30 hosts. /26 only gives 4.

lessons.title: IPv6 essentials
lessons.objective: Read and shorten IPv6 addresses, identify link-local, unique local, and global unicast, and explain SLAAC.
lessons.lab: Run 'ipconfig' on WS01 and 'ip -6 addr' on Linux. Identify each fe80:: link-local address and explain where its interface ID came from. Shorten five long-form IPv6 addresses by hand.

quiz.q: fe80::/10 addresses are…
choices: Link-local — valid only on the local segment
quiz.explain: Every IPv6 interface gets one automatically.

quiz.q: IPv6 addresses are how many bits?
quiz.explain: Eight groups of 16 bits in hex.

quiz.q: SLAAC lets a host…
choices: Get an address from a DHCP server
Build its own address from the router-advertised prefix
quiz.explain: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration — no DHCP server required.

lessons.title: DHCP, DNS, and NAT in depth
lessons.objective: Configure DHCP scopes and reservations, explain DNS record types and resolution, and describe NAT/PAT.

resources.label: Professor Messer — DNS and DHCP videos

lessons.lab: Install the DHCP role on the DC. Create a scope for 10.10.10.100–10.10.10.199 with the DC as DNS and no gateway. Switch WS01 to DHCP and confirm it gets a lease. Create a reservation for WS02 by MAC. In DNS Manager, add an A record 'web' pointing to the Linux box and browse to http://web.lab.nextgen-tech.

quiz.q: A DNS MX record…
choices: Maps a name to an IPv4 address
Identifies mail servers for a domain
Maps an IP to a name
quiz.explain: A = IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, CNAME = alias, PTR = reverse, MX = mail, TXT = text (SPF/DKIM live here).

quiz.q: A DHCP reservation…
choices: Always hands the same IP to a specific MAC address
Is the same as a static IP set on the device
quiz.explain: Central control of 'static' addresses without touching each device.

quiz.q: PAT (port address translation) allows…
choices: One public IP to be shared by many internal hosts
quiz.explain: Your home router does this for every device you own.

lessons.title: Switching: MAC tables, VLANs, and trunks
lessons.objective: Explain how switches learn MACs, why VLANs exist, and how 802.1Q trunking carries multiple VLANs on one link.

resources.label: Professor Messer — VLANs and Trunking videos
Cisco Packet Tracer (free with Networking Academy account)

lessons.lab: In Packet Tracer: one switch, two VLANs (10 and 20), two PCs each. Confirm PCs in the same VLAN ping and PCs in different VLANs do not. Add a second switch with a trunk between them and prove VLAN 10 spans both switches.

quiz.q: A VLAN…
choices: Logically segments one switch into separate broadcast domains
Requires a separate physical switch per network
quiz.explain: Segmentation for security and performance without buying more hardware.

choices: The VLAN tagging standard used on trunk links
quiz.explain: Adds a 4-byte tag with the VLAN ID to each frame on a trunk.

quiz.q: Traffic between two VLANs requires…
quiz.explain: 'Router on a stick' or an SVI on a layer 3 switch.

lessons.title: Spanning tree, link aggregation, and PoE
lessons.objective: Explain why STP prevents loops, what LACP does, and how Power over Ethernet standards differ.

resources.label: Professor Messer — STP, LACP, and PoE videos

lessons.lab: In Packet Tracer, connect three switches in a triangle. Observe which port STP blocks (amber). Unplug the active link and watch it converge. Write two paragraphs on what would happen without STP.

quiz.q: Spanning Tree Protocol prevents…
quiz.explain: Redundant switch links are good; loops are catastrophic. STP blocks the extras.

quiz.q: LACP bundles…
choices: Several physical links into one logical link for bandwidth and redundancy
quiz.explain: 802.3ad / 802.1AX link aggregation.

quiz.q: PoE+ (802.3at) delivers up to about…

lessons.title: Routing fundamentals
lessons.objective: Read a routing table, configure a static route and a default route, and compare OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP conceptually.
lessons.lab: Run 'route print' on WS01 and 'ip route' on Linux; annotate every line. In Packet Tracer, connect two routers with two LANs and make them talk using static routes, then replace the statics with OSPF and confirm the routes appear.

quiz.q: A default route is written as…
quiz.explain: Matches everything not matched by a more specific route.

quiz.q: OSPF is a…
quiz.explain: OSPF builds a full map; BGP is the exterior protocol of the internet.

quiz.q: Administrative distance decides…
choices: Which routing source wins when two protocols offer the same route
quiz.explain: Lower AD wins: connected 0, static 1, OSPF 110, RIP 120.

lessons.title: Firewalls, ACLs, and network services
lessons.objective: Configure basic ACLs and firewall rules, and place services (proxy, load balancer, IDS/IPS, VPN concentrator) in a network design.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Firewalls and Network Appliances videos

lessons.lab: On the Linux box, enable ufw: allow SSH from 10.10.10.0/24 only and HTTP from anywhere in the lab; deny everything else. Prove it from WS01. Then, in Windows Firewall on WS01, block ICMP and confirm pings fail. Restore. Document each rule and why.

quiz.q: A stateful firewall…
choices: Tracks connections and allows return traffic for sessions it has seen
quiz.explain: Stateless (ACLs) need explicit rules both directions; stateful remembers.

quiz.q: An IPS differs from an IDS because it…
choices: Sits inline and can block traffic
quiz.explain: Detection alerts; prevention blocks. Placement matters.

quiz.q: A DMZ (screened subnet) is used to…
choices: Host public-facing servers separated from the internal network
quiz.explain: If a web server is compromised, the attacker is not already inside.

lessons.title: Wireless standards, channels, and design
lessons.objective: Compare 802.11 standards, choose channels to avoid interference, and plan access point placement.
lessons.lab: Use a free Wi-Fi analyzer app to survey your home: list every SSID visible, its channel, band, and signal. Identify which 2.4 GHz channels are congested and move your router to a clear non-overlapping channel (1, 6, or 11). Record before/after speed tests.

quiz.q: Non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the US are…
quiz.explain: Everything else overlaps. This is why crowded apartments have slow Wi-Fi.

quiz.q: Wi-Fi 6 is…
quiz.explain: ac = Wi-Fi 5, n = Wi-Fi 4, ax = Wi-Fi 6/6E, be = Wi-Fi 7.

quiz.q: WPA3 improves on WPA2 mainly by…
choices: Stronger handshake (SAE) resistant to offline password cracking
quiz.explain: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals replaces the crackable PSK handshake.

lessons.title: WAN technologies and remote access
lessons.objective: Compare WAN links (fiber, cable, cellular, satellite, MPLS) and remote access methods (VPN types, SSH, RDP, out-of-band).

resources.label: Professor Messer — WAN Technologies and Remote Access videos

lessons.lab: Install WireGuard or OpenVPN on the Linux box and connect to it from your laptop over the home LAN. Show that once connected you can reach 10.10.10.10 (the DC) from a machine that normally cannot. Document the tunnel config with keys redacted.

quiz.q: A site-to-site VPN…
choices: Connects one laptop to the office
Connects two networks permanently through an encrypted tunnel
quiz.explain: Client-to-site is the laptop case; site-to-site joins offices.

quiz.q: Split tunneling means…
choices: Only traffic for corporate networks goes through the VPN; internet traffic goes direct
quiz.explain: Reduces load on the VPN but means the client is exposed to the internet directly.

quiz.q: Out-of-band management uses…
choices: A separate path (console, dedicated management network, cellular) that works when the production network is down
quiz.explain: How you fix the router that just took down the network.

lessons.title: Network security concepts and attacks
lessons.objective: Identify common network attacks (ARP spoofing, VLAN hopping, rogue DHCP, evil twin, DoS) and the hardening controls that stop them.

resources.label: Professor Messer — Network Attacks and Hardening videos

lessons.lab: Build a hardening checklist for a small business switch and router: change defaults, disable unused ports, port security, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection, management VLAN, SSH only, logging to a central server. Apply what you can to your home router and Packet Tracer switch.

quiz.q: An 'evil twin' attack is…
choices: Two routers with the same IP
A rogue access point mimicking a legitimate SSID to capture traffic
quiz.explain: Users connect to the fake network; the attacker sees everything unencrypted.

quiz.q: DHCP snooping protects against…
choices: Rogue DHCP servers handing out attacker-controlled gateways and DNS
quiz.explain: The switch only trusts DHCP offers from designated ports.

quiz.q: Port security on a switch…
choices: Limits which or how many MAC addresses may use a port
quiz.explain: Stops someone unplugging a printer and plugging in a laptop.

lessons.title: Network troubleshooting tools
lessons.objective: Use ping, traceroute, nslookup/dig, arp, netstat, nmap, iperf, and Wireshark to isolate faults, and know when to use each.
lessons.lab: From the Linux box run 'nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24' then 'nmap -sV 10.10.10.10'. Document every open port on the DC and what service it is. Run an iperf3 test between WS01 and Linux and record throughput. Capture the nmap scan in Wireshark on the DC and describe what a scan looks like on the wire.

quiz.q: traceroute/tracert shows…
choices: Each router hop between you and the destination
quiz.explain: Uses incrementing TTL values to reveal the path.

quiz.q: 'arp -a' displays…
choices: The IP-to-MAC mappings this host has learned
quiz.explain: First place to look for duplicate IPs or ARP spoofing.

quiz.q: iperf measures…
quiz.explain: Separates 'the network is slow' from 'the application is slow.'

lessons.title: Troubleshooting scenarios
lessons.objective: Work realistic tickets — no connectivity, intermittent drops, slow performance, DNS failures, wrong VLAN — using the CompTIA methodology.
lessons.lab: Have your mentor (or a scripted note to yourself) sabotage the lab five ways: wrong gateway, DNS pointed elsewhere, DHCP scope exhausted, duplicate IP, firewall blocking SMB. Diagnose each with the six-step method in under 15 minutes and log each as a ticket in docs/tickets/.

quiz.q: A user can ping by IP but not by name. The problem is most likely…
quiz.explain: IP works, so layers 1–3 are fine; name resolution is failing.

quiz.q: Intermittent connectivity that follows one particular wall jack points to…
choices: Physical cabling or the port on that jack
quiz.explain: If moving the device fixes it, the fault is in the path, not the device.

quiz.q: A new device gets 169.254.x.x. Most likely?
choices: Too many DHCP leases or the client cannot reach the DHCP server
The device is on the wrong VLAN with no DHCP relay
Both A and C are plausible and should be tested
quiz.explain: Both scope exhaustion and VLAN/relay misconfiguration produce APIPA. Test, do not assume.

lessons.title: Capstone: segment the home lab into VLANs
lessons.objective: Move the lab from one flat network into at least three VLANs with inter-VLAN routing, a firewall between them, and a published addressing plan.
lessons.lab: Deploy an OPNsense (or pfSense) VM as the lab router. Make vmbr1 VLAN-aware. Create VLAN 10 Servers (10.10.10.0/24: DC, Linux), VLAN 20 Workstations (10.10.20.0/24: WS01, WS02), VLAN 99 Management (10.10.99.0/24: hypervisor, OPNsense). Move VMs to their VLANs. Write firewall rules: Workstations → Servers allowed for DNS, LDAP, Kerberos, SMB; Servers → Workstations denied except from the DC. Update your addressing table and diagram, and publish both.

quiz.q: After moving WS01 to VLAN 20, it can no longer find the DC. First check?
choices: Does WS01 have an IP in 10.10.20.0/24, a gateway on OPNsense, and DNS pointing to 10.10.10.10 — and does the firewall allow DNS?
quiz.explain: Segmentation adds a router and a firewall to the path; check them in order.

quiz.q: Why put the hypervisor's management interface on its own VLAN?
choices: So a compromised workstation cannot reach the console that controls every machine
quiz.explain: Management-plane isolation is standard in every enterprise you will work in.

quiz.q: Kerberos authentication uses TCP/UDP port…
quiz.explain: 53 DNS, 88 Kerberos, 389 LDAP, 445 SMB — the minimum set a workstation needs to reach a DC.

lessons.title: Exam prep and scheduling
lessons.objective: Close weak domains with practice exams and schedule N10-009.
lessons.lab: Two full timed practice exams. Redo subnetting drills daily until you average under 45 seconds per problem. Schedule the exam when scoring 85%+ twice and set the tracker to Scheduled.

quiz.q: Subnetting speed on the exam matters because…
choices: Several PBQs and questions assume you can subnet quickly, and time is limited
quiz.explain: Automaticity frees time for the harder questions.

quiz.q: Passing Network+ after A+ means…
choices: A+ is renewed under CompTIA's CE stacking
quiz.explain: Higher CompTIA certs renew the lower ones.

quiz.q: The capstone VLAN write-up belongs…
choices: In your GitHub repo as a portfolio piece you will discuss in interviews
quiz.explain: The cert gets you the screen; the documented lab gets you the offer.

courses.title: Linux & Scripting Basics
courses.summary: Enough Linux to be dangerous and enough Bash and PowerShell to automate one boring task and commit it to GitHub. Built on Linux Journey and OverTheWire Bandit.
outcomes: Move confidently in a Linux shell: files, permissions, processes, packages, logs
Complete OverTheWire Bandit through level 20
Write a Bash script and a PowerShell script that each automate a real task
Use Git from the command line and keep scripts in a repo

lessons.title: Navigation, files, and the filesystem tree
lessons.objective: Navigate with cd/ls/pwd, manage files with cp/mv/rm/mkdir, and explain what lives in /etc, /var, /home, /bin, /tmp.

resources.label: Linux Journey — Command Line and The Filesystem

lessons.lab: On the Linux VM, without a GUI: create ~/practice with subfolders a/b/c, touch ten files, move half to c, copy one to /tmp, then delete everything with a single rm -r and explain the flags. Write one line describing each top-level directory in /.

quiz.q: System-wide configuration files live in…
quiz.explain: /etc is where sshd_config, hosts, and most service configs are.

quiz.q: Logs are typically found under…
quiz.explain: /var holds variable data: logs, mail, spool.

quiz.q: 'rm -rf /' would…
choices: Recursively force-delete everything the user can — catastrophic as root
quiz.explain: This is why you snapshot first and why you never run as root by default.

lessons.title: Permissions, users, and sudo
lessons.objective: Read and set rwx permissions with chmod and chown, manage users and groups, and use sudo correctly.

resources.label: Linux Journey — Permissions and User Management

lessons.lab: Create users cooper and myles and a group 'analysts'. Make /srv/shared owned by root:analysts with mode 2770 (setgid). Prove one user's files there are writable by the other and not by a third user. Give 'analysts' sudo rights for only 'systemctl restart nginx' via a sudoers.d file.

quiz.q: -rwxr-x--- means…
choices: Owner rwx, group rx, others nothing
quiz.explain: Three triads: owner, group, others.

quiz.q: The setgid bit on a directory…
choices: Makes new files inherit the directory's group
quiz.explain: Essential for shared team folders.

quiz.q: Editing /etc/sudoers should be done with…
choices: visudo, which checks syntax before saving
quiz.explain: A syntax error in sudoers can lock you out of sudo entirely.

lessons.title: Processes, services, and packages
lessons.objective: Inspect and control processes (ps, top, kill), manage services with systemctl, and install software with apt.
lessons.lab: Install htop and fail2ban with apt. Start a 'sleep 3000 &' background job, find its PID three different ways, and kill it. Use systemctl to check nginx status, stop it, confirm the web page is down from WS01, start it, enable it at boot. Read the journal for nginx with journalctl -u nginx.

quiz.q: systemctl enable nginx…
quiz.explain: enable = at boot; start = now. Use both after install.

quiz.q: kill -9 sends…
choices: SIGKILL, which cannot be caught or ignored
quiz.explain: Try plain kill (SIGTERM) first; -9 is the last resort.

quiz.q: 'apt update' versus 'apt upgrade':
choices: update refreshes the package list; upgrade installs newer versions
quiz.explain: Always update first so upgrade knows what is available.

lessons.title: Text processing and pipes
lessons.objective: Chain grep, cut, sort, uniq, awk, sed, head, tail, and wc with pipes and redirection to answer questions from logs.

resources.label: OverTheWire — Bandit levels 0–12 (text and file tricks)

lessons.lab: From /var/log/auth.log (or journalctl), produce with one pipeline: the top 10 source IPs of failed SSH logins with counts. Then: the count of unique users who logged in successfully today. Save both one-liners to scripts/oneliners.md. Complete Bandit 0–12.

quiz.q: grep -i does…
quiz.explain: -v inverts, -c counts, -r recurses, -n shows line numbers.

quiz.q: 'sort | uniq -c | sort -rn' produces…
choices: Frequency counts of each unique line, most common first
quiz.explain: The single most useful log-analysis pipeline you will ever learn.

quiz.q: '>' versus '>>':
quiz.explain: A misplaced > has destroyed many a log file.

lessons.title: Your first script: variables, arguments, and exit codes
lessons.objective: Write an executable Bash script with a shebang, variables, positional arguments, and meaningful exit codes.
lessons.lab: Write greet.sh that takes a name as $1, prints a greeting with the date, exits 1 with a usage message if no argument is given. Make it executable, run it both ways, and check $?. Run it through ShellCheck and fix every warning.

quiz.q: The first line '#!/bin/bash' is…
choices: The shebang telling the OS which interpreter runs the script
quiz.explain: Without it the script runs in whatever shell the caller uses.

quiz.q: $1 refers to…
quiz.explain: $0 is the script name, $# the count, $@ all arguments.

quiz.q: An exit code of 0 means…
quiz.explain: Non-zero means failure; scripts and CI pipelines depend on this convention.

lessons.title: Conditionals, loops, and functions
lessons.objective: Use if/elif/else, test operators, for and while loops, and functions to control script flow.
lessons.lab: Write hostcheck.sh: loop over every IP in your addressing plan, ping each once, and print UP/DOWN in a table. Add a function that logs results with a timestamp to a file. Complete Bandit 13–20 (you will need SSH keys, ports, and loops).

quiz.q: [ -f "$file" ] tests…
choices: Whether $file exists and is a regular file
quiz.explain: -d directory, -e exists, -x executable, -z empty string.

quiz.q: Why quote variables like "$name"?
choices: To prevent word splitting and globbing when the value has spaces or special characters
quiz.explain: Unquoted variables are the most common Bash bug.

quiz.q: 'for f in *.log; do ...; done' iterates over…
choices: Each file ending in .log in the current directory
quiz.explain: Globbing expands the pattern before the loop runs.

lessons.title: Automate a boring task with Bash
lessons.objective: Pick one real repetitive task in the lab and automate it end to end with logging and error handling, then schedule it with cron.
lessons.lab: Choose one: (a) nightly backup of /etc and /srv/shared to a dated tarball with 7-day retention; (b) daily report of failed SSH logins emailed or written to a shared folder; (c) auto-update with reboot-if-needed and a log entry. Write it with 'set -euo pipefail', log to /var/log/<script>.log, schedule in cron, and verify it ran the next day.

quiz.q: 'set -e' in a script…
choices: Exits immediately if any command fails
quiz.explain: Combined with -u (undefined vars) and -o pipefail, it makes scripts fail loudly instead of silently.

quiz.q: The cron entry '0 2 * * *' runs…
quiz.explain: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

quiz.q: Cron jobs commonly fail because…
choices: The cron environment has a minimal PATH, so commands need full paths
quiz.explain: Works in your shell, fails in cron = almost always PATH or working directory.

lessons.title: PowerShell fundamentals: cmdlets, objects, the pipeline
lessons.objective: Discover cmdlets with Get-Command and Get-Help, and explain why PowerShell pipes objects rather than text.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Introduction to PowerShell (free module)

lessons.lab: On the DC: Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 Name,CPU,Id. Then Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped' | Measure-Object. Then Get-EventLog -LogName Security -Newest 20 | Group-Object EventID. Explain what each pipeline stage receives and outputs.

quiz.q: PowerShell cmdlets follow the naming pattern…
quiz.explain: Consistent naming means you can guess commands you have never seen.

quiz.q: Unlike Bash, PowerShell pipes…
choices: .NET objects with properties, not raw text
quiz.explain: No parsing text columns; you reference $_.Name directly.

quiz.q: To find every cmdlet about services…
quiz.explain: Get-Command and Get-Help are the two discovery tools.

lessons.title: Active Directory with PowerShell
lessons.objective: Query and manage AD users, groups, and computers from the ActiveDirectory module.
lessons.lab: Create a CSV of five fictional new hires (name, department, title). Write New-Users.ps1 that imports it, creates each user in the right OU with a random temporary password, adds them to a department group, and outputs a report. Then write a one-liner listing every account that has not logged in for 90 days.

quiz.q: Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate returns…
choices: All users, including the LastLogonDate attribute which is not returned by default
quiz.explain: Most AD attributes are not returned unless you ask with -Properties.

quiz.q: Why use Import-Csv for bulk user creation?
choices: HR hands you spreadsheets; one script turns a spreadsheet into accounts, repeatably
It is faster than the GUI for one user
quiz.explain: This exact script is in production at most companies.

quiz.q: -WhatIf on a cmdlet…
choices: Shows what would happen without doing it
quiz.explain: Always dry-run bulk changes against AD.

lessons.title: Automate a boring task with PowerShell
lessons.objective: Write a scheduled PowerShell script with parameters, error handling, and logging that solves a real Windows admin task.
lessons.lab: Choose one: (a) daily disk-space report for every domain computer emailed or written to a share; (b) find and disable accounts inactive 90+ days, moving them to a Disabled OU with a log; (c) export the last 24 hours of failed logons (4625) to CSV. Use [CmdletBinding()], param(), try/catch, and Write-Log. Register it in Task Scheduler and confirm it ran.

quiz.q: try { } catch { } in PowerShell catches…
choices: Terminating errors — add -ErrorAction Stop to make non-terminating errors catchable
quiz.explain: The classic gotcha: many cmdlet errors are non-terminating and skip your catch block.

quiz.q: Execution policy 'RemoteSigned' means…
choices: Local scripts run; downloaded scripts must be signed
quiz.explain: Sensible default for admin workstations.

quiz.q: The best place to keep your admin scripts is…
choices: A Git repository with a README per script
quiz.explain: Versioned, documented, and shareable — and a portfolio piece.

lessons.title: Git from the command line
lessons.objective: Init, clone, branch, commit, push, pull, and resolve a merge conflict using Git CLI.
lessons.lab: Create a 'scripts' repo. Set up SSH auth to GitHub. Add your Bash and PowerShell scripts on a branch, open a pull request, and merge it. Then deliberately create a conflict by editing the same line on two branches and resolve it. Write a README with usage for each script.

quiz.q: git add stages changes; git commit…
choices: Records the staged snapshot in local history
quiz.explain: Commit is local. Push sends it to the remote.

quiz.q: A branch is…
choices: A copy of the whole repo
A movable pointer to a commit, letting you work in isolation
quiz.explain: Branches are cheap; use one per change.

quiz.q: Never commit…
choices: Passwords, private keys, or API tokens — use .gitignore and a secrets manager
quiz.explain: Add a .gitignore before your first commit and use git-secrets or pre-commit hooks.

lessons.title: SSH keys, dotfiles, and a reproducible toolbox
