lessons.objective: Manage SSH keys and config for multiple hosts, keep your shell configuration in a dotfiles repo, and use tmux to keep sessions alive.

resources.label: Pro Git — Getting Started with SSH keys (GitHub docs)

lessons.lab: Create ~/.ssh/config with named entries for the Linux box, the hypervisor, and GitHub, each with its own key. Start a dotfiles repo containing .bashrc, .gitconfig, .tmux.conf, and an install.sh that symlinks them. Clone it onto a fresh VM and prove your environment comes up in one command. Start a long job inside tmux, disconnect, reconnect, and confirm it is still running.

quiz.q: ~/.ssh/config lets you…
choices: Define per-host aliases, users, ports, and keys so 'ssh lab' just works
quiz.explain: One config beats memorizing flags for every host.

quiz.q: A dotfiles repo is valuable because…
choices: Your working environment becomes reproducible on any new machine in minutes
quiz.explain: Infrastructure-as-code thinking, applied to your own desk.

quiz.q: tmux protects you from…
choices: Losing a running process when your SSH connection drops
quiz.explain: Detach, reconnect, resume. Essential on flaky Wi-Fi and long jobs.

lessons.title: Course checkpoint: two scripts, one repo, one write-up
lessons.objective: Publish both automation scripts with documentation and a short blog-style write-up explaining the problem, the solution, and what you learned.

resources.label: GitHub Docs — Managing your profile README

lessons.lab: Checklist: Bandit level 20 screenshot in the repo; Bash script scheduled and logged; PowerShell script scheduled and logged; README per script; a 400-word write-up in docs/ titled 'Automating <task>'; your GitHub profile README links to homelab and scripts repos. Send both repo links to your mentor.

quiz.q: The write-up matters because…
choices: Recruiters read code line by line
Explaining what and why in plain English is the skill that gets you hired and promoted
quiz.explain: Communication multiplies technical work.

quiz.q: A good README for a script includes…
choices: Purpose, requirements, usage examples, and what it changes
quiz.explain: Write for the version of you who forgot how it works in six months.

quiz.q: After this course you should be able to…
choices: Read logs, script fixes, and version them — the base skill set for every later course here
quiz.explain: SIEM, detection engineering, and pentesting all assume this floor.

courses.title: Landing the First IT Job
courses.summary: Turn the lab, the certs, and the scripts into a resume, a portfolio, and interview answers for help desk, desktop support, and NOC roles.
outcomes: A one-page resume that passes applicant screening and reads well to a human
A GitHub portfolio a hiring manager can evaluate in two minutes
Confident answers to the 15 most common entry-level IT interview questions
A search-and-apply routine for IT Support Specialist, Service Desk Analyst, Desktop Support Technician, and Junior Systems Administrator roles

lessons.title: The one-page IT resume
lessons.objective: Write a resume that leads with skills and projects, uses the keywords from real job postings, and fits one page.

resources.label: Indeed — search 'IT Support Specialist' near you and read 10 postings

lessons.lab: Read ten local postings for the four target titles. Build a keyword list (Active Directory, Windows 11, Office 365, ticketing, imaging, VPN…). Write a one-page resume: Summary (3 lines), Skills (grouped), Projects (home lab, VLAN segmentation, automation scripts — each with a link and a measurable result), Certifications (with 'in progress' dates), Experience (any job — emphasize customer service and reliability), Education. Save as PDF in a private repo or drive.

quiz.q: For a candidate with no IT job history, the section that should appear first after the summary is…
quiz.explain: Lead with what proves you can do the work. Projects with links are evidence.

quiz.q: Applicant tracking systems (ATS) screen resumes by…
choices: Matching keywords from the job description
quiz.explain: Mirror the posting's language (honestly). 'AD' and 'Active Directory' both belong.

quiz.q: Which project bullet is strongest?
choices: Built and documented a 4-VM Windows domain lab, segmented into 3 VLANs with a firewall; repo linked
quiz.explain: Specific, measurable, verifiable.

lessons.title: GitHub as your portfolio
lessons.objective: Make your GitHub profile read as a portfolio: pinned repos, READMEs with screenshots, a profile README, and consistent commit activity.

resources.label: GitHub Docs — Pinning repositories to your profile

lessons.lab: Pin homelab and scripts. Add a profile README: who you are, what you are studying, links to the two repos and your LinkedIn. Add screenshots to each repo README. Ask a friend who is not in IT to spend two minutes on your profile and tell you what they think you can do.

quiz.q: A hiring manager who opens your GitHub will most likely…
choices: Skim the profile and one README for about two minutes
quiz.explain: Design for the two-minute skim: clear README, screenshots, a diagram.

quiz.q: The commit history in your repos shows…
choices: That you actually did the work over time, not in one paste
quiz.explain: Steady commits are proof of practice.

quiz.q: Which belongs in a public repo?
quiz.explain: Everything else is a security finding against you.

lessons.title: LinkedIn and local networking
lessons.objective: Set up a LinkedIn profile aligned to the resume and attend one local IT or security meetup.

resources.label: Meetup — search 'IT' or 'cybersecurity' in your city

lessons.lab: Headline: 'IT Support | Home lab: Windows domain, VLANs, PowerShell | A+ in progress'. About section = resume summary. Add projects with links. Connect with 20 local IT people with a one-line personal note. Find one meetup in the next 30 days and put it on your calendar.

quiz.q: The best LinkedIn headline for an entry-level candidate…
choices: States the target role plus concrete proof of skill
quiz.explain: Recruiters search headlines. Give them the words.

quiz.q: Local meetups matter because…
choices: Most entry-level hires come through referrals, and meetups create them
quiz.explain: A referral bypasses the resume pile.

quiz.q: A good connection note is…
choices: One sentence: who you are, why you are reaching out, no ask
quiz.explain: Low-pressure, specific, human.

lessons.title: Technical questions for help desk and desktop support
lessons.objective: Answer the standard entry-level technical questions clearly and with the troubleshooting method.
lessons.lab: Record yourself answering these in under 90 seconds each: 'A user can't print.' 'A user says the internet is down.' 'Explain DHCP to a non-technical person.' 'What is Active Directory?' 'How do you reset a user's password and what do you verify first?' 'Walk me through your home lab.' Review the recordings; cut filler words.

quiz.q: 'A user says the internet is down.' Your first move in the interview answer is…
choices: Ask clarifying questions: one site or all? just them or everyone? wired or Wi-Fi? any changes?
quiz.explain: Demonstrating the method matters more than the fix.

quiz.q: Before resetting a password, you should…
choices: Verify the caller's identity per policy
quiz.explain: Help desk password resets are a top social-engineering vector.

quiz.q: When asked something you do not know…
choices: Say so, then explain how you would find out
quiz.explain: Honesty plus a method beats a wrong confident answer every time.

lessons.title: Behavioral questions and the customer-service angle
lessons.objective: Prepare STAR-format stories for teamwork, conflict, learning fast, and handling a frustrated customer.

resources.label: Indeed Career Guide — STAR interview method

lessons.lab: Write five STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result) from any job, school, or sport: a hard customer, a mistake you fixed, a time you learned something fast, working with a difficult teammate, going beyond the ask. Keep each under two minutes spoken. Practice them out loud.

quiz.q: STAR stands for…
quiz.explain: Structure keeps answers concrete and short.

quiz.q: Entry-level IT roles are hired heavily on…
choices: Reliability, communication, and customer service — technical skills can be taught
quiz.explain: Retail, food service, and coaching experience all count if you frame them right.

quiz.q: When describing a mistake, emphasize…
choices: What you did to fix it and what changed afterward
quiz.explain: Ownership plus a process improvement is exactly what managers want.

lessons.title: Mock interview and follow-up
lessons.objective: Complete a full mock interview with your mentor, send a follow-up note, and evaluate an offer.
lessons.lab: 45-minute mock: 10 minutes on your background and lab, 20 minutes technical scenarios, 10 minutes behavioral, 5 minutes your questions for them. Have three questions ready ('What does the first 90 days look like?' 'How are tickets prioritized?' 'How does someone grow from this role?'). Write and send a thank-you note within 24 hours.

quiz.q: 'Do you have any questions for us?' The right answer is…
choices: Two or three prepared questions about the role, team, and growth
quiz.explain: It signals engagement and helps you evaluate them.

quiz.q: A follow-up note should be sent…
choices: Within 24 hours, short, referencing something specific from the conversation
Only if you got the job
quiz.explain: Few candidates do it; it stands out.

quiz.q: When evaluating a first IT offer, weigh most heavily…
choices: Exposure to real systems, a path to grow, and a manager who invests in people
quiz.explain: The first job is a launchpad. Learning velocity beats a few dollars an hour.

lessons.title: Target titles and where to look
lessons.objective: Run a weekly search routine across job boards, MSPs, school districts, hospitals, and local government for the four target titles.
lessons.lab: Build a tracking spreadsheet: company, title, date applied, source, contact, status, next step. Set saved searches for IT Support Specialist, Service Desk Analyst, Desktop Support Technician, Junior Systems Administrator within 40 miles. Add five local MSPs, two school districts, two hospitals, and the county/city IT departments as direct targets.

quiz.q: MSPs (managed service providers) are good first employers because…
choices: You touch many clients' systems fast and learn broadly
quiz.explain: Steep learning curve, wide exposure. A classic launch point.

quiz.q: School districts, hospitals, and local government tend to…
choices: Hire entry-level IT steadily, with stable hours and often tuition or cert reimbursement
quiz.explain: Less glamorous, very reliable, and good for cert funding.

quiz.q: 'Junior Systems Administrator' compared with 'Help Desk'…
choices: Usually expects some experience; apply anyway if you can demonstrate the lab and scripting
quiz.explain: Postings describe the ideal candidate. Documented projects close the gap.

lessons.title: The weekly application routine
lessons.objective: Commit to a tracked weekly cadence of tailored applications, connections, and follow-ups.

resources.label: Your Cargill Academy milestone checklist (My Learning)

lessons.lab: Weekly: 10 quality applications (tailored resume keywords), 5 new LinkedIn connections with a one-line note, 1 follow-up on each open application after 7 days, 1 hour of interview practice. Log every action in your tracker and review the numbers with your mentor each Sunday.

quiz.q: Ten tailored applications a week beats fifty generic ones because…
choices: Tailored keywords pass screening and show effort; volume without fit gets ignored
quiz.explain: Quality and consistency, tracked.

quiz.q: Following up on an application after about a week…
choices: Is normal, shows interest, and often surfaces applications that were never seen
quiz.explain: One polite follow-up per week is expected. Daily is not.

quiz.q: You have applied to 40 roles with no interviews. Best response?
choices: Apply to 100 more of the same
Have your mentor review the resume and portfolio against three postings, then adjust keywords and targets
quiz.explain: Zero responses is a resume or targeting signal, not a talent signal.

lessons.title: Negotiating and accepting the offer
lessons.objective: Evaluate an offer on pay, growth, and learning, negotiate respectfully, and accept in writing.

resources.label: Bureau of Labor Statistics — Computer Support Specialists (pay data)

lessons.lab: Look up the BLS and local salary range for computer support specialists in your metro. Write your walk-away number and your target. Draft a two-paragraph negotiation email asking for a specific figure with a reason (certs in progress, documented lab, shift flexibility). Role-play it with your mentor. Draft the acceptance email too.

quiz.q: When an offer comes in, you should…
choices: Thank them, ask for it in writing, and take 24–48 hours to review
Decline to see if they raise it
quiz.explain: Enthusiasm plus a short review window is standard and expected.

quiz.q: A reasonable entry-level negotiation is…
choices: A specific, researched figure a modest step above the offer, with a reason attached
quiz.explain: Most employers have some room; asking well rarely costs you the offer.

quiz.q: Besides base pay, ask about…
choices: Certification reimbursement, on-call expectations, and shift schedule
quiz.explain: Cert funding alone can be worth thousands over the program.

lessons.title: The first 90 days
lessons.objective: Plan the first 90 days to become reliable, visible, and useful fast.

resources.label: Your Cargill Academy milestone checklist (My Learning)

lessons.lab: Write a 90-day plan: weeks 1–2 learn the ticketing system and shadow every tier; weeks 3–6 own a ticket queue and document three processes nobody wrote down; weeks 7–12 propose one small improvement (a script, a KB article, a checklist) and deliver it. Review with your mentor at day 30, 60, 90.

quiz.q: In your first 90 days, documenting undocumented processes…
choices: Makes you visibly valuable fast and builds the habit this whole program rests on
quiz.explain: The new person who writes things down becomes indispensable.

quiz.q: Shadowing higher tiers early…
choices: Shows you where the interesting problems are and who to learn from
quiz.explain: Ask; most senior techs like teaching someone who is curious.

quiz.q: The most important trait in a new help desk hire is…
choices: Reliability — show up, follow through, close the loop with users
quiz.explain: Trust is built on follow-through, and trust is what gets you access to bigger systems.

lessons.title: Getting certifications funded
lessons.objective: Ask for and secure employer funding for Network+, Security+, and training platforms.

resources.label: CompTIA — Why hire certified (share with your manager)

lessons.lab: In week two, ask your manager how training and certification reimbursement works. Write a one-paragraph business case for Security+ (mapped to a real team need — e.g. phishing tickets, MFA rollout). Track every approved dollar in the Certification Tracker.

quiz.q: When should you ask about certification reimbursement?
choices: Early — in the offer stage or the first weeks — so Network+ and Security+ are employer-funded
quiz.explain: Most employers have a budget; few employees ask.

quiz.q: A business case for a cert should…
choices: Tie the cert to a problem the team actually has
quiz.explain: Managers approve things that solve their problems.

quiz.q: If the employer will not fund certs…
choices: Keep the plan; the program budgets for self-funding and the certs still pay for themselves
quiz.explain: Funding is a bonus, not a dependency.

lessons.title: Turning tickets into portfolio write-ups
lessons.objective: Convert real work into sanitized case-study write-ups that feed the Year 3 'five portfolio write-ups' milestone.

resources.label: GitHub Docs — Basic writing and formatting syntax

lessons.lab: Pick one interesting ticket per month. Write it up in 300–500 words with all identifying details removed: symptom, investigation, root cause, fix, prevention. Get manager permission if there is any doubt about confidentiality. Publish to a 'casebook' repo.

quiz.q: Before publishing a work write-up you must…
choices: Remove all customer, company, and system identifiers, and confirm your employer's policy allows it
Include the company name for credibility
quiz.explain: Confidentiality first. The lesson is portable; the details are not yours to share.

quiz.q: A root-cause write-up is more valuable than a fix log because…
choices: It shows you understand why things break, which is what security roles hire for
quiz.explain: 'Why' is the whole job in security.

quiz.q: One write-up a month gives you, by Year 3…
choices: Well over the five portfolio write-ups in the milestones
quiz.explain: Small, steady, compounding.

courses.title: CompTIA Security+
courses.summary: The cert that turns an IT person into a security candidate. Five domains — concepts, threats, architecture, operations, and governance — mapped onto the lab you already built. Start it three to four months after Network+.
outcomes: Explain the CIA triad, control types, and zero trust in plain language
Recognize the attack types SY0-701 tests and name the mitigation for each
Design a segmented, hardened network and defend the choices
Run the incident response lifecycle against an event in your own lab
Pass SY0-701 and speak about risk, policy, and compliance without bluffing

lessons.title: CIA, AAA, and the control categories
lessons.objective: Define confidentiality, integrity, and availability; separate authentication from authorization and accounting; and sort any control into technical/managerial/operational/physical and preventive/detective/corrective/compensating/deterrent/directive.

resources.label: Professor Messer — SY0-701 Security+ course (free video series)

lessons.lab: Walk your home lab and build a control inventory in a spreadsheet: every control you have already put in place (local admin removed, SSH keys only, logon banner GPO, snapshots, password manager, isolated vSwitch). For each one, fill two columns: category (technical / managerial / operational / physical) and type (preventive / detective / corrective / deterrent / compensating / directive). Argue each classification in one sentence. Expect to find you have almost no detective controls — that gap is what the SIEM course fixes.

quiz.q: A logon banner warning that use is monitored is best classified as which control type?
quiz.explain: It does not stop anyone technically; it discourages. Deterrent controls influence behavior. Exam questions love the banner example.

quiz.q: Backups restore a system after ransomware. That is which control type?
quiz.explain: Corrective controls act after the event to restore normal operation. Detective controls find it; preventive controls stop it.

quiz.q: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Authentication = what you are allowed to do
quiz.explain: AuthN proves identity, AuthZ grants access, accounting logs the activity. The logs are what makes an incident investigable.

lessons.title: Zero trust, least privilege, and defense in depth
lessons.objective: Explain zero trust in terms of control plane and data plane, and show why 'inside the network' is no longer a trust decision.
lessons.lab: Take your lab's four machines and write a one-page zero trust critique: today, any device on 10.10.10.0/24 can reach any other on any port. List five implicit trusts your lab relies on (flat subnet, domain admin used for routine work, no host firewall between clients, unauthenticated nginx, shared local admin password). For each, write the zero trust equivalent you would implement and which lesson later in the Academy covers it.

quiz.q: In zero trust terms, the policy decision point…
choices: Evaluates identity, device, and context and decides whether to allow the request
quiz.explain: The policy engine decides; the policy enforcement point carries the decision out. Control plane decides, data plane moves packets.

quiz.q: Least privilege applied to your lab means…
choices: Every user gets local admin so they can fix their own machine
Your daily account is a standard user and admin work uses a separate account, elevated only when needed
Only one admin account exists for the whole domain
Users may not log in at all
quiz.explain: Separate privileged identities, used deliberately. This is the single highest-value habit you build in the lab.

quiz.q: Defense in depth means…
choices: Layering independent controls so the failure of one does not expose the asset
quiz.explain: Layers that fail independently. Two antivirus products are correlated controls — they fail the same way and fight each other.

lessons.title: Cryptography: symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, PKI
lessons.objective: Choose the right primitive for a job — encryption for confidentiality, hashing for integrity, signatures for authenticity and non-repudiation — and explain how a certificate chain proves identity.

resources.label: Cloudflare Learning — What is a TLS handshake?

lessons.lab: On the Linux box: (1) generate a self-signed certificate with openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 and serve it from nginx over 443; (2) visit it from a Windows client and read the exact browser error; (3) install the certificate into the client's Trusted Root store via GPO or manually, reload, and watch the error disappear. Then run openssl x509 -text -noout on the cert and identify subject, issuer, validity dates, and SAN. Write down why the error appeared and what changed — that is PKI in one paragraph.

quiz.q: You need to prove a downloaded file was not altered, with no secret shared in advance. Use…
choices: A cryptographic hash published by the vendor
quiz.explain: Hashing gives integrity. It is not encryption and it is not reversible — encoding like Base64 gives neither.

quiz.q: In asymmetric cryptography, to send Myles a confidential message you encrypt with…
quiz.explain: Encrypt with the recipient's public key; only their private key opens it. Signing is the mirror image: sign with your private key.

quiz.q: The browser trusted your certificate only after you installed it in the Trusted Root store because…
choices: Trust comes from a chain to a root the client already trusts, not from the certificate itself
quiz.explain: The crypto was fine. What was missing was a trust path. This is exactly how an internal CA works in a real domain.

lessons.title: Change management as a security control
lessons.objective: Describe the approval, impact analysis, backout plan, and maintenance window steps of change management, and explain why unmanaged change is a security problem, not just an ops problem.
lessons.lab: Write a real change request for the next change you make in the lab (for example, enabling the Windows Firewall between clients). Include: requester, description, reason, affected systems, risk if it fails, test plan, backout plan (which snapshot), maintenance window, and approver. Execute the change following your own document. Then deliberately let it fail and use your backout plan. Commit the completed form to docs/changes/ in your homelab repo.

quiz.q: The most security-relevant part of a change record is usually…
choices: The backout plan — it determines whether a failed change becomes an outage or an incident
quiz.explain: Availability is one third of the CIA triad. A change with no rollback is an availability risk you accepted without noticing.

quiz.q: Undocumented configuration drift matters to security because…
choices: You cannot detect an unauthorized change if you never knew the authorized state
quiz.explain: Detection requires a known-good baseline. This is why asset inventory and baselines appear in Domain 4.

quiz.q: Who should approve a standard, low-risk, repeatedly-performed change?
choices: Nobody — standard changes are pre-approved under a defined procedure
The person making the change, silently
quiz.explain: Mature change management pre-approves routine work so the review effort goes where the risk is.

lessons.title: Threat actors, motivations, and attack surface
lessons.objective: Distinguish nation-state, organized crime, hacktivist, insider, and unskilled attackers by resources, motivation, and sophistication, and map which ones actually threaten a small business.
lessons.lab: Build a threat profile for Cargill Consulting in one page: who would realistically attack a small IT consultancy, what they want (credentials to reach client environments, banking access, ransomware payment), and what the entry points are (email, remote access, a client's compromised network, a stolen laptop). Rank the top five by likelihood. Keep this — the GRC lane course turns it into a risk register.

quiz.q: Which threat actor is defined primarily by having legitimate access already?
quiz.explain: The insider's defining feature is authorized access, which is why detective controls and least privilege matter more than perimeter defense against them.

quiz.q: Shadow IT is a risk mainly because…
choices: Systems nobody knows about are not patched, monitored, backed up, or offboarded
quiz.explain: Unmanaged is unprotected. You cannot secure an asset that is not on the inventory.

quiz.q: An attacker's motivation matters to a defender because…
choices: It determines what they will target and how long they will persist, which shapes your controls
It changes which port they scan
It is required by law to document
It does not matter at all
quiz.explain: A ransomware crew wants fast money and moves on; an espionage actor stays quiet for months. Detection strategy differs accordingly.

lessons.title: Social engineering and phishing
lessons.objective: Name the principles social engineers exploit (authority, urgency, scarcity, familiarity, trust, intimidation) and dissect a real phishing email's headers, links, and pretext.
lessons.lab: Take a real phishing email from your own spam folder. Export the full headers and analyze: Return-Path vs From, Received chain, SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, display-name spoofing, the true destination of every link (hover, do not click), and the pretext used. Write it up as a five-paragraph investigation: what arrived, who it claimed to be, what it wanted, the technical indicators, and the verdict. This document is the single most useful thing you can bring to a SOC interview.

quiz.q: An email passes SPF but is still phishing. How?
choices: SPF only validates the sending server for the envelope sender domain — an attacker's own domain can pass SPF perfectly
The recipient's mail server is misconfigured
quiz.explain: Authentication proves the message came from who it says, not that who it says is trustworthy. Look-alike domains pass SPF all day.

quiz.q: Vishing, smishing, and pretexting differ from phishing by…
choices: The channel or technique — voice, SMS, and an invented scenario respectively — not the underlying manipulation
quiz.explain: Same psychology, different delivery. Know the vocabulary — SY0-701 tests the terms directly.

quiz.q: Business email compromise most often succeeds because of which principle?
quiz.explain: The CFO needs this wire transfer before the close of business. Authority plus urgency shuts down verification behavior.

lessons.title: Malware and the attack types that matter
lessons.objective: Identify ransomware, trojans, worms, rootkits, logic bombs, keyloggers, and fileless malware by behavior, and explain the mitigation for each.
lessons.lab: Safe behavior lab, isolated network only, no internet: on LAB-WS01, download the EICAR test file (harmless antivirus test string) and watch Defender react. Then simulate ransomware behavior without malware: write a PowerShell script that recursively renames files in C:\LabData to .locked and drops a README.txt in each folder. Run it, observe what Defender and the event log do or do not show, then restore from snapshot. Write one paragraph on which detection would have caught it and why signature-based antivirus did not.

quiz.q: Fileless malware is difficult to detect because…
choices: It runs in memory using legitimate tools like PowerShell and WMI, leaving little on disk to scan
quiz.explain: Living off the land defeats file-signature scanning. Detection shifts to command-line logging and behavior — the reason you enable PowerShell script block logging in the SIEM course.

quiz.q: The difference between a worm and a virus is that a worm…
choices: Self-propagates across a network without user action
quiz.explain: A virus needs a host and a user; a worm spreads on its own. Network segmentation is the classic worm control.

quiz.q: The most reliable control against ransomware's impact is…
quiz.explain: Prevention will eventually fail. Recoverability is what decides whether an incident is a bad week or a closed business.

lessons.title: Vulnerability management end to end
lessons.objective: Run the cycle — identify, analyze, prioritize with CVSS and context, remediate or accept, verify, report — against real findings on your own lab.
lessons.lab: Install Greenbone/OpenVAS (or Nessus Essentials, free for 16 IPs) on the Linux box and scan the lab subnet. Take the top ten findings and build a remediation plan table: CVE, CVSS base score, whether it appears in CISA KEV, your own contextual severity (is the host internet-facing? does it hold data?), decision (patch / mitigate / accept), owner, and due date. Remediate three, rescan, and show the findings closed. Note where CVSS disagreed with your context-based priority.

quiz.q: A vulnerability scores CVSS 9.8 but exists on an isolated lab VM with no data and no inbound access. The right move is…
choices: Adjust priority using environmental context and exploitability — high base score does not equal high organizational risk
quiz.explain: CVSS base is severity, not risk. Risk needs asset value, exposure, and exploit availability. CISA KEV is the fastest exploitability check.

quiz.q: A false positive in a scan report is…
choices: A real vulnerability the scanner missed
A finding reported that does not actually exist or is not exploitable on that host
quiz.explain: The dangerous twin is the false negative — a real vulnerability the scanner did not report. Credentialed scans reduce both.

quiz.q: After remediation, the step people most often skip is…
choices: Rescanning to verify the finding is actually closed
quiz.explain: Unverified remediation is a hope, not a control. Verification closes the loop and produces the evidence an auditor wants.

lessons.title: Architecture models: on-prem, cloud, virtualization, serverless
lessons.objective: Compare deployment models and explain the shared responsibility line for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Shared responsibility in the cloud

lessons.lab: Draw a shared responsibility table for three things Cargill Consulting actually uses or would use: Microsoft 365 (SaaS), a cloud VM running a client app (IaaS), and your own on-prem lab. For each row — physical, host OS, network controls, application, identity, data — mark who is responsible. Then answer in writing: in a Microsoft 365 account takeover, whose responsibility is it, and why is the answer uncomfortable for most small businesses?

quiz.q: In SaaS, the customer is always responsible for…
quiz.explain: Identity and data never transfer to the provider in any model. That is why 90% of cloud incidents are identity incidents.

quiz.q: A key security advantage of containers over full VMs is…
choices: Small, immutable images with a short lifetime reduce attack surface and make drift obvious
They cannot be accessed over the network
quiz.explain: The advantage is immutability and reduced surface. The trade-off is a shared kernel — container escape is a real risk class.

quiz.q: VM escape refers to…
choices: Code breaking out of a guest to execute on the hypervisor or other guests
quiz.explain: Rare, severe, and the reason isolation boundaries are also patched boundaries. Keep the hypervisor updated.

lessons.title: Secure network design: segmentation, firewalls, IDS/IPS, VPN
lessons.objective: Place controls correctly — screened subnet, internal segmentation, host firewalls, inline IPS versus out-of-band IDS — and explain what each does and does not see.
lessons.lab: Build on the Network+ VLAN work: install pfSense or OPNsense as a VM with an interface in each lab VLAN. Write firewall rules that allow clients to reach the DC on only the ports AD requires (DNS 53, Kerberos 88, LDAP 389, SMB 445, and the rest), deny everything else, and log denies. Verify with a port scan from a client before and after. Save the before/after nmap output and the ruleset to your repo.

quiz.q: An IDS differs from an IPS in that an IDS…
choices: Observes a copy of traffic and alerts, while an IPS sits inline and can block
Requires an agent on each host
quiz.explain: Out-of-band detection versus inline prevention. An IPS failure can break the network; an IDS failure only blinds you.

quiz.q: Internal segmentation limits an attacker mainly by…
choices: Restricting lateral movement once one host is compromised
quiz.explain: Assume breach. Segmentation converts a compromised workstation into a contained problem instead of a domain-wide one.

quiz.q: You allowed only required AD ports and the domain still broke. The most likely cause is…
choices: The dynamic RPC port range (49152–65535) that AD uses after the initial endpoint mapper call on 135
quiz.explain: The RPC dynamic range is the classic AD-through-a-firewall trap, and a genuinely useful thing to know on a help desk.

lessons.title: Protecting data: classification, encryption, DLP, tokenization
lessons.objective: Classify data, choose protection for data at rest, in transit, and in use, and explain masking, tokenization, and hashing as distinct techniques.

resources.label: NIST SP 800-88 — Guidelines for media sanitization

lessons.lab: Classify the data in your own life the way a company would: public, internal, confidential, restricted. Put real examples in each (portfolio repo, lab documentation, resume, password vault, tax documents). For each class, specify storage location, encryption at rest, encryption in transit, who may access it, retention period, and destruction method. Then enable BitLocker on a lab client and record where the recovery key is escrowed — if you cannot answer that, you have just found a real risk.

quiz.q: Tokenization differs from encryption because the token…
choices: Has no mathematical relationship to the original value; the mapping lives in a separate vault
quiz.explain: No key exists that converts the token back — you must reach the vault. Widely used for payment card data to reduce PCI scope.

quiz.q: Data in use means data…
choices: Loaded in memory and being processed
quiz.explain: The hardest state to protect. Answers include secure enclaves and confidential computing, and it is why memory-scraping malware exists.

quiz.q: The most common cause of DLP failure in small organizations is…
choices: Data was never classified, so the tool has no idea what to protect
quiz.explain: Classification is the prerequisite. Tools enforce decisions; they do not make them for you.

lessons.title: Resilience: redundancy, backups, and testing recovery
lessons.objective: Distinguish RTO, RPO, MTTR, and MTBF; design backup strategy to the 3-2-1 rule; and prove recovery works by doing it.

resources.label: Veeam Community Edition (free backup for up to 10 workloads)

lessons.lab: Define RTO and RPO for each lab VM and write them down. Then prove them: destroy the domain controller entirely (delete the VM, not just a snapshot) and restore it from the backup you made in the Home Lab course. Time the whole recovery. Compare actual recovery time against your stated RTO and, if it missed, write what you would change. A restore that has never been tested is a plan, not a capability.

quiz.q: RPO of four hours means…
choices: Recovery must complete within four hours
You can tolerate losing at most four hours of data
Backups run every four hours automatically
The system fails every four hours
quiz.explain: RPO is acceptable data loss (look backward); RTO is acceptable downtime (look forward). Exam questions swap them constantly.

quiz.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule is…
choices: Three admins, two approvals, one change window
Three copies, on two different media, with one offsite
quiz.explain: Modern versions add a fourth: one immutable or offline copy, because ransomware specifically hunts for backups.

quiz.q: High availability and backup are not substitutes because…
choices: HA replicates corruption and ransomware instantly to the standby; backups give you a point in time before the damage
They are in fact the same thing
quiz.explain: A mirrored bad state is still a bad state. HA protects against failure, backup protects against harm.

lessons.title: Hardening, baselines, and asset management
lessons.objective: Apply a published baseline to a Windows host, measure the difference, and explain why asset inventory precedes every other control.

resources.label: CIS Benchmarks (free PDF download after sign-in)

lessons.lab: Download the Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit, import the Windows 11 security baseline GPO into your lab domain, and link it to a test OU with only LAB-WS02 in it. Run the Policy Analyzer to diff baseline against your current settings. Apply it, then work the fallout: note every thing that breaks and decide for each whether to accept the break or document an exception. Write up three settings you changed and what attack each one blocks.

quiz.q: Applying a hardening baseline to production without a pilot group usually causes…
choices: Broken applications and an emergency rollback, which is why you pilot on a test OU first
quiz.explain: Hardening breaks things. The skill is staging it, measuring impact, and documenting accepted exceptions.

quiz.q: Asset inventory is foundational because…
choices: Every other control — patching, monitoring, backup, offboarding — applies only to assets you know exist
quiz.explain: CIS Controls 1 and 2 are inventory of enterprise assets and software, before anything else, for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: Secure disposal of a decommissioned laptop should include…
choices: Cryptographic erase or physical destruction of the drive, plus a certificate of destruction and inventory update
quiz.explain: NIST SP 800-88 defines clear, purge, and destroy. A quick format is none of them.

lessons.title: Identity and access management
lessons.objective: Implement MFA, explain SSO and federation (SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect), and apply provisioning, deprovisioning, and privileged access management.

resources.label: Microsoft Entra — What is Conditional Access?

lessons.lab: In the lab domain: create a tiered admin model. Make a separate Tier-0 account for domain admin work, remove your daily account from Domain Admins, and use Group Policy to deny Tier-0 accounts the ability to log on to workstations (Deny log on locally / through RDP on the Workstations OU). Prove it: try to RDP to WS01 with the Tier-0 account and capture the refusal. Write two sentences on which attack this blocks (hint: credential theft from a compromised workstation).

quiz.q: Which factor combination is true multi-factor authentication?
choices: A password and a code from an authenticator app
A fingerprint and a face scan
quiz.explain: Factors must be from different categories: something you know, have, and are. Two knowledge factors, or two inherence factors, are not MFA.

quiz.q: SAML and OpenID Connect are used for…
choices: Federated authentication — letting one identity provider vouch for a user to another application
quiz.explain: OAuth 2.0 is authorization (delegated access); OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of it. Know the distinction.

quiz.q: The most commonly missed step in the identity lifecycle is…
choices: Deprovisioning when someone leaves or changes roles
quiz.explain: Orphaned accounts and accumulated permissions (privilege creep) show up in nearly every audit and many breaches.

lessons.title: Monitoring, logging, and alerting
lessons.objective: Name the log sources that matter, explain aggregation and correlation in a SIEM, and write an alert that fires on a real event in your lab.

resources.label: Microsoft — Windows Security audit events reference (Events to monitor)

lessons.lab: On the DC, enable auditing of logon events and account management via Group Policy. Then generate real telemetry: fail five logons for a user, lock the account, add a user to Domain Admins, and clear a security log. Find each one in Event Viewer and record the Event ID (4625, 4740, 4728, 1102). Build a table of Event ID, meaning, and why a SOC cares. You will reuse this table directly in the SIEM course.

quiz.q: Security event 1102 (audit log cleared) is high value because…
choices: Legitimate admins rarely clear logs, and attackers do it to cover tracks — it is a strong anti-forensics signal
It means a user logged in
quiz.explain: Rarity plus intent equals a high-fidelity alert. Forwarding logs off the host in real time is the countermeasure.

quiz.q: Correlation in a SIEM means…
choices: Combining events from multiple sources over time to identify a pattern no single event reveals
quiz.explain: One failed logon is noise; 200 failed logons across 40 accounts from one host in two minutes is password spraying.

quiz.q: Why forward logs off the originating host?
choices: An attacker with admin on the host can alter or delete local logs; a copy elsewhere preserves evidence
To make them searchable in Notepad
quiz.explain: Log integrity depends on the attacker not controlling the storage. Write-once and offsite forwarding both serve this.

lessons.title: Incident response and digital forensics
lessons.objective: Run the NIST lifecycle — preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned — and preserve evidence in the correct order of volatility.

resources.label: NIST SP 800-61r2 — Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

lessons.lab: Table-top plus hands-on: declare an incident — a lab user opened a malicious attachment on WS01. Work the lifecycle and document each step with timestamps: isolate WS01 from the lab network (do not power it off), collect volatile data first (running processes, network connections, logged-on users via netstat, tasklist, and Get-Process), then take a disk snapshot, identify persistence, eradicate, restore from clean snapshot, and write a lessons-learned section. Produce a single incident report in your repo, under 1,000 words.

quiz.q: Why isolate a compromised host rather than immediately powering it off?
choices: Shutting down destroys volatile evidence in memory, including running malware and network connections
Isolation is not possible on Windows
quiz.explain: Order of volatility: memory and network state die first. Isolate to stop spread, then collect, then remediate.

quiz.q: Chain of custody documents…
choices: Who handled each piece of evidence, when, and why — so it holds up later
quiz.explain: Any break in the chain can render evidence useless in a legal or HR proceeding. Document handoffs and hashes.

quiz.q: The step most often skipped, and most valuable, is…
quiz.explain: Without the post-incident review, the same incident recurs. The output should be concrete control changes with owners and dates.

sections.title: Domain 5 — Governance, risk, compliance, and exam day

lessons.title: Governance: policies, standards, procedures, guidelines
lessons.objective: Tell the four document types apart, name the common policies an organization needs, and write one real policy for Cargill Consulting.
lessons.lab: Write a real, two-page Acceptable Use Policy for Cargill Consulting: scope, acceptable use, prohibited use, personal devices, remote access, monitoring notice, consequences, and review date. Then write the matching standard (specific: minimum 14-character passphrases, MFA required on all cloud accounts) and one procedure (step-by-step: how to onboard a new contractor). Seeing all three side by side is the point of the exercise.

quiz.q: Which document is mandatory, high-level, and approved by leadership?
quiz.explain: Policy states what and why, standards state the mandatory specifics, procedures give the steps, guidelines are recommended but optional.

quiz.q: Separation of duties means…
choices: Each department has its own network
No single person can complete a sensitive process alone, so fraud requires collusion
Splitting a password between two people
quiz.explain: The related control is mandatory vacation and job rotation — both designed to surface activity a single person could otherwise hide.

quiz.q: Who owns the risk for a system in a well-run organization?
choices: The business data or system owner
quiz.explain: Security advises and implements; the business owns the risk and signs the acceptance. Getting this wrong is a career-long frustration.

lessons.title: Risk management and the risk register
lessons.objective: Run qualitative and quantitative risk assessment, calculate SLE, ARO, and ALE, and choose a treatment: accept, avoid, transfer, or mitigate.

resources.label: NIST SP 800-30 — Guide for conducting risk assessments

lessons.lab: Build a ten-row risk register for Cargill Consulting using the threat profile from lesson 2-1. Columns: risk ID, description, likelihood (1–5), impact (1–5), inherent score, existing controls, residual score, treatment decision, owner, review date. For the top risk, do the math: estimate asset value, exposure factor, SLE (AV × EF), ARO, and ALE (SLE × ARO). Then state what you would spend annually to mitigate it and justify that number against the ALE.

quiz.q: A laptop worth $2,000 is stolen with 25% of value lost after insurance, twice a year. The ALE is…
quiz.explain: SLE = AV × EF = 2,000 × 0.25 = $500. ALE = SLE × ARO = 500 × 2 = $1,000. Expect this exact calculation on the exam.

quiz.q: Buying cyber insurance is which risk treatment?
quiz.explain: Transference shifts financial impact to a third party. Note that it does not transfer reputational damage or regulatory duty.

quiz.q: Residual risk is…
choices: Risk remaining after controls are applied — which the business must formally accept
quiz.explain: Inherent minus control effectiveness equals residual. Someone with authority signs for what is left.

lessons.title: Third-party risk, compliance, and privacy
lessons.objective: Assess a vendor's security, read what an SOC 2 report actually claims, and name the privacy concepts SY0-701 tests.

resources.label: FTC — Privacy and security guidance for business

lessons.lab: Pick a real SaaS product you use (a password manager, a backup service, a ticketing tool). Build a vendor risk assessment: what data would it hold, what is its classification, does the vendor publish an SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate, where is data stored, how is it encrypted, what is the breach notification commitment in the contract, and how would you exit the vendor. Score it and write an approve/conditional/reject recommendation in three sentences.

quiz.q: An SOC 2 Type II report differs from Type I because Type II…
choices: Tests whether controls operated effectively over a period of time, not just their design at a point in time
quiz.explain: Type I is a snapshot of design; Type II is evidence of operation over months. Always ask which one and for what period.

quiz.q: A data processor is…
choices: The party that determines why and how personal data is processed
The party that processes personal data on behalf of, and under instruction from, the controller
quiz.explain: Controller decides, processor executes. This vocabulary carries into GDPR, CCPA, and nearly every privacy regime.

quiz.q: The main reason a right-to-audit clause matters is…
choices: Without it you have no contractual ability to verify a vendor's security claims after signing
quiz.explain: Security requirements that are not in the contract are wishes. Get them in writing before signature, not after an incident.

lessons.title: Exam strategy: PBQs, scheduling, and the last two weeks
lessons.objective: Build a study plan that ends in a scheduled exam, practice performance-based questions under time pressure, and know the day-of mechanics.

resources.label: Jason Dion — Security+ SY0-701 practice exams (Udemy)
Professor Messer — SY0-701 study group and course notes
Pearson VUE — schedule a CompTIA exam (verify current pricing and vouchers)

lessons.lab: Schedule the exam now, six to eight weeks out — an unscheduled exam is a hobby. Then build the plan backward from that date: which domain each week, which Messer videos, which chapters, and two full Dion practice exams in the final two weeks. Rule: any practice question you miss becomes a flashcard with the reason you missed it, not just the right answer. On exam day, do PBQs last — flag them, clear the multiple choice first, then return with the remaining time.

quiz.q: The best use of a missed practice question is to…
choices: Write down why your reasoning failed and what concept you actually misunderstood
Retake the same exam until you score 100%
Skip it, since the real exam differs
quiz.explain: Memorizing answers inflates your score and teaches nothing. The reason for the miss is the study material.

quiz.q: Performance-based questions appear at the start of the exam. You should…
choices: Flag and skip them, finish the multiple choice, then return with the time you have left
quiz.explain: PBQs eat time. Securing the multiple-choice points first protects the score if the clock gets tight.

quiz.q: If you fail, CompTIA's retake policy means…
choices: You cannot retake for a year
You can retake after a short waiting period, and your score report shows the weak domains to target
The second attempt is free automatically
quiz.explain: The score report is the plan for attempt two. Verify current wait periods and retake pricing on CompTIA's site before booking.

courses.title: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity
courses.summary: A cheaper first security certificate and a useful bridge. Five short domains that overlap heavily with Security+, plus ISC2 membership that later counts toward CISSP. Take it while Security+ study is in flight, not instead of it.
outcomes: Explain security principles, the CIA triad, and the ISC2 code of ethics
Describe business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response as three distinct plans
Apply access control concepts and physical security to a real environment
Pass the CC exam and hold an ISC2 membership that feeds the CISSP path later

lessons.title: Why CC, and how it differs from Security+
lessons.objective: Decide where CC fits in your plan, what it costs, and how its exam differs from SY0-701 in depth and format.

resources.label: ISC2 — free CC online self-paced training and exam (One Million Certified in Cybersecurity; verify current availability)

lessons.lab: Compare the CC and Security+ objective lists side by side in a table: domain, overlap with SY0-701, and unique content. Then write a three-sentence decision: are you taking CC before, during, or instead of Security+, and why. Put the decision and the planned date in your certification tracker.

quiz.q: The strongest practical argument for taking CC alongside Security+ study is…
choices: Heavy content overlap means one study effort feeds two exams, and ISC2 membership starts accumulating toward CISSP
CC is harder and proves more
quiz.explain: CC is entry-level and does not replace Security+ with most employers. Its value is cheap reinforcement plus an ISC2 relationship.

quiz.q: ISC2 certifications carry an ongoing obligation that CompTIA certs do not:
choices: An annual maintenance fee plus continuing professional education credits
quiz.explain: Budget the AMF. It is small, but it never stops, and a lapsed membership means a lapsed certification.

quiz.q: The ISC2 code of ethics canons are, in order…
choices: Protect society; act honorably; provide diligent and competent service to principals; advance and protect the profession
Obey your employer; make a profit; avoid liability; keep quiet
Report all incidents; encrypt everything; patch quickly; document
quiz.explain: The order matters and is tested: society first, then honorable conduct, then principals, then the profession.

lessons.title: CIA, privacy, and the risk vocabulary
lessons.objective: Restate the CIA triad with privacy added, and use asset, vulnerability, threat, likelihood, and impact precisely.

resources.label: ISC2 — CC exam outline (domains and weights)

lessons.lab: Take five sentences from a news article about a recent breach and rewrite each using precise vocabulary: name the asset, the vulnerability, the threat actor, the threat event, the likelihood, and the impact. Most reporting blurs vulnerability with threat — find and correct at least two examples.

quiz.q: An unpatched web server is a…
quiz.explain: A vulnerability is a weakness. The threat is the actor or event that could exploit it; risk is likelihood combined with impact.

quiz.q: Non-repudiation means…
choices: Data cannot be read by outsiders
A party cannot credibly deny having performed an action, usually proven by a digital signature or strong logging
quiz.explain: Signatures and tamper-evident logs create non-repudiation. It sits alongside the CIA triad in the CC material.

quiz.q: Privacy and confidentiality differ in that privacy…
choices: Concerns an individual's rights over their personal information, while confidentiality is the control that limits access
quiz.explain: Confidentiality is a means; privacy is a right with legal weight. You can have confidentiality and still violate privacy.

lessons.title: Governance, law, and the ethics that get you fired
lessons.objective: Identify regulations, standards, policies, and procedures, and work through ethical scenarios where the right answer costs you something.
lessons.lab: Write short answers to four scenarios, each citing the specific canon that governs it: (1) you find a client's database exposed while doing unrelated work; (2) your employer asks you to delay disclosing a breach past the notification deadline; (3) a coworker shares an exam dump with you; (4) you can access an ex-partner's account through a system you administer. State the action you would take and the canon that requires it.

quiz.q: Your employer instructs you to conceal a breach from affected customers. The code of ethics says…
choices: Follow employer instructions — they are your principal
Protection of society and the common good outranks your duty to your principal, so you escalate and refuse to conceal
Nothing; ethics do not cover this
quiz.explain: The canons are ranked deliberately. This scenario, in some form, appears on nearly every ISC2 exam.

quiz.q: Using or sharing brain-dump exam material is…
choices: A violation of the code of ethics and grounds for revoking your certification
Only a problem if you get caught
quiz.explain: It is an explicit violation. It also produces candidates who cannot do the job, which is the actual harm.

quiz.q: A regulation differs from a standard in that a regulation…
choices: Carries the force of law with penalties for non-compliance
quiz.explain: HIPAA and GLBA are law; ISO 27001 and CIS are standards you may adopt voluntarily or by contract.

sections.title: Business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response

lessons.title: Three plans, three purposes
lessons.objective: Separate the incident response plan, the business continuity plan, and the disaster recovery plan, and say which one activates when.
lessons.lab: Write a one-page decision tree for Cargill Consulting: for each of six events (ransomware on a client's server, the office loses power for three days, a laptop is stolen, a phishing email is clicked but no malware ran, the accounting SaaS is down for eight hours, a hard drive fails), state which plan activates, who declares it, and the first three actions. Keep it to one page — a plan nobody can read during a crisis is not a plan.

quiz.q: Business continuity planning focuses on…
choices: Restoring IT systems after a disaster
Keeping critical business functions running during a disruption, by any means including manual workarounds
quiz.explain: BCP keeps the business operating; DRP restores the technology. BCP may say answer the phone with a paper notepad.

quiz.q: A business impact analysis produces…
choices: Criticality of each business function with its maximum tolerable downtime, which drives RTO and RPO targets
quiz.explain: The BIA comes before the plan. Without it you protect everything equally, which means you protect nothing adequately.

quiz.q: The first action when an incident is suspected should be…
choices: Follow the plan: notify the defined point of contact and begin documenting with timestamps
quiz.explain: Untrained instinct destroys evidence and spreads the problem. The plan exists to make the first ten minutes boring.

lessons.title: Incident response roles and communication
lessons.objective: Name the roles on an incident team, and draft the internal and external communication that an incident requires.

resources.label: FTC — Data breach response: a guide for business

lessons.lab: Build an incident contact card for Cargill Consulting that fits on an index card: incident commander, technical lead, communications lead, legal/insurance contact, cyber insurance policy number location, and the out-of-band communication channel to use if email and Teams are assumed compromised. Print it. An incident plan stored only on the encrypted file server is a plan you will not have.

quiz.q: Why define an out-of-band communication channel in advance?
choices: If the corporate email or chat is compromised, coordinating the response inside it tells the attacker your plan
quiz.explain: Attackers read incident response threads. Pre-agree on a separate channel and a way to verify identities on it.

quiz.q: The incident commander's job is primarily to…
choices: Coordinate, decide, and own communication so the technical responders can work
quiz.explain: Separating coordination from analysis is what keeps an incident from turning into six people guessing loudly.

quiz.q: Breach notification deadlines are driven by…
choices: Applicable law, regulation, and contract — which vary by jurisdiction and data type, and start running early
quiz.explain: Know which rules apply before an incident. Discovering a 72-hour clock on day four is a bad way to learn.

lessons.title: Recovery, redundancy, and testing the plan
lessons.objective: Describe backup types, redundancy options, and the exercise types — tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, full interruption — that validate a plan.
lessons.lab: Run a 45-minute tabletop with one other person (Cooper, Myles, or a family member playing the business owner). Scenario: ransomware encrypts the file server on a Friday at 4pm and the backup server is also encrypted. Play it out in writing, injecting two complications at 15-minute intervals (the cyber insurance broker cannot be reached; a client asks whether their data was affected). Capture every gap you find as an action item with an owner.

quiz.q: A differential backup contains…
choices: Only data changed since the last incremental backup
All data changed since the last full backup
quiz.explain: Differential restores need the full plus the latest differential. Incremental restores need the full plus every incremental since.

quiz.q: The lowest-cost, lowest-risk way to test a plan is a…
quiz.explain: Tabletops find most planning gaps for the price of a conference room. Full interruption tests find the rest, at real risk.

quiz.q: A warm site is…
choices: A fully equipped, running duplicate ready in minutes
A facility with space, power, and some equipment that needs configuration and data restoration before use
quiz.explain: Cold is space only, warm is partially ready, hot is running. Cost and recovery time move in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Access control models and principles
lessons.objective: Compare DAC, MAC, RBAC, and ABAC and explain least privilege, need to know, and separation of duties in each.

resources.label: NIST — Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) overview

lessons.lab: Classify the access control in systems you touch: NTFS file permissions in your lab, AD security groups, your phone's app permissions, and a cloud service's role assignments. For each, name the model, who can change access, and what happens when someone changes teams. Then find one place in your own lab where access is discretionary and should not be, and fix it.

quiz.q: In a discretionary access control model, permissions are set by…
choices: The data owner, at their discretion
quiz.explain: Windows NTFS is the everyday example. Its flexibility is exactly why permissions sprawl over time.

quiz.q: Role-based access control assigns permissions to…
choices: Roles, which users are then assigned to
quiz.explain: Same principle you applied in the home lab: users into groups, permissions onto groups. Role changes become one membership edit.

quiz.q: Need to know differs from least privilege because need to know…
choices: Restricts access to specific information required for a specific task, even when the person's clearance or role would otherwise allow it
quiz.explain: You can hold the clearance and still have no business reading that record. Auditors test this on HR and medical data.

lessons.title: Physical security controls
lessons.objective: Identify perimeter, building, and equipment controls, and explain tailgating, mantraps, badge systems, and environmental controls.
lessons.lab: Walk the place where your lab lives and write a physical security assessment: who can reach the hardware, is the door locked, is the hypervisor console password protected, is there a UPS, what happens in a power loss, is there a camera, could someone walk out with the box. Score each finding and list three fixes under $100. Your experience in physical security work makes this the section you should be strongest in — write it like a professional assessment.

quiz.q: A mantrap (access control vestibule) primarily prevents…
choices: Tailgating — one authenticated entry, one person
quiz.explain: It enforces one-person-per-authentication physically, which no badge reader alone can do.

quiz.q: An uninterruptible power supply is which control type?
quiz.explain: Availability is security. A dirty shutdown of a domain controller can corrupt the database you depend on.

quiz.q: Physical access to a server generally means…
choices: Nothing, if the OS password is strong
Effective full compromise is possible — boot media, drive removal, and firmware attacks bypass OS controls
Only the keyboard is at risk
The data is protected by the BIOS password
quiz.explain: Physical access beats logical controls, which is why full-disk encryption and locked racks exist.

lessons.title: Network security basics and the exam
lessons.objective: Review the network and security operations content CC tests lightly, then schedule and sit the exam.

resources.label: ISC2 — CC certification exam outline and registration

lessons.lab: Two-week close-out: take the ISC2 self-paced CC course end to end, then sit the practice assessment. Any domain under 80% gets two evenings of review before you book. Schedule the exam, sit it, and record the result and the ISC2 member number in your certification tracker. If you pass, immediately note the AMF due date on a calendar reminder — a lapsed membership quietly ends the certification.

quiz.q: CC's network domain expects you to know…
choices: Core concepts: the OSI model, common ports, firewalls, VPNs, and segmentation at a conceptual level
quiz.explain: It is conceptual. Network+ already took you far past this depth, which is why CC sits comfortably alongside Security+ study.

quiz.q: After passing CC you become a certified member once you…
choices: Pass only — nothing else is needed
Complete endorsement and pay the annual maintenance fee
quiz.explain: CC requires no experience, unlike CISSP, but the endorsement and AMF steps still apply.

quiz.q: The right place to record your exam date and result is…
choices: The Academy certification tracker, with the renewal date
quiz.explain: Renewal dates arrive quietly. Tracking them is a habit that later protects a CISSP worth far more.

lessons.title: Data handling and security awareness
lessons.objective: Apply classification, labeling, retention, and destruction, and explain why awareness training is a control with measurable effect.
lessons.lab: Design a 20-minute security awareness session for a small business client: three topics (phishing, passwords and MFA, reporting an incident), one live demo, one memorable story, and a single call to action. Deliver it to a family member and note where they got bored. Awareness training that nobody remembers is a compliance checkbox, not a control.

quiz.q: The best measure of awareness training effectiveness is…
choices: A change in behavior, such as increased phishing reporting rates and lower click rates over time
quiz.explain: Report rate is the metric most teams forget. A user who reports is a sensor; a user who stays silent is a blind spot.

quiz.q: Data retention schedules exist because…
choices: Keeping data longer than needed increases breach impact and legal exposure, while deleting too early can violate law
quiz.explain: Retention is a two-sided risk. The answer is a documented schedule, followed.

quiz.q: Labeling data supports…
choices: Automated enforcement — DLP, access rules, and retention can act on a label but cannot guess classification
quiz.explain: Classification is the decision, labeling makes the decision machine-readable, tooling enforces it.

lessons.title: Configuration management and patching
lessons.objective: Explain baselines, inventory, and patch management as the operational core of security.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Windows Update for Business

lessons.lab: Build a patch procedure for the lab and follow it once: inventory what needs patching (hypervisor, Windows Server, two clients, Ubuntu, nginx, pfSense if installed), define a schedule, patch a pilot machine first, verify services still work, then patch the rest, and record the date and version of each. Repeat monthly. This document is directly reusable for a real client.

quiz.q: Patching a pilot group first exists to…
choices: Catch a bad update before it reaches every machine
quiz.explain: Vendor updates break things. Rings — pilot, broad, critical — are how you get patched fast without gambling.

quiz.q: A configuration baseline is valuable mainly because…
choices: It defines the known-good state, which makes unauthorized drift detectable
quiz.explain: Detection requires a reference. This is the thread connecting hardening, monitoring, and incident response.

quiz.q: Emergency out-of-band patching is justified when…
choices: A vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild against systems you expose — check CISA KEV
Never; always wait for the window
quiz.explain: Active exploitation changes the math. Your change process should already contain an emergency path with the same rigor, compressed.

lessons.title: Turning CC into leverage
lessons.objective: Use the certification deliberately — resume placement, LinkedIn, ISC2 chapter membership, and the CISSP path it starts.
lessons.lab: Three actions this week: add CC to your resume certifications section with the date earned; update LinkedIn and turn on recruiter visibility for security titles; find the nearest ISC2 chapter or local ISSA/OWASP group and put the next meeting on your calendar. Then log your first CPE credits from the Academy work you have already done — most learners forget CPEs exist until renewal panic.

quiz.q: CPE credits are earned by…
choices: Only by taking paid vendor courses
Documented professional development — courses, conferences, chapter meetings, reading, volunteering — logged with evidence
quiz.explain: Log as you go, with dates and proof. Reconstructing a year of CPEs the week before renewal is miserable and error-prone.

quiz.q: Attending a local chapter meeting is valuable primarily because…
choices: Local practitioners are how entry-level people actually get referred into their first security role
quiz.explain: The referral path beats the application portal at almost every stage of a career, and most of all at the start.

quiz.q: On a resume, CC should appear…
choices: As the headline qualification above everything
In a certifications section alongside Security+ with dates, supported by the projects that prove you can apply it
quiz.explain: Certifications get you screened in; projects get you hired. Keep both on the page and let the projects carry the weight.

courses.title: SOC Analyst Foundations
courses.summary: The hands-on half of Phase 2. Work TryHackMe Pre-Security, Cyber Security 101, and SOC Level 1, back it with Hack The Box Academy fundamentals, and finish investigations on LetsDefend or Blue Team Labs Online until triage feels routine.
outcomes: Triage an alert from queue to verdict with a written justification
Read email headers, PCAPs, and Windows event logs fluently
Map observed activity to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques
Complete TryHackMe SOC Level 1 and a run of LetsDefend or BTLO investigations
Write investigation notes a senior analyst can act on without asking you questions

sections.title: The SOC and the analyst's day

lessons.title: How a SOC actually works
lessons.objective: Describe tiers, shift handover, the alert queue, SLAs, escalation, and where a Tier 1 analyst's authority ends.
lessons.lab: Create a TryHackMe account and complete the Pre-Security path if you have not already, then start Cyber Security 101. As you go, keep a single running notes file in your repo with one heading per room and three bullets: what the room taught, the command or tool that was new, and one sentence you could say in an interview about it. This notes file is the deliverable for the entire course.

quiz.q: A Tier 1 analyst's core responsibility is to…
choices: Triage alerts quickly and accurately, resolve the routine ones, and escalate the rest with context
quiz.explain: Speed plus accuracy plus good escalation notes. Doing Tier 2 work badly is worse than escalating well.

quiz.q: Mean time to detect and mean time to respond measure…
choices: How long it takes to notice an incident and how long to contain it — the two numbers a SOC is judged on
quiz.explain: Every process improvement you propose should tie back to reducing one of these two numbers.

quiz.q: Good shift handover includes…
choices: Open investigations with current hypothesis, what was ruled out, what is pending, and who is waiting on whom
A list of everyone who was late
quiz.explain: What was ruled out is the part everyone omits and the next analyst most needs.

lessons.title: Alert triage: a repeatable method
lessons.objective: Apply a consistent triage process — what fired, what is the asset, what is the user, what happened before and after, what is the verdict — and write it down the same way every time.

resources.label: LetsDefend — SOC analyst training platform (free tier)

lessons.lab: Write your personal triage template as a Markdown file with fixed headings: Alert, Asset, User, Timeline, Evidence, ATT&CK mapping, Verdict (true positive / false positive / benign true positive), Actions taken, Escalation. Then work five LetsDefend or BTLO alerts using it with no deviation. Commit all five completed templates. Consistency is what separates an analyst from someone clicking around.

quiz.q: A benign true positive is…
choices: An alert that fired on nothing
Real activity that matched the detection but was authorized — an admin running the tool legitimately
quiz.explain: The activity happened; the intent was legitimate. Recording it as a false positive corrupts your tuning and hides future abuse.

quiz.q: The first question in triage should be…
choices: What exactly did the detection match on, and on which asset and user?
quiz.explain: Understand the signal before reacting to it. Half of all false positives die at this question.

quiz.q: Closing an alert without documenting why is harmful because…
choices: The same alert will be re-triaged from scratch by the next analyst, and a pattern across alerts becomes invisible
quiz.explain: Your notes are the institutional memory. Three identical closures with notes reveal a tuning opportunity; three without reveal nothing.

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK as a common language
lessons.objective: Map observed behavior to tactics and techniques, and use ATT&CK to reason about what an attacker would do next.
lessons.lab: Take the attack chain you will run later in the SIEM course — phishing document, PowerShell execution, credential dumping, lateral movement over SMB, data staged and exfiltrated — and map each step in ATT&CK Navigator. Export the layer JSON to your repo. Then, for each technique, list one data source that would detect it. You have just designed a detection strategy.

quiz.q: In ATT&CK, a tactic represents…
choices: The attacker's goal at that stage, such as Initial Access or Persistence
quiz.explain: Tactics are the why, techniques are the how, procedures are the specific implementation. Know all three words.

quiz.q: The practical value of mapping alerts to ATT&CK is…
choices: It shows which parts of the kill chain you can and cannot see, exposing coverage gaps
quiz.explain: Coverage mapping turns a pile of detections into a defensible strategy — and drives your next detection engineering work.

quiz.q: You observe T1003 (OS Credential Dumping). The most likely next tactic is…
choices: Lateral Movement using the stolen credentials
quiz.explain: Credentials are stolen to be used. Predicting the next move is how you turn detection into containment.

lessons.title: Reading headers and authentication results
lessons.objective: Parse Received chains, Return-Path, and SPF/DKIM/DMARC results to decide whether a message is what it claims.
lessons.lab: Collect three phishing emails and one legitimate marketing email. For each, produce a header analysis: originating IP and its reputation, the Received chain read bottom to top, SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, From versus Return-Path mismatch, and Reply-To redirection. Write the verdict and the single strongest indicator for each. Include the legitimate one deliberately — knowing what normal looks like is the harder half.

quiz.q: The Received headers should be read…
choices: Bottom to top — the oldest hop is at the bottom
quiz.explain: Each hop prepends its own header. The bottom is the origin, and the hops above it can be forged only up to the first trusted server.

quiz.q: DMARC adds what that SPF and DKIM lack alone?
choices: Alignment between the visible From domain and the authenticated domain, plus a published policy and reporting
quiz.explain: Alignment is the key word. SPF can pass for an envelope domain that has nothing to do with the From address the user sees.

quiz.q: A Reply-To that differs from From most often indicates…
choices: An attempt to route replies to an attacker-controlled mailbox — very common in business email compromise
quiz.explain: Mailing lists do it legitimately, which is why it is an indicator and not a verdict. Weigh it with the rest.

lessons.title: Safely analyzing attachments and URLs
lessons.objective: Detonate and inspect suspicious files and links without infecting yourself, using hashes, sandboxes, and static inspection.
lessons.lab: Using only the isolated lab VM and public sandboxes, analyze the EICAR file and two real phishing URLs from your spam: compute SHA-256, check VirusTotal (search by hash, do not upload client data), run the URL through URLScan, capture the final landing page and any credential form, and record the hosting provider and certificate details. Write a five-line summary with an IOC list: hashes, domains, IPs, URLs.

quiz.q: Why search VirusTotal by hash rather than uploading the file, when the file came from a client?
choices: Uploading makes the file available to other subscribers — a confidential document would be disclosed
quiz.explain: Uploading client data to a public sandbox is a real data-leak incident that analysts cause regularly. Search first, upload only when appropriate.

quiz.q: A file with zero VirusTotal detections is…
choices: Unknown — new or targeted malware is often undetected at first, so behavior still matters
quiz.explain: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Zero detections on a file that also arrived unexpectedly is itself suspicious.

quiz.q: An indicator of compromise is most useful when you…
choices: Sweep the whole environment for it — other victims of the same campaign are the point
quiz.explain: One confirmed phish means the same campaign hit other mailboxes. Scoping is the step that turns triage into incident response.

lessons.title: The phishing walkthrough you will use in interviews
lessons.objective: Produce a polished end-to-end phishing investigation write-up you can narrate in five minutes.
lessons.lab: Write the single best investigation you have done as a public portfolio piece: the alert, the header analysis, the URL and attachment analysis, the scoping query you would run to find other recipients, containment actions (block sender, sinkhole domain, reset credentials for anyone who submitted them), the IOC table, and the lessons learned. Redact anything real. Publish it to your GitHub portfolio and rehearse the five-minute verbal version.

quiz.q: If a user entered credentials on the phishing page, the first containment action is…
choices: Reset the password and revoke active sessions and tokens — a reset alone does not kill an existing session
quiz.explain: Session and refresh tokens survive a password reset. Attackers rely on exactly that gap.

quiz.q: Scoping a phishing campaign means…
choices: Searching mail and proxy logs for every other recipient, click, and credential submission tied to the same indicators
quiz.explain: The reported email is one sample of a campaign. The unreported ones are the incident.

quiz.q: The write-up's most valuable section to a hiring manager is…
choices: Your reasoning — why you reached the verdict and what you would do next
quiz.explain: Tools change. Reasoning is what they are hiring. Make your thinking visible on the page.

lessons.title: Windows event logs for analysts
lessons.objective: Find and interpret the Windows events that matter: logon types, process creation, service installation, and log tampering.

resources.label: Microsoft — Security monitoring recommendations for audit events
Ultimate Windows Security — event ID encyclopedia

lessons.lab: Enable process creation auditing with command line (Event 4688 plus the command-line policy) on LAB-WS01. Run ten commands, some ordinary and some suspicious-looking (whoami, net user, nltest, systeminfo, powershell -enc with a harmless base64 string). Find every one in the event log using Get-WinEvent with an XPath filter, and build a table of Event ID, logon type, process, parent process, and why a SOC would care.

quiz.q: Logon type 3 indicates…
choices: Network logon, such as accessing a file share
quiz.explain: Type 2 is interactive, 3 network, 10 RemoteInteractive (RDP), 5 service. Type 10 from an unusual source is a lateral movement signal.

quiz.q: Parent process matters because…
