choices: Winword.exe spawning powershell.exe is a classic malicious pattern that the child process alone does not reveal
quiz.explain: Process lineage is the heart of endpoint detection. Normal parents for a process are as important as the process itself.

quiz.q: Event 4688 without command-line auditing enabled gives you…
choices: The process name only — the arguments, where the intent lives, are missing
quiz.explain: Enable Include command line in process creation events. Without it, powershell.exe tells you almost nothing.

lessons.title: Network evidence: PCAP and flow
lessons.objective: Use Wireshark and Zeek-style flow data to answer who talked to whom, when, how much, and about what.

resources.label: Wireshark — user guide and sample captures

lessons.lab: Work two exercises from Malware-Traffic-Analysis.net end to end. For each, answer in writing: infected host IP and hostname, the user account, the timeline of the infection, the malicious domains and IPs, what family it looks like, and the evidence for each conclusion. Use Statistics > Conversations to find the beaconing pattern before you read any packet payload.

quiz.q: Beaconing shows up in flow data as…
choices: Small, regular connections to the same destination at near-constant intervals
quiz.explain: Regularity is the tell. Jitter makes it harder but rarely removes the pattern entirely.

quiz.q: With fully encrypted traffic, useful evidence still includes…
choices: Destination, timing, volume, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, certificate details, and SNI
quiz.explain: Metadata carries enormous signal. This is why flow logs remain valuable when payload inspection is impossible.

quiz.q: A workstation making direct DNS queries to an external resolver in an environment with internal DNS is…
choices: Worth investigating — it bypasses internal logging and filtering and may indicate tunneling or malware
quiz.explain: Policy should force DNS through internal resolvers. The exception is the finding.

lessons.title: Hack The Box Academy fundamentals
lessons.objective: Back the TryHackMe work with HTB Academy's information security foundations so both attacker and defender vocabulary are solid.

resources.label: Hack The Box Academy — Information Security Foundations path

lessons.lab: Work the HTB Academy foundational modules on Linux fundamentals, Windows fundamentals, and networking until the tier is complete. Keep the same three-bullet notes per module. Then set a weekly rhythm you can actually sustain: two evenings of platform work, one evening of write-up, every week for the rest of Phase 2. Put it on the calendar as recurring events.

quiz.q: Why should a defender study offensive material?
choices: To switch to the red lane
You cannot detect what you do not understand — detections are written from attacker behavior
quiz.explain: Every good detection engineer can perform the attack they detect. That is the whole argument for the lab attack chain.

quiz.q: The most common reason people stall on these platforms is…
choices: No fixed schedule — progress depends on motivation instead of routine
quiz.explain: Two fixed evenings a week beats occasional six-hour binges. Consistency is the entire strategy.

quiz.q: Write-ups matter because…
choices: They convert completed rooms into evidence and force you to articulate what you learned
quiz.explain: A finished room proves nothing to an employer. A write-up of it proves both skill and communication.

lessons.title: Using threat intelligence without drowning in it
lessons.objective: Distinguish strategic, operational, and tactical intelligence, and apply an IOC feed to a real question.

resources.label: MISP — open source threat intelligence platform

lessons.lab: Pick one active ransomware group from a public report. Build a one-page intelligence profile: initial access methods, tools used, ATT&CK techniques, and published IOCs. Then answer the operational question: given your lab and the logging you have, which of their techniques would you currently detect, and which would you miss? The gap list is your detection backlog.

quiz.q: The pyramid of pain says the most painful indicators for an attacker to change are…
quiz.explain: Hashes change in seconds; behavior is expensive to change. Detections built on TTPs survive far longer.

quiz.q: Strategic threat intelligence is aimed at…
choices: Decision makers — trends and risk to inform investment, not individual alerts
quiz.explain: Know your audience. Feeding a board strategic reporting and a SOC tactical indicators is the difference between useful and ignored.

quiz.q: Blindly importing a large IOC feed into a SIEM usually produces…
choices: Alert noise from stale and low-confidence indicators that erodes trust in the whole system
quiz.explain: Curate by confidence and relevance, and expire indicators. Noise is how detection programs die.

lessons.title: Threat hunting with a hypothesis
lessons.objective: Run a structured hunt: state a hypothesis, choose data, query, analyze, and produce either a detection or a documented negative result.
lessons.lab: Hunt in your own lab: hypothesis — an attacker has established persistence through a scheduled task or run key. Query every endpoint for scheduled tasks and autoruns, baseline what is normal, and identify anything unexplained. Document the hunt formally: hypothesis, data sources, queries used, findings, and outcome (new detection, tuning change, or a clean negative result). A negative result documented is a real deliverable.

quiz.q: A hunt that finds nothing is…
choices: A valid outcome that increases confidence and often exposes logging gaps you did not know you had
A failed hunt to be hidden
quiz.explain: The second-best hunt outcome is discovering you could not have found it anyway. That becomes a logging requirement.

quiz.q: Hunting differs from alerting because hunting is…
choices: Human-driven and hypothesis-led, looking for what the existing detections would miss
quiz.explain: Alerts catch the known. Hunting is the deliberate search for the unknown, and its output should be new alerts.

quiz.q: The prerequisite for effective hunting is…
choices: Knowing what normal looks like in your environment
quiz.explain: Anomaly detection requires a baseline. Spend the first hunts building one.

lessons.title: Handover, metrics, and working in a team
lessons.objective: Write notes and metrics that make you the analyst everyone wants on the other shift.

resources.label: NIST SP 800-61r2 — coordination and information sharing

lessons.lab: Take your five completed LetsDefend or BTLO investigations and produce a weekly SOC report as a senior analyst would read it: alert volume by type, true positive rate, top three noisy detections with a tuning proposal for each, one notable investigation summarized in five lines, and the hours you spent. This single artifact demonstrates more job readiness than any certificate.

quiz.q: A detection producing 95% false positives should be…
choices: Left alone; it might catch something
Tuned with a documented change, or retired — untrusted alerts get ignored, including the 5% that matter
quiz.explain: Alert fatigue is a genuine security failure mode. Propose the tuning with data, and record what you changed.

quiz.q: The most useful metric for a small SOC to track first is…
choices: Time from alert to verdict, and the true positive rate per detection
quiz.explain: Measure what you want to improve. Packet counts change nothing about how the team works.

quiz.q: When you are unsure about a verdict, the right move is…
choices: Close it as false positive to keep the queue clean
Escalate with your analysis, your uncertainty stated plainly, and what you already ruled out
quiz.explain: Stating uncertainty clearly is a senior behavior. Silent closures to protect metrics are how breaches get missed.

lessons.title: Complete the TryHackMe SOC Level 1 path
lessons.objective: Finish the full path and consolidate every module into one revision document.
lessons.lab: Finish SOC Level 1 completely, including the capstone rooms. Then write a single consolidated revision document organized by function — email, endpoint, network, SIEM, threat intel, incident response — pulling the best command, query, and insight from every room into the right section. Six pages maximum. This becomes your reference sheet on the job.

quiz.q: The best time to write the consolidated notes is…
choices: As you go, then consolidated at the end while the material is fresh
Only if you fail an interview
quiz.explain: Notes written later are thinner and wrong in places. Consolidation at the end is for structure, not recall.

quiz.q: Completing a learning path proves…
choices: That you can do the job unsupervised
Familiarity with the tools and concepts — the proof of capability is your write-ups and your reasoning in interviews
Equivalent to two years of experience
quiz.explain: Do not oversell platform completion, and do not undersell it either. Pair it with artifacts.

quiz.q: The capstone rooms matter most because…
choices: They force you to combine skills under ambiguity, which is exactly what real alerts do
They are required for the certificate
quiz.explain: Isolated skills are easy. Unlabeled problems are the job.

lessons.title: Build the portfolio of investigations
lessons.objective: Publish five polished investigations that demonstrate range: phishing, malware on an endpoint, suspicious logon, network anomaly, and a hunt.
lessons.lab: Create a public repo named security-investigations. Publish five write-ups, one per category, each under 900 words with a consistent structure: scenario, evidence, analysis, verdict, containment and recommendations, ATT&CK mapping, IOCs. Add a README that indexes them and states the tools used. Link the repo from your resume and LinkedIn. Five good write-ups beat twenty rooms completed.

quiz.q: Write-ups from training platforms should avoid…
choices: Publishing flags, answers, or solution spoilers where the platform's rules forbid it
quiz.explain: Respect each platform's write-up policy. Describe method and reasoning rather than dumping answers.

quiz.q: The README of a portfolio repo should…
choices: Index the investigations, state the skills demonstrated, and let a reader find the best one in ten seconds
quiz.explain: Assume ten seconds of attention. Make the strongest piece obvious and easy to reach.

quiz.q: Range across categories matters because…
choices: It shows you can work the whole queue, not just the one alert type you practiced
quiz.explain: SOC queues are mixed. Demonstrate breadth deliberately.

lessons.title: Ready check: a timed mock shift
lessons.objective: Prove readiness by working a simulated shift under time pressure and producing shippable documentation.
lessons.lab: Block three hours. Work the LetsDefend alert queue as though it were a real shift: triage every alert you can, use your template every time, escalate what needs escalation with written context, and finish with a handover note for the imaginary next shift. Record how many alerts you closed, your accuracy, and where you got stuck. Repeat monthly until the pace feels normal.

quiz.q: Under time pressure, the first thing to protect is…
choices: Accuracy and documentation on the alerts you do work
quiz.explain: A wrongly closed true positive costs far more than a queue that runs long. Speed comes from familiarity, not from cutting analysis.

quiz.q: If the queue is longer than your shift, you should…
choices: Prioritize by asset criticality and alert severity, and hand over the rest with context
quiz.explain: Triage means prioritizing under constraint. Silent mass closure is the failure mode that ends careers.

quiz.q: The mock shift is worth repeating monthly because…
choices: Speed under pressure is a trained skill, and the exercise keeps exposing the gaps your notes have not closed
quiz.explain: Deliberate, timed practice is what converts knowledge into performance.

courses.title: SIEM in the Home Lab
courses.summary: Stand up Wazuh or Security Onion, forward Windows domain logs into it, attack your own lab from Kali, and write up exactly what the SIEM caught and what it missed. The most convincing single project on an entry-level security resume.
outcomes: Deploy a SIEM and onboard Windows and Linux log sources
Verify log flow and diagnose the gaps that silently break detection
Execute a realistic attack chain against your own lab from Kali
Produce a detection coverage report mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
Publish a write-up that shows both the detections that fired and the ones that did not

lessons.title: Wazuh, Security Onion, or Splunk free
lessons.objective: Pick a platform for the right reasons and size the VM so it does not fall over.

resources.label: Splunk Free — download (verify current ingest limit)

lessons.lab: Write a decision record as docs/decisions/002-siem.md: which platform, three reasons, and the resource cost. Wazuh is the recommended default — it is free, includes agents, file integrity monitoring, and ready-made rules, and runs in about 8 GB of RAM. Security Onion gives you Zeek and Suricata network visibility but wants 16 GB. Splunk teaches the query language employers ask about but limits ingest. Choose, size the VM, and record what you gave up.

quiz.q: The main practical constraint on a home lab SIEM is…
choices: RAM — search and indexing engines are memory hungry
quiz.explain: Under-provisioned SIEMs swap, fall behind, and drop events. Give it the RAM before you blame the software.

quiz.q: The strongest argument for learning Splunk specifically is…
choices: It is free forever at any volume
SPL appears in a large share of SOC job descriptions, so the query language itself is a hiring signal
It is the easiest to install
quiz.explain: The skill is transferable even when the tool is not. Learn one query language deeply and the next is faster.

quiz.q: Security Onion adds what that Wazuh alone does not?
choices: Full network visibility via Zeek and Suricata, plus PCAP retention
quiz.explain: Endpoint plus network is the complete picture. Many labs run Wazuh for endpoint and add Zeek separately.

lessons.title: Install the SIEM and secure it
lessons.objective: Deploy the server, place it correctly on the lab network, and lock down access to it.
lessons.lab: Build the SIEM VM (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk) at 10.10.10.50 on the lab network. Install Wazuh with the quickstart script. Then secure it as you would in production: change default credentials, restrict dashboard access to your management workstation, enable HTTPS with the certificate you generated in Security+ lesson 1-3, and snapshot as siem-clean. Document the admin password location — the password manager, not the README.

quiz.q: A SIEM is a high-value target because…
choices: It holds the evidence of everything, and an attacker who controls it controls what defenders can see
It uses a lot of RAM
quiz.explain: Compromising the SIEM is both intelligence and anti-forensics. Harden it before you onboard anything.

quiz.q: Storage sizing for a SIEM is driven mainly by…
choices: Events per second multiplied by average event size multiplied by retention period
quiz.explain: EPS times size times retention. Know this formula — it appears in interviews and in every budget conversation.

quiz.q: Taking a snapshot named siem-clean before onboarding is useful because…
choices: Onboarding mistakes and rule experiments are easy to undo without a full reinstall
quiz.explain: The habit from the Home Lab course carries forward. Snapshot before every risky configuration change.

lessons.title: Onboard Windows and Linux log sources
lessons.objective: Install agents, forward the right channels, and prove events are arriving.
lessons.lab: Deploy the Wazuh agent to LAB-DC01, LAB-WS01, LAB-WS02, and the Ubuntu server. On Windows, forward the Security, System, Application, Sysmon (once installed), and Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational channels. On Linux, forward auth.log and the nginx access log. Then verify: generate one distinctive event on each host (a failed logon, a sudo command) and find it in the dashboard within 60 seconds. Record the search that found it.

quiz.q: The most common cause of an agent showing connected but sending no events is…
choices: The log channel is not configured for collection, or the local audit policy never generates the event
The SIEM is out of disk
The agent is the wrong version
quiz.explain: Connected is not collecting. Always verify end to end with a deliberately generated event.

quiz.q: Sysmon adds value over the default Windows logs by…
choices: Recording process creation with hashes and parent lineage, network connections, and registry changes in far richer detail
quiz.explain: Sysmon plus a good configuration (SwiftOnSecurity's is the common starting point) is the single biggest endpoint visibility upgrade available for free.

quiz.q: Time synchronization across log sources matters because…
choices: Correlating events across hosts requires a common timeline; clock skew makes causality impossible to establish
quiz.explain: Same reason Kerberos cares. Point everything at the DC or an NTP source, and record UTC.

lessons.title: Sysmon and a real endpoint configuration
lessons.objective: Install Sysmon with a curated configuration and understand what each event ID gives you.
lessons.lab: Install Sysmon on both Windows clients and the DC using the SwiftOnSecurity configuration. Confirm the Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational channel is forwarded. Then build a reference table of the event IDs you will actually use: 1 process creation, 3 network connection, 7 image loaded, 8 CreateRemoteThread, 11 file created, 13 registry value set, 22 DNS query. For each, write one attacker behavior it exposes.

quiz.q: Sysmon Event ID 1 is especially valuable because it records…
choices: Process creation with full command line, hashes, and parent process
quiz.explain: Command line plus lineage plus hash is the foundation of most endpoint detections.

quiz.q: Sysmon Event ID 22 (DNS query) helps detect…
choices: Command and control beaconing and DNS tunneling, by revealing which process resolved which domain
quiz.explain: Process-attributed DNS is powerful: your network resolver sees the query but not which process made it.

quiz.q: Running Sysmon with the default configuration is discouraged because…
choices: The default is effectively everything or nothing — a curated config filters the noise so the SIEM stays usable
quiz.explain: Tuning at the source is cheaper than tuning at the SIEM. Start from a community config and adjust.

lessons.title: Dashboards, searches, and saved queries
lessons.objective: Build the handful of searches and views you would actually open at the start of a shift.
lessons.lab: Build and save six searches: failed logons by account in the last hour; successful logon after five or more failures for the same account; new service installed; account added to a privileged group; PowerShell with encoded command; outbound connection to a non-lab IP. Pin them into a single dashboard called Morning Check. Screenshot it. Then write what each one would look like as noise versus as a real finding.

quiz.q: The search successful logon after repeated failures detects…
choices: A user who forgot their password only
Possible successful brute force or password spray — the transition is what matters, not either event alone
quiz.explain: This is correlation in its simplest form and a genuinely high-value detection. A forgetful user is the false positive you tune around.

quiz.q: A dashboard is most useful when it…
choices: Answers a small set of specific questions you ask regularly
quiz.explain: Dashboards that show everything get ignored. Build for a question, not for decoration.

quiz.q: Saved searches matter because…
choices: Repeatability — the same query every time makes changes in the environment visible, and they become scheduled alerts later
quiz.explain: Today's saved search is tomorrow's alert rule. Write them as if they will be promoted.

lessons.title: Alert rules and tuning
lessons.objective: Convert searches into alert rules with thresholds and exclusions, and tune the noisy ones honestly.
lessons.lab: Promote three of your saved searches into alert rules with sensible thresholds. Run the lab normally for 48 hours and count how many alerts each produces. For every noisy rule, write a tuning change — narrower scope, a time window, an exclusion for a known service account — and document the reason. Never tune by excluding the thing you were trying to detect; write down why each exclusion is safe.

quiz.q: The risk of tuning by broad exclusion is…
choices: You may exclude exactly the activity an attacker will use, creating a permanent blind spot nobody remembers
quiz.explain: Every exclusion needs a written justification and a review date. Attackers love service account exclusions.

quiz.q: Sigma rules are useful because they are…
choices: Vendor-neutral — written once and converted to Splunk, Elastic, Wazuh, or Sentinel queries
quiz.explain: Sigma is to detections what ATT&CK is to behavior: a shared language. It comes back in the Detection Engineering course.

quiz.q: A good alert rule includes…
choices: The query, the rationale, the expected true positive rate, the ATT&CK mapping, and what the analyst should do next
quiz.explain: An alert without response guidance creates work instead of reducing it. Write the triage steps into the rule.

lessons.title: Kali on the lab network
lessons.objective: Add a Kali VM to the isolated lab and perform reconnaissance that your SIEM should notice.

resources.label: Kali Linux — downloads and VM images

lessons.lab: Build the Kali VM at 10.10.10.66 on the isolated network only — never bridged to your home LAN. Run a full TCP scan of the lab subnet with nmap -sS -p- and a service scan of the DC. Then go to the SIEM: did anything fire? Record exactly what you saw, what you did not, and why. Most default configurations see very little host-based evidence of a scan, which is the lesson.

quiz.q: Kali must stay on the isolated network because…
choices: It runs slowly on bridged networks
Attack tooling on your home LAN can hit family devices and, in some cases, your ISP's network — legally and practically a bad idea
It would not reach the lab
quiz.explain: Only ever attack systems you own and have isolated. This rule does not bend.

quiz.q: A port scan is often invisible to endpoint logging because…
choices: Scanning touches the network stack without creating process or logon events the host audits by default
Scans are too fast to log
quiz.explain: This is why network sensors exist. It is also the first coverage gap your report should name.

quiz.q: Which SYN scan characteristic makes it comparatively quiet on the target?
choices: It never completes the TCP handshake, so many applications never log a connection
It sends only one packet in total
quiz.explain: No full connection, no application log entry. Firewall and flow logs still see it.

lessons.title: The attack chain: access, execution, persistence
lessons.objective: Run a realistic multi-stage attack against your own lab and capture the telemetry at every stage.

resources.label: Atomic Red Team — small tests mapped to ATT&CK

lessons.lab: Use Atomic Red Team on LAB-WS01 to execute one atomic test per tactic, in order: T1059.001 PowerShell execution, T1053.005 scheduled task persistence, T1087 account discovery, T1003 credential dumping simulation, T1021.002 SMB lateral movement to WS02. Record the exact time of each test in a table. Then go to the SIEM and, for each technique, note whether an alert fired, whether the raw telemetry exists but no rule matched, or whether nothing was recorded at all. That three-way distinction is the entire deliverable.

quiz.q: The three-way outcome — alerted, telemetry present but no rule, nothing recorded — matters because…
choices: The fixes are completely different: tune the rule, write a rule, or add a log source
quiz.explain: Most teams only count alerts and never discover the middle case, which is usually the cheapest to fix.

quiz.q: Atomic Red Team tests are preferable to real malware in a lab because…
choices: They reproduce the technique safely and repeatably, with documented cleanup, and will not spread
quiz.explain: Safe, documented, reversible. Run real malware only in a lab you are prepared to lose entirely.

quiz.q: Recording the exact time of each test is essential because…
choices: Without your ground truth timeline you cannot tell a missed detection from a detection you simply did not find
quiz.explain: Ground truth is what makes the exercise a measurement rather than an impression.

lessons.title: Detection gaps and closing them
lessons.objective: Turn every miss into either a new rule, a new log source, or a documented accepted gap.
lessons.lab: For each technique that went undetected, do one of three things and record which: write a detection rule (start from a Sigma rule and convert it), add the missing log source, or write an accepted-gap note explaining why detection is impractical here. Re-run the full attack chain afterward and produce a before/after coverage table. Aim to move at least four techniques from missed to detected.

quiz.q: A detection you wrote should always be validated by…
choices: Re-running the attack and confirming the rule fires, then confirming it does not fire during normal operations
quiz.explain: Both halves matter. An untested rule is a belief, and a rule that fires constantly is worse than none.

quiz.q: An accepted gap should be documented because…
choices: An undocumented gap is indistinguishable from an oversight, and future staff will assume coverage that does not exist
quiz.explain: Explicit risk acceptance is a professional act. Silent gaps are how organizations are surprised.

quiz.q: Converting a community Sigma rule to your SIEM still requires…
choices: Field mapping to your log sources and tuning to your environment's normal
quiz.explain: Sigma standardizes logic, not your field names or your baseline. Expect real work per rule.

sections.title: Write it up and ship it

lessons.title: The coverage report
lessons.objective: Produce a professional detection coverage report with an ATT&CK Navigator layer.
lessons.lab: Write a report a manager could read: executive summary in five sentences, environment description with the network diagram, methodology, results table (technique, executed at, telemetry, detection, outcome), an ATT&CK Navigator layer coloring detected versus undetected, the fixes you applied, remaining gaps with recommendations, and an appendix of the rules you wrote. Keep the body under 2,000 words. Export the Navigator layer JSON into the repo.

quiz.q: The executive summary should state…
choices: What you tested, what the coverage was before and after, and the top two remaining risks — in plain language
quiz.explain: Assume the reader stops after the summary. Put the decision-relevant facts there.

quiz.q: A Navigator layer is a good artifact because…
choices: It communicates coverage and gaps at a glance in a format the industry already reads
quiz.explain: Shared visual vocabulary. It also makes progress over time obvious when you re-test in six months.

quiz.q: Reporting the gaps you could not close is…
choices: The most credible part of it — every real environment has gaps, and naming them shows judgment
quiz.explain: A report with 100% coverage and no gaps reads as either untested or dishonest to anyone experienced.

lessons.title: Publish and present the project
lessons.objective: Turn the project into a portfolio piece and a five-minute talk.

resources.label: GitHub Docs — writing a good README

lessons.lab: Publish a repo called siem-lab: README with the architecture diagram and a one-paragraph summary, the report, the detection rules, the Navigator layer, and screenshots with sensitive values redacted. Then rehearse the five-minute version out loud: what you built, what you attacked it with, what you found, what you fixed, and what you would do next with more time. Record it once and watch it back.

quiz.q: The strongest closing line of the five-minute version is…
choices: What I would do next with more time and why — it shows you understand the work is never finished
quiz.explain: Interviewers probe for judgment about what matters next. Have that answer prepared.

quiz.q: Screenshots in a public repo must be checked for…
choices: Real hostnames, public IPs, tokens, usernames, and anything identifying your actual home network
quiz.explain: Redact before publishing. Private lab RFC 1918 addresses are fine; credentials and real identifiers are not.

quiz.q: This project belongs on your resume as…
choices: A project entry with a link and a measurable result, such as detection coverage raised from 3 of 12 techniques to 9 of 12
quiz.explain: Never inflate a project into employment. Do quantify it — numbers make a project entry credible.

lessons.title: Keep it running
lessons.objective: Turn a one-time project into an ongoing lab practice that keeps producing evidence of skill.
lessons.lab: Set a monthly recurring routine and put it on the calendar: run three new atomic tests, review alert volume and tune one noisy rule, verify all agents are still reporting, and add a paragraph to a running CHANGELOG in the siem-lab repo. Enable file integrity monitoring on the DC's SYSVOL and one Linux directory this month. A repo with twelve months of dated entries is far more persuasive than a repo with one big commit.

quiz.q: Agents silently stopping is common. The control for it is…
choices: An alert on agent heartbeat loss — detection fails silently otherwise
quiz.explain: Monitor the monitoring. A dead sensor looks exactly like a quiet network.

quiz.q: File integrity monitoring on SYSVOL is useful because…
choices: Changes to scripts and policies stored there affect every domain machine, making it a high-value attacker target
quiz.explain: A malicious logon script in SYSVOL runs everywhere. Watch what has leverage.

quiz.q: A dated changelog across many months demonstrates…
choices: Sustained practice and operational discipline — the traits that separate a hobbyist from a hire
quiz.explain: Consistency over time is the rarest and most convincing signal in an entry-level portfolio.

courses.title: Landing the First Security Role
courses.summary: Convert Security+, the SIEM project, and your investigation write-ups into a SOC Analyst I offer. Internal moves, targeted applications, and the phishing walkthrough that carries the technical interview.
outcomes: A security-targeted resume and LinkedIn presence backed by real artifacts
A worked plan for the internal move, which is the highest-probability path
Rehearsed answers for the standard SOC interview questions
A five-minute phishing investigation walkthrough delivered from memory

lessons.title: Titles, levels, and what they actually want
lessons.objective: Identify the entry-level security titles worth applying to and read a job posting for what is genuinely required versus aspirational.

resources.label: LinkedIn Jobs — search SOC Analyst I

lessons.lab: Collect fifteen postings across SOC Analyst I, Security Operations Analyst, Junior Security Administrator, Information Security Analyst, and Security Engineer I. Build a frequency table of every required skill and tool mentioned. Rank them. Then honestly mark which of the top ten you can evidence today with a project or a cert, which you could learn in a month, and which are out of reach. That table is your study plan and your application filter.

quiz.q: A posting asks for three years of experience for a Tier 1 role. You should…
choices: Apply if you meet most of the technical requirements — posted experience minimums are frequently aspirational, especially at Tier 1
quiz.explain: Apply and let them decide. Never falsify experience — a lie found later ends the job and the reference.

quiz.q: Which signal in a posting most reliably indicates a genuine entry-level role?
choices: The word junior in the title only
A described training path, shift structure, and mentorship, rather than a demand for independent incident ownership
quiz.explain: Real Tier 1 roles describe how you will be trained and supervised. Postings demanding independent ownership at entry level are mislabeled.

quiz.q: Security Engineer I differs from SOC Analyst I mainly in that engineering roles…
choices: Build and maintain tooling and controls rather than working an alert queue
quiz.explain: Know which one you want. The SIEM project reads well for both, but you should tailor which half you emphasize.

lessons.title: The internal move
lessons.objective: Plan the transition from your current IT role into security at the same employer, which is the most common route in.
lessons.lab: Write a one-page internal proposal for your current or next employer: the security work you would take on (phishing triage, vulnerability report review, access reviews, onboarding hardening), how many hours a week, what it saves the team, and what you are asking for in return (title change, security tooling access, exam funding). Request a meeting with your manager and deliver it. Make it easy to say yes to.

quiz.q: The internal move usually beats external applications because…
choices: You already have a track record, a reference, and institutional knowledge, which outweigh a thin security resume
quiz.explain: The employer's risk is lower because they know you. That is exactly the barrier external applications hit.

quiz.q: The proposal should lead with…
choices: The problem you will solve for the team
quiz.explain: Frame it as their gain, not your ambition. Your goals belong in the closing paragraph, not the opening.

quiz.q: If the answer is no, the right follow-up is…
choices: Ask what would need to change for it to be a yes, and by when — then work that list and come back
quiz.explain: A no with conditions is a roadmap. A no with no conditions tells you to look outside, which is also useful information.

lessons.title: The security resume rebuild
lessons.objective: Restructure the resume around security evidence without erasing the IT experience that makes you credible.

resources.label: Indeed — search IT Support Specialist and SOC Analyst postings for language

lessons.lab: Rewrite the one-page resume for security: summary naming the target role; Certifications with Security+ and dates; Projects section leading with the SIEM lab (with the coverage number) and the investigations repo; Experience rewritten so help desk work reads in security terms (account provisioning and deprovisioning, MFA enrollment, phishing report handling, patch deployment, asset inventory); Skills grouped by tool. Have one person who hires read it and give you 15 minutes of criticism.

quiz.q: Help desk experience should be described as…
choices: Identity lifecycle work, MFA enrollment, endpoint hardening, and first-line phishing handling — same work, correct vocabulary
quiz.explain: Translate honestly. You did do access management; call it what the industry calls it, without inflating the scope.

quiz.q: The projects section should appear…
choices: Above experience for a career changer, because the projects are the security evidence
quiz.explain: Lead with the strongest evidence for the role you want. Experience still matters and stays on the page.

quiz.q: Including a measurable result in a project bullet matters because…
choices: Numbers make claims checkable and memorable — raised detection coverage from 3 of 12 to 9 of 12 ATT&CK techniques
quiz.explain: Specificity signals that the work actually happened. Vague project bullets read as coursework.

lessons.title: The phishing walkthrough
lessons.objective: Deliver a five-minute phishing investigation from memory, structured so the interviewer can follow every decision.
lessons.lab: Rehearse and time the walkthrough: (1) the alert and how it reached you, (2) header analysis and what it proved, (3) URL and attachment analysis with the tools named, (4) the verdict and the evidence for it, (5) scoping — how you found the other recipients, (6) containment — block, reset, revoke sessions, (7) what you recommended afterward. Five minutes, no notes. Deliver it to two different people and fix the parts where they lost the thread.

quiz.q: The part interviewers most often probe is…
choices: Why you reached your verdict and what would have changed your mind
quiz.explain: They are testing reasoning under uncertainty. Have the counterfactual ready: here is what would have made me escalate instead.

quiz.q: If asked about a step you did not perform, the right answer is…
choices: Say you have not done it, describe how you would approach it, and name what you would need
quiz.explain: Honest gaps plus a method are respected at Tier 1. A confident fabrication is discovered in the follow-up question.

quiz.q: Revoking sessions and tokens after a credential phish matters because…
choices: It is faster than a password reset
A password reset alone leaves existing sessions valid, so the attacker keeps access
quiz.explain: This exact detail is a frequent interview discriminator between candidates who read about it and candidates who did it.

lessons.title: Technical questions you will actually get
lessons.objective: Prepare crisp answers to the recurring SOC interview questions without sounding rehearsed.
lessons.lab: Write and rehearse three-sentence answers to: what happens when you type a URL into a browser; explain TCP handshake and what a SYN flood does; how does Kerberos authentication work at a high level; what is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption; how would you investigate a user reporting a slow machine that might be infected; what is lateral movement and how would you detect it; what does a 4625 followed by a 4624 mean; how do you decide whether an alert is a true positive. Say each one out loud until it is natural.

quiz.q: A three-sentence answer is preferred because…
choices: It shows you can find the level of detail that fits the question, and invites a follow-up rather than filling the silence
quiz.explain: Answer, then stop. The follow-up question is where you demonstrate depth, and it also tells you what they care about.

quiz.q: 4625 followed by 4624 for the same account indicates…
choices: Failed logon(s) followed by a successful one — worth investigating for brute force or a user who finally remembered
quiz.explain: Know the ID pairs cold. They are cheap points in an interview and daily work in the job.

quiz.q: When you do not know an answer, the best response is…
choices: Say you do not know, then reason out loud about how you would find out
Change to a topic you know
quiz.explain: How you handle not knowing is a real evaluation criterion — you will not know things every day on the job.

lessons.title: Offers, shift work, and the first 90 days
lessons.objective: Evaluate an offer realistically — including shift patterns — and plan the first ninety days so you become useful quickly.

resources.label: Bureau of Labor Statistics — Information security analysts

lessons.lab: Build an offer evaluation sheet before you need it: base pay, shift pattern and differential, on-call expectations, training budget and exam funding, tooling you would learn, mentorship structure, and the realistic path to Tier 2. Score two hypothetical offers with it — one higher paying with rotating nights and no training budget, one lower paying with day shift and funded certifications — and write which you would take and why. Then draft your first-90-days plan: learn the environment, ask for the runbooks, shadow, and find one small thing to improve by day 60.

quiz.q: Rotating night shift is worth accepting when…
choices: The role offers real mentorship, funded certifications, and a defined path off nights — trading schedule for career velocity, with an end date
quiz.explain: Nights are common at entry level and physically costly. Accept them with a stated timeline, not indefinitely.

quiz.q: The most valuable thing to ask for in the first week is…
choices: The runbooks, the escalation policy, and permission to shadow a senior analyst
quiz.explain: Learn their process before proposing changes. Credibility earned in month one funds the improvements in month three.

quiz.q: A good day-60 improvement to propose is…
choices: Tuning one noisy detection or documenting an undocumented procedure — small, evidenced, and obviously useful
quiz.explain: Small wins with data behind them build the trust that larger proposals need.

sections.title: The search routine and the community

lessons.title: A weekly application routine you can sustain
lessons.objective: Run a repeatable weekly job-search cycle instead of sporadic bursts of applications.

resources.label: LinkedIn Jobs — saved searches and alerts
USAJOBS — federal and contractor security roles

lessons.lab: Set up the machine: saved searches with email alerts on LinkedIn and Indeed for your five target titles within your commute radius plus remote. Build a tracking spreadsheet with columns for company, role, date applied, source, referral contact, tailored resume version, status, and next action date. Then commit to the weekly rhythm: five tailored applications, two outreach messages, one portfolio improvement. Quality over volume — fifty generic applications lose to five tailored ones.

quiz.q: Tailoring a resume per application means…
choices: Adjusting the summary line and reordering skills and projects to mirror that posting's priorities
Adding every keyword whether true or not
quiz.explain: Ten minutes of reordering, not an hour of rewriting. Keyword stuffing you cannot defend in an interview backfires.

quiz.q: Tracking applications in a spreadsheet matters because…
choices: Follow-up is where offers come from, and without a next-action date you will not follow up
quiz.explain: The follow-up message a week later converts far better than the application itself.

quiz.q: A referral changes your odds mainly because…
choices: It moves your resume from the pile to a human who has a reason to read it
quiz.explain: Referrals get you read, not hired. The interview is still yours to earn.

lessons.title: Showing up: BSides, ISSA, OWASP, and local groups
lessons.objective: Use local security community events as the referral network they actually are.
lessons.lab: Find the nearest BSides, ISSA, OWASP, and DEF CON group meetings and put the next three on your calendar. Attend one this quarter. Go with a specific plan: talk to three people, ask each what their team is struggling with, and follow up on LinkedIn within 48 hours with one useful sentence referencing the conversation. Volunteer at the next BSides — volunteers meet everyone, including the people who hire.

quiz.q: The most effective thing to do at a local security event is…
choices: Ask people about their work and follow up afterward with something useful
Sit at the back and take notes
quiz.explain: Curiosity builds relationships; resumes at a meetup do not. The job conversation comes later and comes to you.

quiz.q: Volunteering at a conference is recommended because…
choices: Volunteers work alongside organizers and speakers, which produces real relationships fast
quiz.explain: It also gives you an easy reason to talk to everyone, which solves the hardest part of networking.

quiz.q: Attendance at chapter meetings also gives you…
choices: CPE credits toward ISC2 and other certification renewals, if you log them
quiz.explain: Log them as you attend. Renewal requirements are much easier to meet when CPEs accumulate passively.

lessons.title: Your public presence
lessons.objective: Make LinkedIn and GitHub do work for you while you sleep.

resources.label: LinkedIn — Open to Work and recruiter visibility settings

lessons.lab: Rebuild both profiles in one sitting. LinkedIn: headline naming the target role and your strongest evidence, an about section written in first person that tells the career-change story in five sentences, featured links to the SIEM lab and investigations repos, Security+ in the certifications section, and recruiter visibility on. GitHub: a profile README that indexes your three best repos with one line each. Then post once about the SIEM project — what you built, what surprised you, what you would do differently.

quiz.q: A LinkedIn headline should contain…
choices: The role you are targeting plus your strongest proof point, because recruiters search on it
quiz.explain: The headline is a search field and a billboard. Make both jobs work: target role, plus evidence.

quiz.q: Posting about your own project is worth doing because…
choices: It creates a public, dated record of your work that hiring managers and connections actually see
quiz.explain: One honest post about real work beats ten reshares. Write it the way you would explain it to a colleague.

quiz.q: What should NOT appear on a public profile or repo?
choices: Employer-identifying details of real incidents, client names, or any internal data
quiz.explain: Discretion is itself a hiring signal. A candidate who leaks their employer's details in a write-up will do it again.

lessons.title: Blue, red, or GRC — an honest comparison
lessons.objective: Compare the three lanes on daily work, hiring volume, pay trajectory, and temperament rather than on which sounds most exciting.
lessons.lab: Build a comparison table with rows for daily work, tools, certifications, typical entry route, local job volume (count real postings in your area for each lane this week), on-call burden, and what a bad day looks like. Fill it from postings and from conversations with people doing the work. Then write your ranked preference with two sentences of reasoning per lane. Revisit it in six months — the answer is allowed to change.

quiz.q: The lane with the largest volume of entry-level roles is generally…
quiz.explain: Defense has the most seats and the clearest entry path. Red team roles are comparatively few and rarely entry level.

quiz.q: GRC suits someone who…
choices: Writes clearly, enjoys structured reasoning about risk, and can hold a room of stakeholders to a standard
quiz.explain: GRC is not a lane for people avoiding technical work — the good ones are technical and persuasive.

quiz.q: Choosing a lane means…
choices: Concentrating effort for the next two or three years; lateral moves between lanes are common later
quiz.explain: Focus beats breadth at this stage. The cross-lane knowledge you already have becomes an advantage later, not a waste.

lessons.title: Try before you commit
lessons.objective: Test each lane with a small, time-boxed project before committing years of study to it.

resources.label: TryHackMe — SOC Level 1 and offensive paths

lessons.lab: Spend one weekend on each lane. Blue: work five LetsDefend alerts and write one investigation. Red: complete two easy Hack The Box machines and write a methodology note. GRC: run a CIS Controls Implementation Group 1 self-assessment against your own home lab and produce a findings report with prioritized recommendations. Rank which weekend you would happily repeat every week for two years. That ranking is worth more than any career quiz.

quiz.q: The best test of a lane is…
choices: Whether the routine daily work still appeals after you have actually done it for a full day
quiz.explain: Every lane has a glamorous version and a Tuesday-afternoon version. Choose based on Tuesday.

quiz.q: A GRC weekend project produces…
choices: A real assessment artifact — findings, evidence, and prioritized recommendations — which is exactly what GRC hiring managers want to see
quiz.explain: GRC portfolios are rare and therefore powerful. A CIS or NIST CSF self-assessment of your own lab is a legitimate sample of work.

quiz.q: If you enjoy all three roughly equally, the sensible default is…
choices: Start blue — the largest hiring volume, and it produces the context that makes red and GRC work better later
Wait until someone decides for you
quiz.explain: Defense gives you environment knowledge that both other lanes build on. It is also the easiest to get paid to learn.

lessons.title: Set the Phase 3 plan
lessons.objective: Commit the lane decision to a dated plan with a certification target, a budget, and a project.

resources.label: CompTIA — continuing education and CEU stacking

lessons.lab: Write the Phase 3 plan on one page: chosen lane, the first certification and target exam month, the estimated cost and who is paying, the weekly study hours you will actually protect, the lab project that will accompany it, and the checkpoint date where you review whether it is working. Enter the certification into the Academy tracker with status Studying and a target date. Share the page with your mentor so someone else knows the date.

quiz.q: A plan with no dates is…
choices: An intention — dates are what convert study into a scheduled exam
quiz.explain: The same rule as Security+: book the exam. An unscheduled certification drifts indefinitely.

quiz.q: Telling someone else your target date helps because…
choices: External accountability substantially raises follow-through, and they can check in when motivation dips
quiz.explain: Cooper and Myles should hold each other to dates. The pairing is one of the biggest advantages of doing this together.

quiz.q: The checkpoint date exists to…
choices: Decide honestly whether the plan is working and change it early rather than abandoning it quietly
quiz.explain: Plans fail silently. A scheduled review turns quitting into a decision you make deliberately or not at all.

courses.title: CompTIA CySA+
courses.summary: The analyst cert that follows Security+ for the blue lane. Behavioral analytics, vulnerability management at scale, incident response, and — the domain people underestimate — reporting and communication. CS0-003 also renews your Security+ through CompTIA CEU stacking.
outcomes: Analyze system and network telemetry for malicious behavior rather than matching signatures
Run a vulnerability management program including scan configuration, prioritization, and validation
Lead the technical half of an incident from detection through post-incident reporting
Write findings and metrics that non-technical stakeholders act on
Pass CS0-003 and renew Security+ automatically with the CEUs

lessons.title: System and network baselines
lessons.objective: Establish what normal looks like for processes, network flows, accounts, and scheduled tasks, so anomalies become visible.
lessons.lab: Build a written baseline of your lab domain: every running service on the DC, every scheduled task on each client, every account and its last logon, every listening port, and normal outbound destinations. Capture it with PowerShell (Get-Service, Get-ScheduledTask, Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate, Get-NetTCPConnection) and save the output to the repo with a date. Repeat monthly and diff. The diff is where findings live.

quiz.q: Behavioral analysis beats signature matching against…
choices: Novel or targeted activity for which no signature exists yet
quiz.explain: Signatures cover the known. Behavior — a service account logging in interactively at 3am — catches what has no signature.

quiz.q: The main challenge of anomaly detection is…
choices: Establishing a trustworthy baseline in an environment that legitimately changes
quiz.explain: If the baseline was captured after a compromise, you baseline the attacker. Baselines need dates and a known-good basis.

quiz.q: A service account with interactive logons should be treated as…
choices: Suspicious — service accounts should authenticate as services, and interactive use often means credential theft or misuse
quiz.explain: High-value detection, low false positive rate once tuned. Pair it with a deny-interactive-logon policy on those accounts.

lessons.title: Malicious activity indicators on endpoints
lessons.objective: Recognize the endpoint patterns CS0-003 tests: abnormal process behavior, unauthorized changes, privilege escalation, and persistence.
lessons.lab: On LAB-WS01, use Autoruns and Process Explorer to inventory every autostart location and every running process with its signature status and parent. Then plant three benign persistence mechanisms yourself (a Run key, a scheduled task, a new service) and find them all again using only the SIEM. Time how long each takes to find and note which was hardest — that one is your detection gap.

quiz.q: An unsigned binary running from %APPDATA% with a parent of winword.exe is…
choices: A strong indicator of malicious document execution warranting immediate investigation
quiz.explain: Location plus signature status plus parent lineage together make the case. Any one alone is weaker.

quiz.q: Which persistence mechanism generally produces the clearest log evidence?
quiz.explain: 7045 is loud and rare. WMI subscriptions and DLL hijacks are far quieter, which is exactly why attackers prefer them.

quiz.q: Unexpected outbound traffic from a host at consistent intervals suggests…
quiz.explain: Backups are also periodic — which is why you compare against the baseline of known scheduled jobs before calling it.

lessons.title: Network and cloud activity analysis
lessons.objective: Interpret flow data, DNS, proxy logs, and cloud audit logs to spot exfiltration, tunneling, and identity abuse.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Entra ID sign-in logs

lessons.lab: Generate and then detect DNS exfiltration in your lab: from LAB-WS01, use a simple script to encode a small file into subdomain queries against a domain your Linux box is authoritative for. Capture the traffic with Zeek or Wireshark, then write the detection logic — query length, entropy, query volume per host per domain, unique subdomain count. Document both the attack and the detection.

quiz.q: DNS tunneling is attractive to attackers because…
choices: DNS is almost always permitted outbound and is often unmonitored, even in restrictive environments
quiz.explain: Low bandwidth, high availability. The detection is behavioral: volume, entropy, and subdomain diversity per domain.

quiz.q: An impossible travel alert in cloud sign-in logs means…
choices: The same identity authenticated from geographically distant locations in less time than travel would allow — possible credential compromise
quiz.explain: VPNs cause false positives, which is why it is an indicator to investigate, not an automatic incident.

quiz.q: Data exfiltration over HTTPS to a legitimate cloud storage provider is hard to catch because…
choices: It is encrypted and the destination is on every allowlist
quiz.explain: The answer is volume anomaly detection and DLP on the endpoint, not blocking the destination.

lessons.title: Tooling: EDR, SOAR, and automation
lessons.objective: Explain what EDR, SOAR, and scripted automation do for an analyst, and automate one real piece of your own workflow.
lessons.lab: Automate your own enrichment: write a PowerShell or Python script that takes an IP or hash and returns a short report — VirusTotal reputation via the free API, WHOIS, geolocation, and whether it appears in your SIEM in the last 7 days. Use it on five indicators from a past investigation and measure the time saved. Commit the script with a README and rate limiting handled properly.

quiz.q: The main risk of automated containment (auto-isolating a host) is…
choices: A false positive can take a critical system offline, so automation needs confidence thresholds and scoping
quiz.explain: Automate enrichment aggressively, automate action carefully. Start with high-confidence detections and non-critical assets.

quiz.q: EDR differs from traditional antivirus mainly by…
choices: Recording rich endpoint telemetry and enabling investigation and response, not just blocking
quiz.explain: The R is the point: response and the retrospective visibility that makes scoping possible.

quiz.q: The best first automation for an analyst is usually…
choices: Enrichment — gathering the context you always gather by hand
quiz.explain: Enrichment is safe, saves minutes on every alert, and never causes an outage when it is wrong.

lessons.title: Scanning: types, configuration, and scope
lessons.objective: Configure credentialed and uncredentialed scans appropriately, understand scan impact, and choose scope deliberately.
lessons.lab: Run the same scan twice against your lab — once uncredentialed, once with domain credentials — and compare the findings count and the detail. Document the difference. Then deliberately scan during a busy moment and note any performance impact on the VMs. Write a scan policy for the lab: scope, schedule, credentials handling, and who is notified before a scan runs.

quiz.q: A credentialed scan is preferred because it…
choices: Sees installed patch levels and configuration directly, producing far fewer false positives and negatives
quiz.explain: Uncredentialed scanning guesses from banners. Credentialed scanning reads the truth from inside.

quiz.q: Scanning production systems requires…
choices: Change approval, a maintenance window for aggressive checks, and a rollback contact — some checks crash fragile systems
quiz.explain: Legacy and embedded devices fall over under scanning. That is a real outage caused by a security tool.

quiz.q: Asset discovery matters to vulnerability management because…
choices: Unscanned assets are unmeasured risk — the scan report only covers what you told it to look at
quiz.explain: Coverage percentage is the metric most programs never report, and the one that matters most.

lessons.title: Prioritization beyond CVSS
lessons.objective: Combine CVSS, exploitability (KEV, EPSS), asset criticality, and exposure into a defensible priority order.
lessons.lab: Take 25 findings from your lab scan and build a prioritization model in a spreadsheet: CVSS base, EPSS score, KEV listed yes/no, asset criticality 1-3, internet exposed yes/no. Compute a composite score with weights you can defend, and sort. Compare your top ten against the scanner's top ten by CVSS alone and write a paragraph on where and why they differ.

quiz.q: EPSS estimates…
choices: The probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild in the near term
quiz.explain: CVSS says how bad it would be; EPSS says how likely it is. Together with asset context they make a real priority.

quiz.q: A vulnerability in CISA KEV should be treated as…
choices: Low priority if CVSS is medium
High priority regardless of CVSS — it is confirmed exploited in the wild
quiz.explain: Confirmed exploitation outranks theoretical severity. Federal agencies have mandated remediation deadlines for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: Compensating controls affect prioritization because…
choices: They reduce exploitability or impact, which can justify a later patch date with documented reasoning
quiz.explain: A vulnerable service reachable only from a jump host behind MFA is a different risk from the same service exposed to the internet.

lessons.title: Validation, exceptions, and closing the loop
lessons.objective: Verify remediation, handle risk acceptance formally, and report progress with metrics that survive scrutiny.

resources.label: NIST SP 800-40r4 — Guide to enterprise patch management planning
CIS Controls v8 — continuous vulnerability management

lessons.lab: Build the program artifacts: a remediation SLA table by severity, an exception request form (what, why, compensating controls, expiry date, approver), and a monthly metrics report with mean time to remediate by severity, percentage of assets scanned, and the count of open exceptions past expiry. Fill them in with your lab's real numbers. The expired-exceptions count is the metric that makes auditors pay attention.

quiz.q: A risk exception must always include…
choices: An expiry date and a named approver with the authority to accept that risk
quiz.explain: Permanent exceptions are the norm in badly run programs. An expiry date forces periodic re-justification.

quiz.q: Mean time to remediate is most useful when reported…
choices: Segmented by severity, because a 30-day average hides critical findings sitting open for 90 days
quiz.explain: Averages hide the tail. Segment, and report the worst outlier alongside the average.

quiz.q: Rescanning after remediation is required because…
choices: A patch can fail, be rolled back, or not apply to every instance — verification is the only proof
quiz.explain: Trust the evidence, not the ticket status. Closed-without-verification is how findings reappear months later.

lessons.title: Application and infrastructure vulnerability concepts
lessons.objective: Recognize the vulnerability classes CS0-003 tests — injection, XSS, insecure deserialization, race conditions, misconfiguration — and how they are found.
lessons.lab: Work the PortSwigger Web Security Academy free labs on SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and access control, at least two each. Then host OWASP Juice Shop on your Linux box and find five flaws yourself without walkthroughs. Write each up as a finding: description, impact, evidence, remediation, and severity. This is both CySA+ preparation and a reusable portfolio piece.

quiz.q: The root cause of SQL injection is…
choices: Untrusted input concatenated into a query instead of being parameterized
quiz.explain: Parameterized queries or prepared statements are the fix. Input filtering alone is a mitigation, not a cure.

quiz.q: Stored XSS is more severe than reflected XSS because…
choices: The payload persists server-side and executes for every user who views the affected content, with no phishing required
quiz.explain: Reflected XSS needs the victim to follow a crafted link. Stored XSS waits for them.

quiz.q: Security misconfiguration is consistently in the OWASP Top 10 because…
choices: Defaults, verbose errors, unnecessary features, and unpatched components accumulate in every real deployment
It is easy to exploit only in labs
quiz.explain: It is a process failure as much as a technical one, which is why hardening baselines and configuration management appear in every framework.

lessons.title: Attack frameworks and the analyst's mental model
lessons.objective: Apply the Cyber Kill Chain, the Diamond Model, and ATT&CK, and know when each is the right lens.
lessons.lab: Take the SIEM lab attack chain and describe it three ways: as kill chain phases, as a Diamond Model event set (adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim), and as ATT&CK techniques. Write one paragraph on what each model made obvious that the others did not. Frameworks are tools, not doctrine — this exercise shows you why practitioners use all three.

quiz.q: The Diamond Model's four core features are…
quiz.explain: Its power is pivoting: from one known infrastructure you find other victims and other capabilities.

quiz.q: The Cyber Kill Chain is most criticized for…
choices: Being linear and perimeter-focused, which fits less well for insider threats and post-compromise activity
quiz.explain: It remains useful for communicating early-stage disruption opportunities. ATT&CK covers post-compromise far better.

quiz.q: The practical reason to map an incident to a framework during response is…
choices: It prompts you to look for the stages you have not yet found, rather than stopping at the first indicator
quiz.explain: Frameworks are checklists against your own tunnel vision. Found execution but no initial access? Keep looking.

lessons.title: Containment, eradication, and recovery decisions
lessons.objective: Make the hard calls — isolate now or watch, reimage or clean, when to reset the domain — and justify them.

resources.label: Microsoft — recovering from systemic identity compromise

lessons.lab: Write three decision memos, one page each, for scenarios in your lab: (1) a single workstation with commodity malware; (2) credential theft with lateral movement to a second host; (3) evidence the domain controller was accessed with Domain Admin credentials. For each, state your containment action, your eradication approach, what you would need to declare recovery complete, and what you would tell the business owner about downtime. Scenario three should conclude that only a full credential reset restores trust.

quiz.q: Once an attacker has obtained Domain Admin, the only reliable recovery includes…
choices: A full credential reset including the krbtgt account (twice), because forged Kerberos tickets survive password changes otherwise
quiz.explain: Golden Ticket attacks are why krbtgt is reset twice with replication in between. This is the single most important AD recovery fact.

quiz.q: Choosing to observe rather than immediately isolate is justified when…
choices: The risk of tipping off the attacker outweighs the ongoing harm, and you need scope before acting — a decision made with the business, not alone
quiz.explain: It is a legitimate strategy with real risk. It needs authority, a time limit, and documented reasoning.

quiz.q: Cleaning rather than reimaging a compromised endpoint is risky because…
choices: You cannot prove every persistence mechanism was removed, and rootkits can hide from the tools you are using to check
quiz.explain: Reimage from known-good media is the default for a reason. Cleaning is an exception justified by specific constraints.

lessons.title: Forensic fundamentals for an analyst
lessons.objective: Acquire and examine evidence correctly — memory, disk, and logs — without destroying it.

resources.label: Autopsy — open source digital forensics platform

lessons.lab: Practice acquisition on your own lab: capture a memory image of LAB-WS01 while the Atomic Red Team persistence test is active, then analyze it with Volatility — process list, network connections, injected code, and command lines. Separately, examine the host with Eric Zimmerman's tools: prefetch, shimcache, and the MFT. Document hashes of every acquired artifact before and after analysis to demonstrate integrity.

quiz.q: The order of volatility says to collect…
choices: Registers and cache, then memory, then network state, then disk, then backups — most volatile first
quiz.explain: Every action you take changes memory. Collect the most perishable evidence before it is gone.

quiz.q: Hashing evidence at acquisition establishes…
choices: Integrity — later comparison proves the evidence was not altered during analysis
quiz.explain: Hash at acquisition, work on a copy, re-hash to prove nothing changed. It is also what makes findings defensible.

quiz.q: Prefetch files are useful because they show…
choices: Evidence that a program executed, when, and how many times — even if the binary is gone
quiz.explain: Execution artifacts survive deletion of the executable. Shimcache and Amcache serve similar roles.

lessons.title: Post-incident: root cause and lessons learned
lessons.objective: Run a blameless post-incident review that produces control changes with owners and dates.
lessons.lab: Write a full post-incident report for your lab attack chain: timeline with timestamps, root cause (not the proximate cause — keep asking why), what worked, what did not, dwell time, and five action items each with an owner and a due date. Then actually complete two of the action items in the lab and mark them closed. A post-incident report with no completed actions is theatre.

quiz.q: Blameless review means…
choices: The focus is on the system and process failures that allowed a human error to cause harm, so people report honestly
quiz.explain: Blame produces hiding, hiding produces repeat incidents. Accountability lives in the action items, not in the blame.

quiz.q: Dwell time measures…
choices: How long the attacker was present before detection — the metric that most directly reflects detection capability
quiz.explain: Reducing dwell time is the core purpose of detection engineering. Track it incident over incident.

quiz.q: An action item without an owner and a date is…
choices: Acceptable if the team is small
A wish — it will not be done, and the same incident will recur
quiz.explain: Name and date, every time, tracked to closure in the same place you track vulnerabilities.

sections.title: Domain 4 — Reporting, communication, and the exam

lessons.title: Writing for people who do not do this job
lessons.objective: Produce vulnerability and incident reports that a business owner reads, understands, and acts on.
lessons.lab: Take the most technical finding from your vulnerability work and write it three ways: a one-paragraph executive summary with business impact and a recommended decision; a half-page technical summary for the system owner with remediation steps; and the full technical detail with evidence. Give the executive version to a non-technical family member and ask them what they would do. If they cannot answer, rewrite it.

quiz.q: An executive summary should state business impact in terms of…
choices: Consequences the business cares about — downtime, data loss, regulatory exposure, cost — and the decision being requested
quiz.explain: Translate technical severity into business consequence and a specific ask. Otherwise the report is filed, not acted upon.

quiz.q: Stakeholder identification matters because…
choices: It is a CompTIA objective only
Different audiences need different detail and different asks — system owners, executives, legal, and customers are not the same reader
quiz.explain: One report for all audiences satisfies none. Write the same facts at three altitudes.

quiz.q: Reporting metrics without context is risky because…
choices: A number with no trend or target invites misinterpretation — 40 open criticals means nothing without last month's figure and the SLA
quiz.explain: Always pair a number with a trend and a target. That is what makes it a decision input rather than an anxiety generator.

lessons.title: Metrics, KPIs, and the security program view
lessons.objective: Choose metrics that drive behavior — coverage, dwell time, MTTR, SLA compliance — and present them honestly.

resources.label: CIS Controls v8 — measures and metrics
NIST SP 800-55 — performance measurement for information security

lessons.lab: Build a one-page monthly security dashboard for your lab as if it were a client: asset coverage percentage, detection coverage against ATT&CK, open findings by severity with trend, MTTR by severity, exceptions past expiry, phishing report rate, and one narrative paragraph. Produce it twice, a month apart, so the trend column is real. Bring this to interviews — very few entry-level candidates have ever produced a metrics report.

quiz.q: A metric becomes harmful when…
choices: It is used as a target in a way that incentivizes gaming — closing alerts fast rather than correctly
quiz.explain: Goodhart's law in a SOC: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Pair speed metrics with quality metrics.

quiz.q: Coverage metrics matter because…
choices: Every other metric is meaningless if it is calculated over a fraction of the environment you do not know the size of
quiz.explain: MTTR across 60% of assets is an unknown number. Report coverage alongside every other figure.

quiz.q: Phishing report rate is a better metric than click rate alone because…
choices: It measures whether users act as sensors, which is the behavior you actually want, not just the absence of a bad one
quiz.explain: Track both. Rising reports with falling clicks is a program that is working.

lessons.title: Exam preparation and CEU stacking
lessons.objective: Build the study plan for CS0-003, practice its performance-based questions, and use the CEUs to renew Security+.

resources.label: CompTIA — CySA+ certification and exam objectives
Jason Dion — CySA+ CS0-003 practice exams

lessons.lab: Schedule the exam eight to ten weeks out. Build the plan backward, one domain per two weeks, with your own lab work as the practical half. CySA+ performance-based questions are log-analysis heavy — practice reading unfamiliar log formats under time pressure using samples from the SIEM you built. In the final two weeks, sit two full practice exams and turn every miss into a flashcard with the reasoning. After passing, confirm in your CompTIA account that Security+ renewed automatically through CEU stacking.

quiz.q: CompTIA CEU stacking means…
choices: Passing a higher-level CompTIA certification renews the lower ones within the same renewal window
quiz.explain: CySA+ renews Security+ and Network+. This is why sequencing CompTIA certifications well saves real money.

quiz.q: CySA+ PBQs differ from Security+ PBQs by being…
choices: More analysis-driven — you read logs, scan output, and code snippets and draw conclusions rather than configure settings
quiz.explain: Practice with real log excerpts. Speed at reading unfamiliar formats is the trainable skill.

quiz.q: The most common reason candidates fail CS0-003 is…
choices: Treating it as a memorization exam rather than practicing analysis of real artifacts
quiz.explain: It is an analyst exam. The lab hours you have already logged are your best preparation.

courses.title: ISACA CISA
courses.summary: The Certified Information Systems Auditor is the anchor certification of the GRC lane. Five domains covering the audit process, governance, acquisition and implementation, operations, and protection of information assets — taught through the auditor's mindset of evidence and independence.
outcomes: Plan and execute an IS audit using a risk-based approach
Gather and evaluate evidence to support audit conclusions
Evaluate IT governance, controls, and their effectiveness
Communicate findings and follow up on remediation
Pass the CISA exam and understand its experience requirement

lessons.title: What an auditor actually does
lessons.objective: Adopt the auditor's mindset: independence, objectivity, evidence over assertion, and the difference between auditing and doing.
lessons.lab: Audit one control in your home lab as an independent auditor would, not as its builder. Take the control objective 'only authorized users can administer the domain' and gather evidence: the Domain Admins membership list, the last review date, and whether a process exists to review it. Write a finding with condition, criteria, cause, effect, and recommendation. Notice how different this is from configuring the control — that gap is the auditor's mindset.

quiz.q: Auditor independence matters because…
choices: An auditor evaluating their own work cannot be objective, so audit and implementation must be separated
quiz.explain: You cannot audit what you built. Independence is the foundation of an audit opinion's credibility.

quiz.q: The five elements of a well-formed audit finding are…
choices: Condition, criteria, cause, effect, and recommendation
quiz.explain: Condition (what is), criteria (what should be), cause, effect, recommendation. This structure is tested and used daily.

quiz.q: An auditor who finds a problem should…
choices: Document it and recommend remediation — fixing it would compromise independence and is not the auditor's role
quiz.explain: Auditors assess and recommend; management remediates. Crossing that line destroys the independence the role depends on.

lessons.title: Risk-based audit planning
lessons.objective: Plan an audit using risk to allocate effort, and define scope, objectives, and materiality.
lessons.lab: Build a risk-based audit plan for a hypothetical small business's IT: list the auditable areas (identity, backups, patching, vendor access, physical security), score each on risk, and allocate your audit hours proportionally. Justify why the highest-risk area gets the most attention. Write the audit charter, scope, and objectives for the top area. This is exactly how real audit programs decide where to look.

quiz.q: Risk-based auditing means…
choices: Directing audit effort toward the areas of highest risk, because resources are finite
quiz.explain: You cannot audit everything deeply. Risk decides where the limited hours produce the most assurance.

quiz.q: Materiality in an audit context refers to…
choices: The threshold at which a finding is significant enough to affect conclusions or decisions
quiz.explain: Not every deviation matters. Materiality keeps the audit focused on what actually affects the assurance provided.

quiz.q: An audit charter establishes…
choices: The audit function's authority, responsibility, and scope, granting it the mandate to access what it needs
quiz.explain: Without a charter granting authority and access, an auditor cannot compel the evidence the audit requires.

lessons.title: Evidence, sampling, and testing controls
lessons.objective: Gather sufficient appropriate evidence, use sampling correctly, and test both control design and operating effectiveness.
lessons.lab: Test a control for both design and operating effectiveness in your lab. Take 'privileged access is reviewed quarterly': first assess whether the control is well designed (does a review process exist and would it catch a problem?), then test whether it actually operated (is there evidence of reviews having happened, with dates and sign-offs?). Document both. A well-designed control that never operates is a common and important finding.

quiz.q: Design effectiveness and operating effectiveness differ in that design asks…
choices: Whether the control would work if operated, while operating effectiveness asks whether it actually operated as intended over the period
quiz.explain: A control can be well designed but never performed. Testing both is why SOC 2 Type II covers a period, not a moment.

quiz.q: Sampling is used in audit because…
choices: It is more accurate than full testing
Testing every instance is often impractical, so a representative sample supports a conclusion about the population
quiz.explain: Sampling risk — that the sample misrepresents the population — is managed by sample size and selection method.

quiz.q: The most reliable audit evidence is generally…
choices: Evidence the auditor obtains directly or that is generated by an independent system, over evidence provided by the auditee
quiz.explain: Source and independence determine reliability. Auditor-obtained system logs beat a manager saying it works.

lessons.title: IT governance and frameworks
lessons.objective: Evaluate IT governance structures and apply COBIT and related frameworks to assess how IT is directed and controlled.
lessons.lab: Assess the 'governance' of your own home lab and portfolio as if it were an organization: is there a documented strategy, are decisions recorded (your decision records), is there a change process, are roles defined, and how is risk managed? Map your practices to a few COBIT governance objectives and identify the gaps. Write it as a maturity assessment with a target state.

quiz.q: IT governance is primarily concerned with…
choices: Ensuring IT supports and aligns with organizational objectives, with clear accountability and risk management
quiz.explain: Governance is direction and oversight — the board and executive layer — distinct from operational management.

quiz.q: COBIT is best described as…
choices: A framework for the governance and management of enterprise IT, mapping objectives to processes and controls
quiz.explain: It is the auditor's reference for evaluating whether IT is governed well. Know its structure at a conceptual level.

quiz.q: A maturity model helps an audit by…
choices: Describing the current capability level against a defined scale, making improvement targets concrete
quiz.explain: Maturity levels turn 'this is weak' into 'this is level 2, target level 4', which management can act on.
