lessons.title: Auditing acquisition, development, and implementation
lessons.objective: Evaluate how systems are acquired, developed, and implemented, including project governance and testing.
lessons.lab: Audit a change you made in your lab as an SDLC-style implementation: was there a documented requirement, a test before production, an approval, a rollback plan, and post-implementation verification? Map it against the phases of a software or system development lifecycle and identify which controls were present and which were missing. Write findings for the gaps.

quiz.q: An auditor reviewing a system implementation checks primarily for…
choices: Whether appropriate controls existed at each phase — requirements, testing, approval, and post-implementation review
quiz.explain: The audit follows the lifecycle, verifying that controls governed each phase, not judging the technical choices themselves.

quiz.q: Testing in a non-production environment before deployment is a control because it…
choices: Catches defects and unintended impacts before they affect live systems and data
quiz.explain: Same principle as the pilot group in patching. Separation of test and production is a control an auditor verifies.

quiz.q: Post-implementation review verifies…
choices: That the project was under budget
Whether the implemented system actually met its objectives and controls operate as intended
quiz.explain: The step organizations skip most. Did it deliver what was intended, and do the controls work in production?

lessons.title: Business continuity and resilience audit
lessons.objective: Audit business continuity and disaster recovery capabilities, including the BIA, plans, and testing evidence.
lessons.lab: Audit the resilience of your lab: is there a business impact analysis (which VMs matter and how much downtime is tolerable), documented recovery procedures, evidence that a recovery was actually tested (you did this in Security+), and defined RTO/RPO? Write an audit report on the DR capability with findings and a maturity rating. Connect it to the recovery test you already performed — you have the evidence.

quiz.q: An auditor assessing DR asks first for…
choices: Evidence that recovery has actually been tested, not just that a plan document exists
quiz.explain: An untested plan is a finding. Auditors want evidence of a successful test with dates and results.

quiz.q: The business impact analysis is foundational to DR audit because…
choices: Without it, there is no defensible basis for the recovery priorities, RTOs, and RPOs the plan claims
quiz.explain: The BIA justifies the plan's priorities. A plan with RTOs not traceable to a BIA is a finding.

quiz.q: RTO and RPO in the plan should be…
choices: Validated against actual recovery test results — a stated one-hour RTO that testing shows takes six hours is a finding
quiz.explain: Stated versus demonstrated capability is a classic audit gap, and exactly what your recovery test measured.

sections.title: Protection of information assets and the exam

lessons.title: Auditing information security controls
lessons.objective: Evaluate logical and physical access controls, network security, and data protection from the auditor's evidence-based perspective.
lessons.lab: Audit the access controls across your lab against CIS Controls: account management, access control management, and audit log management. For each, gather evidence of the control's existence and operation, rate it, and write findings. You built these controls in earlier courses — now assess them independently. The shift from builder to assessor is the whole point of the GRC lane.

quiz.q: When auditing access controls, the strongest evidence of the review control is…
choices: Dated, signed records of actual access reviews with evidence that changes were made as a result
A screenshot of the user list
quiz.explain: A policy is design; dated review records with resulting actions are operating effectiveness. Auditors want the latter.

quiz.q: A control auditors frequently find missing is…
choices: Timely removal of access when people leave or change roles — deprovisioning
quiz.explain: Orphaned accounts and privilege creep appear in nearly every access audit. It ties back to the IAM lifecycle from Security+.

quiz.q: The auditor's role regarding a discovered access gap is to…
choices: Document the finding with evidence and recommend remediation, leaving the fix to management
quiz.explain: Independence again: assess and recommend, do not remediate. The consistency of this principle is what CISA tests.

lessons.title: Reporting findings and follow-up
lessons.objective: Write audit reports that drive action, rate findings appropriately, and track remediation to closure.
lessons.lab: Compile your lab findings into a formal audit report: executive summary, scope and methodology, findings each rated by risk with the five elements and management response, and a follow-up plan with owners and dates. Then simulate the follow-up: pick two findings, remediate them in the lab, and document the closure evidence. The follow-up phase is what makes an audit improve anything rather than just describe problems.

quiz.q: A management response section in an audit report captures…
choices: Management's agreement or disagreement with each finding and their committed remediation with a date and owner
quiz.explain: The response is where accountability is established. A finding management accepts with a date is one that gets fixed.

quiz.q: Audit follow-up exists to…
choices: Verify that agreed remediation was actually completed and effective, closing the loop
quiz.explain: Without follow-up, findings are noted and forgotten. Verification of closure is what produces improvement.

quiz.q: Management's decision to accept a risk rather than remediate is…
choices: A legitimate option that the auditor documents, provided the acceptance is made by someone with appropriate authority
quiz.explain: The business owns the risk and may accept it. The auditor's job is to ensure the decision is informed and properly authorized.

lessons.title: Exam preparation and the experience requirement
lessons.objective: Plan for the CISA exam and understand the work-experience requirement for full certification.

resources.label: ISACA — CISA Questions, Answers and Explanations (QAE) database

lessons.lab: Build the study plan around ISACA's domain weightings and the QAE question database — CISA is heavily terminology and mindset driven, so practice thinking like an auditor rather than a technician. Schedule the exam, and separately map your path to the five years of experience CISA requires (waivers exist for education and other certs). You can pass the exam before you have the experience; the certification is granted once experience is met. Record both dates in the tracker.

quiz.q: CISA's experience requirement means…
choices: You cannot take the exam without it
You can pass the exam first, but full certification requires the qualifying work experience (with possible waivers)
quiz.explain: Pass now, certify when experience is met — commonly five years of IS audit, control, or security work with waivers available.

quiz.q: CISA exam questions reward candidates who…
choices: Choose the answer an independent, risk-focused auditor would give — often the one about evidence, process, or governance
quiz.explain: When two answers seem right, the auditor's mindset — independence, evidence, risk — usually points to the intended one.

quiz.q: The best single practice resource for CISA is generally…
choices: ISACA's official QAE database, because it teaches the exam's specific way of reasoning
quiz.explain: The QAE explanations train the mindset. CISA is as much about how ISACA thinks as about the facts.

courses.title: TCM Practical Network Penetration Tester
courses.summary: The best-value entry to the red lane. TCM's PNPT is a five-day practical exam ending in a real report and a debrief — external recon, Active Directory attacks, and the writing that turns access into a deliverable. The bundled training is included in the price.
outcomes: Run OSINT and external reconnaissance against a defined scope
Exploit a network and pivot through an Active Directory environment
Chain misconfigurations rather than relying on single CVEs
Write a professional penetration test report with an executive summary and evidence
Pass the PNPT exam including the live debrief

lessons.title: Authorization is the whole job
lessons.objective: Internalize that everything in this lane is illegal without written authorization, and understand scope, rules of engagement, and the get-out-of-jail letter.

resources.label: TCM Security Academy — PNPT and PEH course
EC-Council — rules of engagement overview (concept reference)

lessons.lab: Write a rules-of-engagement document for a hypothetical Cargill Consulting client engagement: scope (which IPs and domains are in and out), timing window, permitted techniques (no denial of service, no social engineering unless specified), data handling, emergency contacts, and the authorization signature block. This is not busywork — a missing signature is the difference between a penetration test and a felony.

quiz.q: The single document that legally separates penetration testing from a crime is…
choices: Written authorization from someone with the authority to grant it, defining scope and rules of engagement
quiz.explain: No signed authorization, no test. This holds without exception, in every jurisdiction, for every engagement.

quiz.q: A system in the target's building but not listed in scope should be…
choices: Tested anyway, since it is on site
Left alone and flagged to the client — out of scope means out of scope
Added to scope by the tester
quiz.explain: Scope discipline protects you and the client. Third-party systems in particular may belong to someone who never consented.

quiz.q: The emergency contact in the rules of engagement exists because…
choices: A test can cause an outage or trigger a real incident response, and someone must be reachable to stop or coordinate immediately
quiz.explain: Tests break things and set off alarms. Both sides need a way to reach each other fast.

lessons.title: The attacker's lab: Kali and a vulnerable domain
lessons.objective: Build the isolated attack lab you will practice in: Kali plus a deliberately vulnerable Active Directory environment.

resources.label: GOAD — Game of Active Directory vulnerable lab

lessons.lab: On your hypervisor's isolated network, stand up Kali and a vulnerable AD lab. Reuse your Home Lab domain and deliberately weaken it (Kerberoastable service accounts, a user with a weak password, unconstrained delegation) or deploy GOAD if you have the resources. Confirm Kali can reach the targets and nothing can reach your home network. Snapshot everything as pentest-clean. Document the intended weaknesses so you know what success looks like.

quiz.q: Practicing offensive techniques must happen on…
choices: Systems you own or are explicitly authorized to attack, fully isolated from other networks
quiz.explain: The isolation rule from the SIEM course applies with even more force here. Your practice must never touch anything you do not own.

quiz.q: Deliberately weakening your AD lab is useful because…
choices: It makes the lab realistic — real domains accumulate exactly these misconfigurations
quiz.explain: You are recreating the conditions PNPT and real engagements exploit: chained misconfigurations, not exotic zero-days.

quiz.q: A clean snapshot before practice matters because…
choices: Attacks leave the environment in a changed state, and you want a fast reset to a known baseline
quiz.explain: Same discipline as every other course. Reset, re-attack, refine.

lessons.title: Methodology and note-taking
lessons.objective: Adopt a repeatable methodology and a note-taking system that produces the report as a byproduct of the test.

resources.label: Obsidian or CherryTree for structured pentest notes

lessons.lab: Set up a note structure before you touch a target: a section per phase (recon, enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation, pivoting, cleanup), and for every finding a template capturing the command run, the output, a screenshot, the timestamp, and the affected host. Practice on one machine in your lab. The rule: if it is not in the notes, it did not happen and cannot go in the report.

quiz.q: Good pentest notes are structured so that…
choices: The report can be assembled from them directly — every finding already has its evidence, command, and screenshot
quiz.explain: The report is the deliverable. Notes that were not taken during exploitation cannot be reconstructed accurately afterward.

quiz.q: Screenshotting every significant step matters because…
choices: Reproducible evidence is what makes a finding credible and remediable — a claim without proof is disputed
quiz.explain: Include the timestamp and the host. Evidence is the currency of the profession.

quiz.q: A methodology helps most by…
choices: Ensuring you do not skip enumeration steps under time pressure — most missed findings are missed enumeration
quiz.explain: Thorough, boring enumeration finds more than clever exploitation. The methodology is what keeps you thorough when rushed.

lessons.title: OSINT and external footprinting
lessons.objective: Gather intelligence on a target from public sources — people, domains, credentials, and technology — before touching anything.
lessons.lab: Run an OSINT exercise against yourself or a consenting family member with permission: enumerate email addresses, breached passwords (haveibeenpwned), social media exposure, and any technical footprint. Produce an intelligence report as you would for a client, then write the remediation advice. Doing this to yourself first teaches both the offensive technique and the personal defensive lesson.

quiz.q: OSINT precedes active scanning because…
choices: It is passive and low-risk, and it shapes the active phase — knowing the tech stack and employee names focuses everything after
quiz.explain: Reconnaissance quality determines the whole engagement. Passive first, active second.

quiz.q: Breached credentials are valuable to an attacker because…
choices: Password reuse means a credential leaked from one service often unlocks another, including corporate accounts
quiz.explain: Credential stuffing is one of the most common initial access techniques. It is also why MFA and password managers matter so much.

quiz.q: Performing OSINT on yourself first is recommended because…
choices: It is required for the exam
It teaches the technique safely and reveals your own exposure, which you can then reduce
quiz.explain: You learn the tooling and improve your own security posture at once. Only ever OSINT others with authorization.

lessons.title: Scanning, enumeration, and initial access
lessons.objective: Enumerate services thoroughly and gain a foothold through a misconfiguration or weak credential.
lessons.lab: Against your lab, run the full enumeration flow: nmap discovery and service scan, then per-service enumeration for everything you find (SMB shares, web directories, exposed logins). Get an initial foothold through the weakness you planted — a weak SMB password or an exposed web application. Document every enumeration command even when it found nothing; the negative results are part of the methodology and the report.

quiz.q: Thorough enumeration means…
choices: Investigating every discovered service specifically, since the foothold is usually in a service a quick scan under-examined
quiz.explain: The famous maxim: enumeration is the key. Most missed footholds are under-enumerated services.

quiz.q: A full-port scan (-p-) is worth the extra time because…
choices: Services on non-standard high ports are common and are exactly where a quick top-1000 scan misses the way in
quiz.explain: Administrators hide services on odd ports believing it is security. Full scans find them.

quiz.q: Recording enumeration commands that found nothing is worthwhile because…
choices: It documents coverage — the client learns what was checked, and you avoid re-checking during a long engagement
quiz.explain: Scope of testing is itself a deliverable. What you checked and found secure has value to the client.

lessons.title: Web application attacks for the foothold
lessons.objective: Exploit the common web vulnerabilities that frequently provide initial access on real engagements.
lessons.lab: Host a vulnerable web app (OWASP Juice Shop or DVWA) on your lab and gain server access through it: find a file upload flaw or command injection, get a reverse shell, and stabilize it. Then chain: from the web shell, enumerate the host for the next step. Document the full chain from the web request to the shell prompt.

quiz.q: A web application is often the initial access vector because…
choices: It is deliberately exposed to the internet, so its vulnerabilities are reachable in a way internal systems are not
quiz.explain: Exposure plus complexity. The application is the door the organization chose to leave open.

quiz.q: Stabilizing a reverse shell (upgrading to a full TTY) matters because…
choices: A raw shell lacks job control and interactive features, and drops easily — a stable shell makes the rest of the work possible
quiz.explain: The python pty and stty trick is a rite of passage. An unstable shell wastes enormous time.

quiz.q: File upload vulnerabilities lead to code execution when…
choices: The application stores an uploaded executable script in a location the web server will run
quiz.explain: Upload plus a reachable execution path equals a shell. The fix is validating type, renaming, and storing outside the web root.

lessons.title: AD enumeration and BloodHound
lessons.objective: Map an Active Directory environment and identify attack paths to Domain Admin.

resources.label: TCM Security — Practical Ethical Hacking (AD section)

lessons.lab: From a low-privileged foothold in your lab domain, run SharpHound to collect AD data and analyze it in BloodHound. Identify the shortest path from your compromised user to Domain Admin. Document each edge in the path and what technique exploits it. This graph-based approach is exactly how modern AD attacks and the PNPT exam work.

quiz.q: BloodHound is powerful because it…
choices: Reveals attack paths through relationships — group memberships, sessions, and ACLs — that are invisible when viewed one object at a time
quiz.explain: The attacker thinks in graphs. Defenders who adopt BloodHound see the same paths and cut them.

quiz.q: The value of finding the shortest path to Domain Admin is…
choices: It focuses effort on the misconfigurations that actually matter, rather than exploiting everything
It is required by the exam
quiz.explain: Efficiency and clarity. The report can then recommend cutting exactly those edges.

quiz.q: SharpHound collection can be noisy, so on a real engagement you would…
choices: Be aware it generates significant logging and consider stealth versus thoroughness based on the rules of engagement
quiz.explain: Understanding the noise you make is part of the craft, and disabling a client's logging is out of scope unless explicitly authorized.

lessons.title: Kerberoasting, credential attacks, and lateral movement
lessons.objective: Execute the core AD attacks — Kerberoasting, password spraying, pass-the-hash — and move laterally.
lessons.lab: In your lab: request service tickets and Kerberoast the service account you made vulnerable, crack it offline with hashcat, then use the credential to move laterally with Impacket's tools. Practice pass-the-hash with a captured NTLM hash. Document each attack, the exact commands, and — importantly for the report — the specific misconfiguration that enabled it and how to fix it.

quiz.q: Kerberoasting works because…
choices: Any domain user can request a service ticket, which is encrypted with the service account's password hash and can be cracked offline
quiz.explain: The fix is long, random, managed service account passwords. It is why gMSAs exist and why this is a top real-world finding.

quiz.q: Pass-the-hash is possible because…
choices: NTLM authentication accepts the hash itself as proof of identity, so the plaintext password is never needed
quiz.explain: You authenticate with the hash directly. Credential Guard and disabling NTLM where possible are the defenses.

quiz.q: For the report, each AD attack must be paired with…
choices: The specific misconfiguration that enabled it and a concrete remediation, so the finding is actionable
quiz.explain: The client cannot patch a technique; they can fix a misconfiguration. Findings must be remediable.

lessons.title: Pivoting and post-exploitation
lessons.objective: Pivot through networks, establish access to isolated segments, and demonstrate impact responsibly.
lessons.lab: Add a second, isolated subnet to your lab reachable only through a compromised host. Establish a pivot with Ligolo-ng or chisel, enumerate the hidden segment, and reach a target you could not touch directly. Document the pivot clearly with a diagram — reviewers and clients frequently misunderstand pivoting, so the diagram is the finding.

quiz.q: Pivoting demonstrates to a client that…
choices: A single compromised host exposes network segments the perimeter was assumed to protect — impact, not just access
quiz.explain: It is how you show that flat internal networks turn one foothold into total exposure. It makes the case for segmentation.

quiz.q: Demonstrating impact responsibly means…
choices: Exfiltrating all data to prove the point
Proving access to sensitive systems without causing damage or removing real data — a screenshot of access, not a copy of the crown jewels
quiz.explain: Prove reachability and access; do not cause harm. The rules of engagement define exactly how far to go.

quiz.q: A pivot diagram belongs in the report because…
choices: The attack path across segments is the hardest thing for a non-tester to visualize, and the visualization drives the remediation
quiz.explain: Communication is the deliverable. A clear diagram of how you crossed the network is often the report's most valuable page.

lessons.title: The penetration test report
lessons.objective: Write a report that serves both an executive and an engineer, with an accurate risk rating for every finding.

resources.label: TCM Security — sample penetration test report

lessons.lab: Write a full report on your lab engagement: executive summary (business-level, no jargon), scope and methodology, findings each with risk rating, evidence, reproduction steps, and remediation, an attack narrative telling the story of the compromise, and an appendix. Have someone non-technical read the executive summary and tell you the top risk. If they cannot, rewrite it. The report is what PNPT actually grades.

quiz.q: The executive summary of a pentest report should…
choices: State the business risk and the most important recommendations in language a non-technical decision maker acts on
quiz.explain: The executives decide the budget and rarely read past the summary. That page determines whether anything gets fixed.

quiz.q: A finding's risk rating should reflect…
choices: How hard it was to exploit
Likelihood and business impact in context — not the CVSS base score alone
The tester's opinion of severity only
quiz.explain: Same principle as vulnerability management. A critical CVE on an unreachable box is not a critical finding.

quiz.q: The report matters more than the compromise because…
choices: The client is paying for actionable improvement, and access they cannot understand or remediate is worthless to them
The exam grades only the report
quiz.explain: The value delivered is the report. PNPT grades it precisely because it is the actual professional product.

lessons.title: The debrief and exam logistics
lessons.objective: Prepare for the PNPT's distinctive live debrief and plan the five-day exam.

resources.label: TCM Security Academy — full PNPT course bundle

lessons.lab: Do a full dry run: give yourself five days against your lab, produce the complete report, then record a 15-minute debrief presentation as if to the client's technical staff — walk through the attack path, the key findings, and the top three remediations, taking questions from an imaginary panel. The PNPT debrief trips up strong hackers who cannot explain their work. Rehearse until you can.

quiz.q: The PNPT live debrief tests…
choices: Whether you can explain your findings and reasoning to people, which is central to the actual job
quiz.explain: It is the feature that makes PNPT respected. Consultants who cannot communicate do not last, however good their exploitation.

quiz.q: The PNPT exam format is…
choices: A five-day practical engagement producing a report, followed by a live debrief
quiz.explain: It mirrors a real engagement end to end, which is why it transfers so well to actual consulting work.

quiz.q: If you fail the exam, TCM's model typically allows…
choices: A retake, often with a free second attempt included in the bundle — verify current terms
quiz.explain: Check current policy, but the value proposition — training plus exam plus a retake for around $500 — is why PNPT leads the lane on cost.

lessons.title: After PNPT: the offensive portfolio
lessons.objective: Build a public portfolio that demonstrates offensive skill without publishing anything harmful.
lessons.lab: Publish a sanitized methodology repository: your enumeration checklists, your report template, and write-ups of retired Hack The Box machines (only retired ones, respecting platform rules). Never publish anything targeting a real system you do not own. Add a clear ethics statement to the README. This portfolio plus PNPT is a strong junior penetration tester application, and it feeds directly into the Offensive Lab and OSCP courses.

quiz.q: Publishing offensive write-ups requires care to…
choices: Only cover authorized or retired targets, respect platform rules, and never provide a roadmap against a real victim
quiz.explain: Ethics is the profession's foundation. A tester who publishes attacks on real, non-consenting targets is unhireable and possibly a criminal.

quiz.q: An ethics statement in an offensive portfolio signals…
choices: Professional maturity — the judgment employers most need to trust before granting offensive access
quiz.explain: The whole lane runs on trust. Demonstrating that you understand the boundaries is a hiring signal, not boilerplate.

quiz.q: Methodology checklists are valuable in a portfolio because…
choices: They show disciplined, repeatable process — which distinguishes a professional tester from someone who got lucky on a box
quiz.explain: Process is the profession. A polished checklist demonstrates exactly the reliability a consultancy needs to bill for.

courses.title: ISC2 SSCP
courses.summary: The Systems Security Certified Practitioner is ISC2's hands-on operational security certification — a technical complement to the GRC lane that also fits blue-team work. Seven domains spanning access controls, operations, risk, incident response, cryptography, network, and systems security.
outcomes: Implement and administer access controls across identity systems
Run security operations and administration from a practitioner's seat
Apply risk identification, monitoring, and incident response operationally
Configure network and systems security controls correctly
Pass the SSCP and progress the ISC2 membership begun with CC

lessons.title: Implementing access controls
lessons.objective: Administer the access control models and identity mechanisms operationally, from provisioning through authentication to review.
lessons.lab: Implement the full identity lifecycle in your lab domain and document it as an operations runbook: provisioning a new user with least privilege, enforcing MFA, the authentication flow, periodic access review, and deprovisioning on departure. This is the practitioner counterpart to the CISA audit of the same controls — SSCP is about running them, CISA about assessing them.

quiz.q: SSCP differs from CISA in emphasis by being…
choices: Hands-on and operational — implementing and administering controls, where CISA assesses them
quiz.explain: SSCP is the practitioner's cert. It sits comfortably in both the GRC and blue lanes because operating controls underlies both.

quiz.q: Enforcing least privilege at provisioning is better than removing excess access later because…
choices: Access granted is rarely revoked, so starting minimal prevents the privilege creep that reviews then have to catch
quiz.explain: Default-minimal is far more reliable than default-broad plus cleanup. Prevention beats detection here.

quiz.q: A single sign-on system centralizes authentication, which means…
choices: It is a high-value target and single point of failure, so it must be hardened and monitored accordingly
quiz.explain: Convenience concentrates risk. SSO plus strong MFA and monitoring of the identity provider is the operational answer.

lessons.title: Security operations and administration
lessons.objective: Run day-to-day security operations: asset management, configuration management, change control, and security awareness.
lessons.lab: Build the operational security documentation set for your lab: an asset inventory, a configuration baseline, a change control log, and a data handling procedure. Operate them for two weeks — record every change through the log, update the inventory as things change. SSCP is about the disciplined daily operation of these controls, and the documentation is the evidence.

quiz.q: Configuration management supports security by…
choices: Maintaining a known-good baseline so unauthorized changes become detectable and systems stay hardened
quiz.explain: The baseline is the reference for detection — the same thread running through hardening, monitoring, and audit.

quiz.q: Change control is a security control because…
choices: Unmanaged changes introduce vulnerabilities and outages, and undocumented change defeats detection
quiz.explain: Same lesson as Security+ domain 1. Change management protects availability and integrity, not just process tidiness.

quiz.q: Data handling procedures define…
choices: How data is classified, stored, transmitted, retained, and destroyed according to its sensitivity
quiz.explain: Operationalizing classification is a practitioner responsibility. The classification decision drives the handling rules.

lessons.title: Risk identification, monitoring, and analysis
lessons.objective: Identify risks operationally, implement continuous monitoring, and analyze the results.

resources.label: NIST SP 800-137 — information security continuous monitoring

lessons.lab: Set up continuous monitoring for one risk in your lab end to end: choose the risk (unauthorized privileged access), define what to monitor, configure the monitoring in your SIEM, establish the alerting, and document how you would analyze and respond to a hit. This connects the SIEM work from Phase 2 to the risk framing of the GRC lane — monitoring is where the two meet.

quiz.q: Continuous monitoring differs from periodic assessment by…
choices: Providing ongoing, near-real-time visibility rather than a point-in-time snapshot that is stale the next day
quiz.explain: Point-in-time audits and continuous monitoring complement each other. SSCP practitioners run the continuous side.

quiz.q: Effective monitoring requires defining, before configuring the tool…
choices: What specifically you are trying to detect and what a meaningful result looks like
quiz.explain: Monitoring without a defined objective produces noise. Decide the question, then build the detection — the detection engineering lesson.

quiz.q: Risk identification at the operational level focuses on…
choices: Concrete technical and process risks the practitioner can observe and act on — misconfigurations, gaps, and anomalies
quiz.explain: SSCP operates at the technical layer. Strategic risk is CRISC and CISM territory.

lessons.title: Incident response and recovery operations
lessons.objective: Perform the operational incident response tasks — detection, response, forensics support, and recovery — from the practitioner seat.
lessons.lab: Write and rehearse operational incident response runbooks for your lab covering the practitioner's tasks: initial detection and validation, containment steps, evidence preservation basics, and recovery. Run one against a simulated incident (reuse the Security+ or SIEM scenario). SSCP tests the operational execution of incident response, complementing the process and governance view from the management certs.

quiz.q: The SSCP practitioner's role in incident response is primarily to…
choices: Execute the operational steps — detect, contain, preserve evidence, and recover — following the established plan
quiz.explain: Practitioners do; management directs. SSCP tests the hands-on execution.

quiz.q: Preserving evidence during operational response means…
choices: Following order of volatility and documenting handling so the evidence remains usable for later analysis or proceedings
quiz.explain: The volatility and chain-of-custody principles from Security+ apply directly at the operational level.

quiz.q: Recovery is considered complete when…
choices: The system is powered back on
The system is restored to known-good state, the vulnerability is addressed, and monitoring confirms normal operation
quiz.explain: Powering on a still-vulnerable system invites reinfection. Recovery includes remediation and verification.

lessons.title: Cryptography in practice
lessons.objective: Apply cryptographic controls operationally — key management, certificate administration, and choosing the right mechanism.
lessons.lab: Operate a small PKI in your lab: stand up an internal certificate authority (Windows AD Certificate Services or an openssl-based CA), issue certificates to your lab hosts, and document the full key lifecycle — generation, distribution, storage, rotation, revocation. Then practice revocation: revoke a certificate and confirm clients reject it. Key management is where cryptography actually succeeds or fails operationally.

quiz.q: Most cryptographic failures in practice come from…
choices: Poor key management — keys stored insecurely, never rotated, or not revocable — rather than broken math
quiz.explain: The algorithms are usually fine. Key generation, storage, rotation, and revocation are where operational security lives or dies.

quiz.q: Certificate revocation matters because…
choices: A compromised or superseded certificate must be made untrusted before its expiry, or it remains usable by an attacker
quiz.explain: Issuing certificates is easy; revoking them reliably (CRL, OCSP) is the operational challenge SSCP tests.

quiz.q: A private key should be…
choices: Shared with the team for convenience
Generated and stored so that only the intended holder can access it, never transmitted, and protected at rest
quiz.explain: The private key never leaves its holder. The same rule as SSH keys in the Home Lab course, applied to PKI.

lessons.title: Network and systems security, and the exam
lessons.objective: Configure network and endpoint security controls operationally, then plan and sit the SSCP exam.

resources.label: ISC2 — SSCP exam outline and requirements

lessons.lab: Consolidate the network and systems hardening you have done across earlier courses into an SSCP-aligned operational review: firewall rules, segmentation, endpoint hardening, and secure protocols. Confirm each is documented and operating. Then schedule the exam. SSCP requires one year of experience for full certification (with a degree waiver available); like CC, you can pass first and certify when experience is met. Record both in the tracker and note the AMF alongside your CC membership.

quiz.q: SSCP's experience requirement is…
choices: One year of cumulative work experience in an SSCP domain, with a waiver available for a relevant degree
quiz.explain: Lower than CISSP's five years, which is part of why SSCP is a sensible earlier ISC2 milestone.

quiz.q: Holding CC and then SSCP benefits you because…
choices: Both build your ISC2 membership and CPE history, laying groundwork toward CISSP later
quiz.explain: The ISC2 relationship compounds. Membership, CPEs, and endorsement experience all feed the eventual CISSP path.

quiz.q: SSCP fits both the GRC and blue lanes because…
choices: Operating security controls competently underlies both assessing them (GRC) and defending with them (blue)
quiz.explain: That dual fit is why the certification data lists it under both lanes. Practitioner skill is foundational to each.

courses.title: Microsoft Security Operations Analyst
courses.summary: SC-200 covers the Microsoft defender stack most employers already own: Defender for Endpoint, Defender XDR, Entra ID Protection, and Microsoft Sentinel with KQL. Cheap exam, free renewal, and the KQL you learn transfers to every job that touches Azure.
outcomes: Investigate and respond to incidents in Microsoft Defender XDR
Write KQL queries and analytics rules in Microsoft Sentinel
Configure data connectors, workbooks, and automation playbooks
Mitigate identity threats with Entra ID Protection and Conditional Access
Pass SC-200 and renew it free online each year

sections.title: Get the environment and learn KQL

lessons.title: Build a free Microsoft lab tenant
lessons.objective: Stand up a Microsoft 365 developer tenant and an Azure free account so every later lesson has somewhere to run.
lessons.lab: Create the developer tenant and an Azure subscription. Add five test users, enable security defaults, and set a spending limit and budget alert on the Azure subscription immediately — a Sentinel workspace left ingesting can produce a real bill. Record the tenant name, admin account location (password manager), and the cost guardrails you set in your repo.

quiz.q: The first thing to configure in a new Azure subscription used for learning is…
choices: A budget with alerts and, where available, a spending limit
quiz.explain: Cloud labs bill by consumption. Learners who skip this step discover Sentinel ingest pricing the expensive way.

quiz.q: A developer tenant is appropriate for SC-200 study because it…
choices: Is identical to production in every way
Provides licensed Microsoft 365 features in an isolated environment you can safely misconfigure
quiz.explain: It is a sandbox with real features. Check current program terms — eligibility and renewal rules change.

quiz.q: Test users matter because…
choices: Identity detections, risky sign-ins, and Conditional Access cannot be exercised meaningfully with one account
quiz.explain: You need subjects to attack and policies to apply differently. One admin account teaches you almost nothing.

lessons.title: KQL from zero to useful
lessons.objective: Write Kusto queries that filter, summarize, join, and time-window data well enough to investigate independently.

resources.label: Kusto Detective Agency (free KQL challenge game)

lessons.lab: Work the Kusto Detective Agency cases until you can write joins and summarize without reference. Then write five queries against your own tenant: sign-ins by location in the last 7 days; failed sign-ins per account with a count over 5; processes run per device; outbound connections to rare destinations; and one query joining identity data to device data. Save all five into a reusable KQL file in your repo with comments.

quiz.q: In KQL, the operator used to aggregate rows into counts and groups is…
quiz.explain: summarize count() by Account is the backbone of nearly every hunting query. where filters, project selects, extend computes.

quiz.q: Filtering early in a KQL query matters because…
choices: Query cost and speed depend on how much data passes through each step — filter on time first, then fields
quiz.explain: Always constrain the time range first. In a paid workspace, sloppy queries cost money as well as patience.

quiz.q: The bin() function is used to…
choices: Group values into fixed-size buckets, most often time buckets for trend analysis
quiz.explain: summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) is how you build a timeline and spot beaconing intervals.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender XDR: the unified incident view
lessons.objective: Navigate the Defender portal, understand how alerts correlate into incidents, and work an incident end to end.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Microsoft Defender XDR overview
Microsoft Learn — investigate incidents in Defender XDR

lessons.lab: Onboard one Windows VM from your home lab to Defender for Endpoint (the free trial supports this). Run the Microsoft-provided attack simulations from the Evaluation and tutorials section. Work the resulting incident fully: read the attack story graph, examine each alert, review the evidence tab, take a response action (isolate the device), then undo it. Write down how the graph differed from reading raw events in Wazuh.

quiz.q: An incident in Defender XDR is…
choices: A correlated collection of alerts, assets, and evidence believed to belong to the same attack
quiz.explain: Correlation is the product's core value: one incident instead of forty alerts describing the same intrusion.

quiz.q: Device isolation in Defender for Endpoint…
choices: Cuts network connectivity while keeping the Defender agent connected so you can continue investigating
quiz.explain: Containment without losing visibility or volatile evidence — exactly the incident response principle from Security+.

quiz.q: Automated investigation and response is valuable but requires…
choices: Configured approval levels — full automation on a high-value server can cause an outage from a false positive
quiz.explain: Same lesson as SOAR: automate enrichment freely, automate action with scoping and thresholds.

lessons.title: Workspace, connectors, and ingest cost
lessons.objective: Deploy Sentinel, connect data sources, and manage the cost model that governs every real deployment.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Sentinel costs and billing

lessons.lab: Create a Log Analytics workspace and enable Sentinel (the free trial covers a limited period and volume — check current terms). Connect the Entra ID sign-in and audit logs and the Defender XDR connector. Then do the exercise everyone skips: estimate monthly ingest for your tenant, and compute what the same volume would cost for a 200-person business. Write the number down. Cost is why real SOCs care which logs they collect.

quiz.q: Sentinel is billed primarily on…
choices: Volume of data ingested and retained
quiz.explain: This drives every architecture decision: which logs, which retention tier, and what gets filtered before ingest.

quiz.q: A basic or auxiliary log tier is useful for…
choices: High-volume, low-value data you rarely query but must retain — at lower cost with query limitations
quiz.explain: Tiering is how large environments stay affordable. Verify current tier names and limits — Microsoft changes them.

quiz.q: Before enabling a new connector in production you should…
choices: Estimate its daily volume and decide whether the detection value justifies the ingest cost
quiz.explain: Every connector is a recurring bill. Collect what you will detect on or need for investigation, not everything possible.

lessons.title: Analytics rules, incidents, and workbooks
lessons.objective: Create scheduled analytics rules from KQL, tune them, and visualize with workbooks.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — create custom analytics rules
Azure Sentinel GitHub — community detections and workbooks

lessons.lab: Enable three out-of-the-box analytics rules and write two of your own from your KQL file — one for impossible travel or risky sign-in follow-through, one for a suspicious process on an onboarded device. Configure entity mapping so incidents show accounts and hosts properly, set incident grouping, and build a workbook showing sign-in trends and alert volume. Trigger each rule deliberately and confirm the incident appears with the right entities.

quiz.q: Entity mapping in an analytics rule matters because…
choices: It is required to save the rule
It lets Sentinel correlate incidents, build investigation graphs, and let you pivot on accounts, hosts, and IPs
quiz.explain: Unmapped rules produce incidents you cannot pivot from. It is the most commonly skipped field and the most useful.

quiz.q: Incident grouping is used to…
choices: Combine related alerts over a time window into one incident rather than flooding the queue
quiz.explain: A rule that fires 400 times during a password spray should produce one incident, not four hundred.

quiz.q: Starting from community rules in the Azure-Sentinel repository is sensible because…
choices: They encode well-tested detection logic that you then map to your fields and tune to your baseline
They are free of false positives
quiz.explain: Same as Sigma: borrow the logic, own the tuning.

lessons.title: Automation with playbooks
lessons.objective: Build a Logic Apps playbook that enriches and responds to an incident automatically.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — automate threat response with playbooks

lessons.lab: Build two playbooks. First, enrichment: on incident creation, look up the source IP reputation, add the result as a comment, and tag the incident. Second, response with a human gate: on a high-severity identity incident, post an adaptive card to Teams or send an email asking an analyst to approve disabling the account, and act only on approval. Test both, and document the approval step as the control that prevents an automated outage.

quiz.q: A human approval step in a response playbook exists to…
choices: Prevent an automated action from causing harm when the detection is wrong
quiz.explain: Approval gates are how teams adopt automation safely and build trust in it over time.

quiz.q: Automation rules differ from playbooks in that automation rules…
choices: Handle incident-level logic — assigning, tagging, closing, and triggering playbooks — without building a Logic App
quiz.explain: Use automation rules for triage logic, playbooks for anything that needs to reach another system.

quiz.q: The first playbook most SOCs should build is…
choices: Enrichment that adds the context an analyst always looks up by hand
quiz.explain: Safe, immediately valuable, and it builds the team's confidence before anything destructive is automated.

lessons.title: Entra ID Protection and Conditional Access
lessons.objective: Detect and respond to identity risk, and enforce access decisions with Conditional Access policies.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

lessons.lab: Create Conditional Access policies in report-only mode first: require MFA for all users, block legacy authentication, and require compliant or hybrid-joined devices for admin roles. Review the report-only impact data before enabling. Then simulate risk — sign in through Tor or a VPN from another country — and work the risky sign-in through to remediation. Always exclude one break-glass account from every policy and document where its credentials live.

quiz.q: A break-glass account excluded from Conditional Access exists because…
choices: A misconfigured policy can lock every administrator out of the tenant permanently
It is faster to sign in
quiz.explain: It is the single most important Conditional Access practice. Store the credentials offline, monitor its use, and review it regularly.

quiz.q: Report-only mode lets you…
choices: Log policy evaluation without enforcing it, so you can measure impact before turning it on
Run the policy twice as fast
Apply the policy to reports only
quiz.explain: Every new policy goes to report-only first. Enforcement without measurement is how tenants break on a Friday afternoon.

quiz.q: Blocking legacy authentication is high value because legacy protocols…
choices: Cannot enforce MFA, making them the preferred path for password spray attacks
quiz.explain: It is the highest-impact single change in most tenants. Check usage reports before blocking so you know what breaks.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud and workload protection
lessons.objective: Use Defender for Cloud's secure score and workload protections, and interpret cloud security posture findings.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Microsoft Defender for Cloud

lessons.lab: Deploy one deliberately weak Azure VM (public IP, RDP open to the internet, no NSG restrictions) and let Defender for Cloud assess it. Record the secure score, the recommendations generated, and the severity ordering. Remediate them one at a time and watch the score move. Then delete the VM — never leave RDP exposed to the internet, even briefly, and note in your write-up how quickly the brute force attempts appeared.

quiz.q: Cloud security posture management focuses on…
choices: Misconfigurations and compliance drift across cloud resources, which cause the majority of cloud breaches
quiz.explain: Cloud incidents are predominantly configuration and identity failures, not exotic exploits.

quiz.q: Secure score is best used as…
choices: A prioritized, trackable to-do list whose trend over time matters more than the number
quiz.explain: Chasing the number leads to gaming. Use it to sequence work and to show progress.

quiz.q: RDP exposed to the internet is dangerous because…
choices: It is continuously scanned and brute forced within minutes, and it is a leading ransomware entry vector
quiz.explain: Use a bastion, VPN, or just-in-time access. This is one of the most consistent findings in breach reporting.

lessons.title: Threat hunting in the Microsoft stack
lessons.objective: Run proactive hunts with advanced hunting queries, bookmarks, and hunting livestreams.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — advanced hunting in Defender XDR
Microsoft Learn — hunt for threats in Sentinel

lessons.lab: Run three hunts with written hypotheses against your tenant and onboarded device: (1) processes launched from Office applications; (2) sign-ins from previously unseen countries for each account; (3) new scheduled tasks or services created in the last 14 days. Bookmark anything interesting, promote one hunt into a scheduled analytics rule, and document all three with hypothesis, query, result, and action.

quiz.q: A bookmark in Sentinel hunting is used to…
choices: Preserve an interesting result with your notes so it can be attached to an incident later
quiz.explain: Bookmarks are how a hunt becomes evidence. Without them the finding lives only in your memory.

quiz.q: Promoting a hunting query to an analytics rule is appropriate when…
choices: It reliably identifies behavior worth alerting on, with an acceptable false positive rate
quiz.explain: Hunting is exploratory; alerting demands precision. Validate the false positive rate before promotion.

quiz.q: Advanced hunting in Defender XDR queries…
choices: Raw endpoint, identity, email, and cloud app telemetry across the stack, usually with 30 days of retention
quiz.explain: Know the retention window — it defines how far back an investigation can reach without exporting to Sentinel.

lessons.title: Study plan and exam mechanics
lessons.objective: Work the official learning path, practice with the free assessment, and schedule SC-200.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — SC-200 study guide and practice assessment
Microsoft — exam scheduling via Pearson VUE

lessons.lab: Complete every module on the official SC-200 learning path, then take the free practice assessment. Anything under 80% gets a second pass plus a hands-on task in your tenant. Schedule the exam five to six weeks out at $165 (verify current price and check whether your employer or a Microsoft event offers a discount voucher). Record the date in the Academy tracker with status Scheduled.

quiz.q: Microsoft's official practice assessment is valuable because it…
choices: Is free, matches the current objective domains, and reports weak areas by skill
quiz.explain: It is a calibration tool, not a question bank. Use the skill breakdown to direct your review.

quiz.q: Microsoft role-based certifications renew…
choices: Free online each year through a short unproctored assessment, within a renewal window
Every three years for a fee
quiz.explain: Free annual renewal is a genuine advantage over CompTIA's CEU model — but the window is easy to miss, so calendar it.

quiz.q: SC-200 questions are weighted toward…
choices: Applied scenarios across Defender XDR, Sentinel, and Entra — with real KQL
quiz.explain: Hands-on tenant time is the study method. Reading alone reliably fails this exam.

lessons.title: Turning the Microsoft stack into a portfolio
lessons.objective: Publish your KQL library, detections, and playbooks as public evidence of capability.
lessons.lab: Publish a repo called sentinel-detections: your KQL query library organized by data source, the analytics rules you wrote as ARM templates or YAML, the playbook definitions, the workbook JSON, and a README explaining each detection's purpose, ATT&CK mapping, and known false positives. Redact tenant identifiers. This repo is directly relevant to almost every blue-lane job posting that mentions Microsoft.

quiz.q: Each published detection should document…
choices: Purpose, ATT&CK mapping, data sources required, known false positives, and response guidance
quiz.explain: The metadata is what makes a detection usable by someone else, and what shows a hiring manager you think like an engineer.

quiz.q: Before publishing tenant artifacts you must remove…
choices: Tenant IDs, subscription IDs, workspace names, real usernames, and internal hostnames
quiz.explain: Identifiers are the leak risk. The logic is the value and is safe to share.

quiz.q: The strongest signal this repo sends is…
choices: That you can build and document detections other people could run — the core of a detection engineering role
That you write a lot of code
quiz.explain: It is the natural bridge into the Detection Engineering Lab course and into SOC Level 2 work.

lessons.title: SC-200 or AWS — choosing your cloud
lessons.objective: Decide whether to follow SC-200 with more Microsoft depth or branch to AWS, based on where the local jobs are.
lessons.lab: Count the evidence rather than guessing: search your local market and remote listings for Azure, Entra, Sentinel, and Defender versus AWS, GuardDuty, and CloudTrail. Record the counts. Interview one person working in each if you can. Then write your decision and the follow-on certification with a target quarter, and enter it in the tracker. Revisit if your employer's stack changes — the employer's cloud usually settles the argument.

quiz.q: The best basis for choosing a cloud certification is…
choices: What your employer or target employers actually run, measured by real job postings
quiz.explain: Certifications are hiring signals. Signal in the language the local market speaks.

quiz.q: Skills learned on one cloud transfer to another because…
choices: The concepts — identity, logging, network controls, posture management, shared responsibility — are the same, only the product names change
quiz.explain: The second cloud is always much faster than the first. Depth in one beats shallow coverage of both.

quiz.q: SC-100 is a reasonable next step when…
choices: You have operational experience and are moving toward architecture and design decisions
You want a red team role
quiz.explain: It is an expert-level design exam. Taking it too early produces a certificate you cannot back up in interviews.

courses.title: OffSec PEN-200
courses.summary: The OSCP is the industry's benchmark offensive certification: a 24-hour hands-on exam plus a report. PEN-200 is demanding and expensive, and the culture is Try Harder. Approach it after PNPT with a plan, not on impulse.
outcomes: Enumerate and exploit Linux and Windows hosts without automated exploit tools
Perform manual privilege escalation on both operating systems
Move through an Active Directory set as the exam requires
Manage time and stress across a 24-hour practical exam
Pass the OSCP and produce a report that meets OffSec's standard

lessons.title: Is OSCP the right investment now?
lessons.objective: Evaluate the cost, time, and prerequisites honestly before committing, and decide whether to do it now or later.
lessons.lab: Write an honest decision memo: the cost (roughly $1,649 for the course plus one exam attempt — verify current pricing and bundle options), the realistic hours (150+ over two to three months), the prerequisite skills you already have from PNPT, and whether an employer will fund it. Decide now-or-later with a date. OSCP is a serious commitment; the worst outcome is buying the lab time and letting it lapse unused.

quiz.q: The most common reason people waste money on OSCP is…
choices: Buying lab time before they have the prerequisite skills or a sustained schedule to use it
quiz.explain: PNPT first, then a genuine block of protected time. Lab time is a depreciating asset; do not start the clock unprepared.

quiz.q: Doing PNPT before OSCP is sensible because…
choices: It builds the foundational skills and confidence far more cheaply, so OSCP lab time is spent learning OSCP-specific depth
quiz.explain: Sequencing saves money and reduces the odds of an expensive first-attempt failure.

quiz.q: Employer funding for OSCP is worth pursuing because…
choices: It is a common professional development benefit, and a funded attempt removes the financial pressure that harms exam performance
quiz.explain: Ask, with a written case tied to your role. Many security teams budget for it as standard.

lessons.title: The Try Harder mindset and time management
lessons.objective: Build the persistence and structured problem-solving OSCP demands, and a note and time discipline that survives a 24-hour exam.

resources.label: TJ Null — OSCP-like Hack The Box list (community)

lessons.lab: Practice the discipline before the exam: pick a hard HTB machine and give yourself a strict time box with a rule that you take a break and re-enumerate rather than tunnel when stuck. Keep a running log of every dead end. The skill OSCP actually tests is systematic persistence under pressure, not memorized exploits — build the habit now.

quiz.q: When stuck on a target for a long time, the OSCP-effective response is to…
choices: Step back, re-enumerate systematically, and question an assumption — the missed detail is almost always in enumeration
quiz.explain: Fixation is the enemy. Re-enumeration with fresh eyes finds the overlooked service or credential far more often than persistence with one idea.

quiz.q: Try Harder as a philosophy means…
choices: Develop independent problem-solving and resourcefulness rather than expecting to be handed the answer
quiz.explain: It is about self-sufficiency, not self-destruction. Breaks and sleep improve performance on a 24-hour exam.

quiz.q: A dead-end log during practice is useful because…
choices: It builds the habit of tracking what you have ruled out, which prevents re-treading the same ground during the exam
quiz.explain: Under exam pressure, forgetting what you already tried wastes precious hours. The log is your memory.

lessons.title: Manual exploitation without the easy button
lessons.objective: Exploit targets manually — modifying public exploit code and avoiding the exam-restricted automated tools.

resources.label: GTFOBins — Unix binaries for privilege escalation

lessons.lab: Take a public exploit from Exploit-DB that does not work out of the box against a lab target, and debug it: fix the target IP and port, adjust offsets or payloads, and get it working. Do this three times with different exploits. On the exam, Metasploit use is restricted to a single machine, so manual exploitation and the ability to fix broken public code are non-negotiable skills.

quiz.q: OSCP restricts automated exploitation tools to…
choices: A single target — everything else must be exploited manually
quiz.explain: Verify the current exam rules, but the intent is fixed: prove you can exploit manually, not just run a framework.

quiz.q: Public exploits frequently fail against a target because…
choices: They need adaptation — correct offsets, the right payload, target-specific parameters — which is a core tested skill
quiz.explain: Reading and fixing exploit code separates OSCP candidates from script users. Practice it deliberately.

quiz.q: GTFOBins is used to find…
choices: Ways to abuse legitimate Unix binaries — often via sudo or SUID misconfigurations — for privilege escalation
quiz.explain: A misconfigured sudo entry plus GTFOBins is one of the most common Linux privesc paths on the exam and in reality.

lessons.title: Linux privilege escalation
lessons.objective: Enumerate a Linux host thoroughly and escalate from a low-privilege shell to root through misconfiguration.
lessons.lab: Set up three lab Linux hosts each with a different privesc path: a SUID binary, a writable cron job, and a sudo misconfiguration. From a low-privilege shell, enumerate manually first (do not rely only on linPEAS), find the path, and escalate. For each, write the enumeration finding, the exploitation, and the remediation. Manual enumeration understanding is what lets you succeed when the automated script output is overwhelming.

quiz.q: A SUID binary is dangerous when…
choices: It runs as its owner (often root) and can be abused to execute arbitrary commands with that privilege
It is owned by a user
quiz.explain: find / -perm -4000 lists them. GTFOBins tells you which are abusable. A classic first privesc check.

quiz.q: Relying only on automated enumeration scripts is risky because…
choices: They produce overwhelming output, and understanding what matters requires knowing the manual checks the script automates
They are illegal on the exam
quiz.explain: Use the scripts, but be able to read their output critically. The signal is buried in the noise.

quiz.q: A writable file referenced by a root cron job leads to privesc because…
choices: You can insert commands that the scheduler will execute as root on the next run
It requires no privileges to view
quiz.explain: Writable script plus privileged scheduler equals code execution. The fix is correct file ownership and permissions.

lessons.title: Windows privilege escalation
lessons.objective: Escalate on Windows through service misconfigurations, token abuse, and unquoted service paths.
lessons.lab: Build lab Windows hosts with escalation paths: an unquoted service path with a writable directory, a service you can reconfigure, and a scenario for potato-style token abuse where SeImpersonatePrivilege is held. Escalate each to SYSTEM manually and document. Windows privesc is where many exam attempts stall, so drill it until each path is second nature.

quiz.q: An unquoted service path is exploitable when…
choices: The path contains spaces and an attacker can write to an earlier directory in the path, causing Windows to run their binary as the service account
The service has a long name
quiz.explain: Windows tries each space-separated fragment. A writable C:\Program.exe wins over C:\Program Files\... — the fix is quoting the path.

quiz.q: SeImpersonatePrivilege matters because…
choices: It enables potato-family attacks that impersonate a SYSTEM token, a very common path on service accounts
quiz.explain: Web and database service accounts often hold it. Knowing this single privilege unlocks many Windows targets.

quiz.q: The most reliable Windows privesc approach is to…
choices: Enumerate systematically — services, privileges, installed software, patches — then choose the path the evidence supports
quiz.explain: Same discipline as Linux. Enumeration first; the escalation follows from what you find.

lessons.title: Active Directory in the OSCP exam
lessons.objective: Handle the exam's AD set: initial access, lateral movement, and reaching the domain controller.
lessons.lab: Practice the exam-style AD chain against your lab under time pressure: gain a foothold, harvest credentials, move laterally, and reach the domain controller — end to end, in one sitting, fully documented. The exam's AD set carries significant points and must be completed as a chain, so rehearse it as one continuous flow rather than isolated techniques.

quiz.q: The AD portion of the OSCP exam is best treated as…
choices: A connected chain worth substantial points that should often be attempted early while you are fresh
The same as the standalone machines
quiz.explain: Its point weight and chained nature make it strategically important. Verify current exam structure, then plan your attack order around it.

quiz.q: Credential reuse across the AD set is common, so after each compromise you should…
choices: Harvest and test every credential against other hosts — reuse is frequently the intended path forward
quiz.explain: Loot thoroughly. The next step is often a credential you already have but have not tried yet.

quiz.q: Documenting the AD chain as you go is essential because…
choices: The report requires clear reproduction steps, and reconstructing a multi-host chain from memory after 20 hours is error-prone
quiz.explain: No documentation, no points, however complete the compromise. Screenshot and note at every step.

lessons.title: The 24-hour exam plan
lessons.objective: Build a concrete plan for the exam window: order of attack, break schedule, point targets, and stop conditions.
lessons.lab: Write your exam-day plan: confirm the current passing point threshold, decide your attack order, schedule meals and sleep (yes, sleep — a two to four hour break improves performance), set a rule for when to move on from a stuck target, and prepare the proctoring environment in advance. Do a full 24-hour dry run against a practice set at least once before the real thing.

quiz.q: Scheduling sleep during a 24-hour exam is wise because…
choices: Fatigue destroys the systematic thinking the exam depends on; rested re-enumeration outperforms exhausted persistence
quiz.explain: Candidates routinely solve on the second day what they could not see exhausted on the first. Plan the break in advance.

quiz.q: A stop condition for a stuck machine helps because…
choices: A pre-set time limit forces you to bank points on other targets rather than sinking the whole exam into one host
quiz.explain: Time is the real adversary. A fixed rotation across targets protects your point total.

quiz.q: Preparing the proctoring setup in advance matters because…
choices: Technical problems with ID verification, webcam, or screen sharing can cost exam time or invalidate the attempt
quiz.explain: Read the proctoring requirements days ahead. Losing an hour to a webcam problem is an avoidable disaster.

lessons.title: The OSCP report
lessons.objective: Produce a report that meets OffSec's specific requirements, with reproducible steps for every point claimed.

resources.label: OffSec — exam report and submission guidelines

lessons.lab: Using OffSec's template, write a full report from your dry-run exam: for every compromised host, the enumeration, the exploitation with commands and screenshots, the privilege escalation, and the proof file contents. The rule that catches people: a compromise you cannot reproduce in the report earns no points, regardless of whether you actually got the shell. Reproducibility is the standard.

quiz.q: Points on the OSCP are awarded based on…
choices: The report demonstrating the compromise with reproducible steps and the required proof — an undocumented shell scores zero
quiz.explain: This surprises people every exam. The report is the submission; the live compromise is only evidence you must capture.

quiz.q: Screenshots in the report must show…
choices: The proof file contents alongside identifying context such as the IP and whoami output, per the current requirements
quiz.explain: Follow the exact proof requirements in the current guide — they are specific, and missing them costs the points.

quiz.q: The report is due…
choices: Within the stated window after the exam (commonly 24 hours) — so notes must be report-ready during the exam, not written from scratch after
quiz.explain: You will be exhausted. Notes taken well during the exam make the post-exam report assembly manageable.

lessons.title: After OSCP: leveraging the credential
lessons.objective: Use the OSCP to open doors and decide the offensive career direction from here.

resources.label: Bureau of Labor Statistics — Information security analysts

lessons.lab: Update your resume and LinkedIn with OSCP the day you pass, and write one honest reflection post on what the process taught you. Then plan the next step: junior penetration tester or red team roles now, and Phase 4 offensive certifications (OSEP, CRTO) once you have engagement experience. Enter the target and timeframe in the tracker. OSCP opens the door; real engagements make the career.

quiz.q: OSCP is respected by employers primarily because…
choices: Its hands-on, proctored, report-based format makes it hard to fake — passing proves demonstrated skill
quiz.explain: The difficulty is the point. A credential that cannot be crammed carries real signal.

quiz.q: The right next offensive step after OSCP is usually…
choices: Gaining real engagement experience first, then advanced certifications like OSEP or CRTO when the work calls for them
quiz.explain: Experience before the next expensive cert. OSEP and CRTO reward people who already work in the field.

quiz.q: A reflection post after passing is worthwhile because…
choices: It demonstrates communication and self-awareness, and marks the milestone publicly for your network
quiz.explain: The lane over-indexes on technical bravado. Thoughtful communication stands out and ages well.

courses.title: AWS Security Specialty (alternative to SC-200)
courses.summary: The AWS route through Phase 3 for anyone whose employer runs on AWS rather than Microsoft. Detection and response with CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Detective, plus the IAM and encryption depth the specialty exam demands. Take this or SC-200, not both.
outcomes: Read CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs well enough to reconstruct an incident
Operate GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Detective as a working detection stack
Design IAM policies and KMS key policies that hold up to review
Respond to a compromised access key and a compromised EC2 instance
Pass AWS Certified Security – Specialty

lessons.title: A safe AWS lab account
lessons.objective: Create an AWS account configured so you can experiment without a surprise bill or an exposed root account.
lessons.lab: Open the account, then immediately: enable MFA on the root user and lock the credentials away, create an IAM admin user for daily work, set a billing budget at $10 with email alerts, enable Cost Anomaly Detection, and turn on IAM Access Analyzer. Record every step in a runbook. The root account should not be used again for the rest of this course.

quiz.q: The root user should be used for…
choices: Only the handful of tasks that require it, with MFA enforced and credentials stored offline
quiz.explain: Root cannot be restricted by IAM policy. Compromise of root is total compromise of the account.

quiz.q: A billing budget with alerts is a security control because…
choices: Cryptomining after a credential compromise usually shows up first as an unexpected bill
quiz.explain: Cost anomalies are a genuine detection signal in cloud environments, often faster than any security alert.

quiz.q: IAM Access Analyzer identifies…
choices: Resources shared with external principals — buckets, roles, and keys accessible outside your account
quiz.explain: External exposure is the top cloud finding class. Turn it on in every account, day one.

lessons.title: CloudTrail, Config, and VPC Flow Logs
lessons.objective: Enable the three logging services that make investigation possible, and understand what each does and does not record.
lessons.lab: Enable a multi-region CloudTrail trail delivering to an S3 bucket with object lock, enable AWS Config with a few managed rules, and turn on VPC Flow Logs for your default VPC. Then perform ten actions in the console and find every one of them in CloudTrail using Athena or the event history. Write down which of your actions produced a data event rather than a management event and why they are billed differently.

quiz.q: By default, CloudTrail records…
choices: Management events (control plane API calls); data events such as S3 object access must be enabled explicitly and cost extra
quiz.explain: This gap surprises investigators constantly — no record of which objects were read during an exfiltration.

quiz.q: Object lock on the CloudTrail bucket protects against…
choices: An attacker with sufficient privileges deleting the evidence of their own activity
quiz.explain: Immutable log storage is the cloud equivalent of forwarding logs off the host. Ideally to a separate logging account.

quiz.q: VPC Flow Logs record…
choices: Connection metadata — source, destination, ports, bytes, and accept or reject — but no payload
quiz.explain: Metadata only. For payload you need traffic mirroring, which costs considerably more.

lessons.title: Organizations, SCPs, and account structure
lessons.objective: Explain multi-account architecture and use service control policies as a guardrail rather than a permission grant.

resources.label: AWS — Organizations and service control policies

lessons.lab: Design a multi-account structure on paper for a small consultancy: management, log archive, security tooling, production, and development. Draw which logs flow where and who has access to what. Then write three SCPs in JSON: deny disabling CloudTrail, deny use of unapproved regions, and deny deleting the log archive bucket. Explain in writing why an SCP cannot grant a permission.

quiz.q: A service control policy…
choices: Sets the maximum available permissions — the effective permission is the intersection of the SCP and the IAM policy
Applies only to the root user
quiz.explain: SCPs are a ceiling, not a grant. Even root in a member account cannot exceed them, which is what makes them a real guardrail.

quiz.q: A separate log archive account is recommended because…
choices: It keeps evidence outside the blast radius of a compromise in the account being investigated
quiz.explain: Separation of the evidence store from the environment it records is a principle, not an AWS quirk.

quiz.q: Restricting unapproved regions helps security by…
choices: Shrinking the area you must monitor — attackers commonly spin up resources in unused regions to avoid notice
quiz.explain: Cryptomining in an unwatched region is a classic post-compromise move. Deny regions you do not use.

lessons.title: GuardDuty
lessons.objective: Enable GuardDuty, interpret its finding types, and tune it without creating blind spots.
lessons.lab: Enable GuardDuty and generate sample findings. For each of ten finding types, write what data source produced it (CloudTrail, VPC Flow, DNS logs, EKS audit, or runtime monitoring), what an attacker would have done to trigger it genuinely, and what your first three triage steps would be. Then create one suppression rule and document precisely why it is safe.

quiz.q: GuardDuty analyzes…
choices: CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and optional sources such as S3 data events and runtime monitoring
quiz.explain: Enabling it requires no log configuration of your own — it reads those sources directly, which is why it is the fastest detection win in AWS.

quiz.q: A finding of CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS most likely means…
choices: An instance is resolving mining pool domains, usually indicating compromise
quiz.explain: Unless you knowingly run mining software, treat it as compromise and start with how the instance was reached.

quiz.q: Suppression rules are risky because…
choices: They hide findings permanently — an overly broad rule can mask a real compromise indefinitely
quiz.explain: Same discipline as SIEM tuning: narrow scope, written justification, review date.

lessons.title: Security Hub, Detective, and Inspector
lessons.objective: Aggregate findings, investigate them, and scan workloads for vulnerabilities.
lessons.lab: Enable Security Hub with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard and the CIS benchmark. Record your starting score and the top ten failed controls. Remediate five, and document the change and the score movement for each. Enable Inspector and review the findings on a test EC2 instance. Compare how the three services present the same underlying problem.

quiz.q: Security Hub's primary role is…
choices: Aggregating and normalizing findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and partners, plus running posture standards
quiz.explain: It is the single pane and the compliance scorecard. The detection comes from the services feeding it.

quiz.q: Detective is used to…
choices: Investigate them — it builds behavior graphs from your logs so you can answer what else this principal did
quiz.explain: Finding to context in a few clicks. It substantially shortens scoping, which is the slow part of cloud incidents.

quiz.q: Inspector differs from GuardDuty in that Inspector…
choices: Continuously scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure
quiz.explain: Vulnerability management versus threat detection. Both belong in the stack and answer different questions.

lessons.title: Responding to cloud incidents
lessons.objective: Work the two incidents every AWS responder sees: a leaked access key and a compromised EC2 instance.

resources.label: AWS — what to do if you inadvertently expose an access key

lessons.lab: Write and rehearse two runbooks against your own account. Leaked key: identify the key's activity in CloudTrail, deactivate rather than delete it first (preserving the ability to attribute activity), review everything it did, check for persistence such as new IAM users, roles, or trust policies, then rotate and delete. Compromised instance: isolate with a deny-all security group, preserve a volume snapshot and a memory capture if possible, detach the instance profile, then terminate. Test each runbook end to end.

quiz.q: Deactivating rather than immediately deleting a leaked key first is useful because…
choices: It stops the access while keeping the key ID resolvable for attribution during the investigation
quiz.explain: Stop the bleeding, preserve the ability to answer what it did. Delete once the investigation is complete.

quiz.q: After a credential compromise, checking for new IAM users, roles, and trust policy changes matters because…
choices: Attackers establish persistence in IAM so that rotating the original key does not remove their access
quiz.explain: Rotating the key while leaving a backdoor role is the classic incomplete remediation in cloud incidents.

quiz.q: Isolating an EC2 instance is best done by…
choices: Applying a security group with no allowed traffic, keeping the instance running for evidence
quiz.explain: Stopping loses memory. Same volatility principle as the on-premises case.

lessons.title: IAM policy evaluation logic
lessons.objective: Read and write IAM policies confidently, and evaluate how identity, resource, permission boundary, and SCP interact.
lessons.lab: Write three policies and test each in the Policy Simulator: least-privilege read access to one S3 bucket with a condition requiring TLS; an EC2 policy scoped by resource tag; and a permission boundary limiting what a delegated admin can grant.
